docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: This repository holds a book and the code that the book describes. A contribution can therefore take two forms, and the two are reviewed by different standards: a page is judged by whether its claims can be verified, a source file by whether it compiles clean.

docs.title: 1. What is worth sending
docs.text:
Four kinds of contribution are accepted without discussion:

  • A reproducible defect. A page states a fact — a sizeof value, a warning text, an exit status — and the reader's compiler disagrees. Send the compiler version, the command, and the output. If the page is wrong, it is fixed; if the page is right and the compiler differs, the page gains a note about the version.
  • A lab that is ambiguous. The README.md asks for something that two careful readers interpret differently. That is a documentation defect, not a reader defect.
  • A field note. A defect from your own code, in the shape described in section 4. These are the most useful contributions because they carry a real compiler response.
  • A missing prerequisite link. A page assumes a fact it never establishes and never links to.

Feature requests for the site design, the theme, or the build system are out of scope: the theme is inherited and deliberately left alone.

docs.title: 2. Rules for source files
docs.text:
Every example obeys five rules. A pull request that breaks one is returned with the rule cited, not with the fix applied.

  1. One translation unit. The file compiles alone, with its own main. No example depends on another example's object file.
  2. Four-line header. LAB, Build, Expect, Probe, in that order. Build is a command that works from the file's own directory; Expect includes the exit status; Probe names one change worth making.
  3. Zero warnings. -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic for C, the same for C++, plus -Wconversion where the chapter is about conversions. The build does not pass -Werror, because a reader who cannot run the program also cannot read the warning; zero warnings is the review rule, and check.sh prints what it sees so the rule stays visible.
  4. No writes into the source tree. Output goes to build/ or /tmp. A committed binary is a bug.
  5. Deterministic output. Same input, same bytes out. Where randomness is part of the lesson, the seed is fixed and printed.

Dependencies are limited to the C and C++ standard libraries. A third-party library may appear only in a chapter whose subject is that library, and then it is optional.

docs.title: 3. Rules for pages
docs.text:
Pages are written in English and are judged on density rather than length. Five to nine kilobytes of prose, tables and code is the target; a page below that is usually missing evidence, and a page above it usually contains a paragraph that belongs on another page.

Three requirements apply to every page:

  • Every claim has evidence. A number from a sizeof, a warning copied verbatim from a compiler, a timing from a stated machine, or an assertion that runs. A claim without evidence is removed, however plausible.
  • Links resolve to a subsection. [Heap](c/heap.md#realloc-may-move-the-block) is acceptable; "see the next chapter" is not. A link into a page that does not exist is a build error, not a promise.
  • No repeated paragraph. The same explanation does not appear on two pages. One page owns it; the other links to the anchor.

Structure is not templated. The memory chapters run as a continuous argument; the craft chapters open with a failure; the build chapters are organised around commands and artefacts; the biology chapters around data flow. A page is allowed to look unlike its neighbour. It is not allowed to look unlike itself halfway through.

docs.title: 4. Field note format
docs.text:
A field note records a defect from real code, and has five parts in a fixed order:

### The original code
<the snippet, with the file it came from>

### What the tool said
<compiler or runtime output, verbatim, including the flag name>

### Why it happened
<the classification: syntax, ownership, boundary, aliasing, lifetime>

### The smallest fix
<the corrected lines, and nothing else>

### Where the lesson transfers
<link to the chapter that generalises the rule>

The verbatim tool output is the part that makes a field note worth reading. Paraphrased warnings teach nothing, because the reader will meet the real text, not the paraphrase.

docs.title: 5. Workflow
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/GuiHui-huimy/CorCraft.git
cd CorCraft
git switch -c page/heap-realloc-note
make -f tools/Makefile test
bash tools/run_labs.sh

Both commands must exit zero before a pull request is opened. A documentation-only change still runs them, because a page that contradicts a passing test is the failure mode this repository exists to avoid.

In the pull request, state which chapter is affected, what the reader could not do before, and which command demonstrates the difference. A diff without a reproduction is not reviewable.

docs.title: 6. Review standard
docs.text: A change is accepted when three questions have answers: does it build clean, does the affected page still state only what the code exhibits, and can a reader who has not seen the change follow the result. The third question is the one that rejects most submissions, and the one worth asking before writing the second paragraph.

docs.title: 7. See also
docs.text:

  • Linux Toolchain for the compiler versions the standards assume.
  • How I Use AI to Build a Project for using a model while drafting, without letting it invent the evidence.

docs.title: License
docs.text:
Two licences apply to this repository, and the split is deliberate: the prose is the part I want to protect as a book, the code is the part I want people to take. This page states where the boundary sits, how to attribute, and which files I did not write.

The short version: the text and images are CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, the code is MIT, and the names and logo are reserved. If you only need one sentence, that is it. The rest of this page is the reasoning and the details a careful reader will want before reusing something.

docs.title: 1. What each licence covers
docs.text:
Path or content Licence docs/**/*.md — every chapter, exercise and note CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 docs/assets/images/* — diagrams and the logo as an image CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, except the logo as a mark Code blocks inside a page MIT code/, labs/, tools/ MIT CMakeLists.txt, mkdocs.yml, .gitignore MIT docs/material/templates, plugins, extensions MIT, from MkDocs Material "C/C++ Craft", "CorCraft", the logo, the site identity Not licensed; reserved

The reason a code block inside a chapter is MIT while the paragraph around it is CC is practical. Readers copy snippets into their own projects, and a snippet that arrives under a non-commercial copyleft licence is a snippet most people cannot use. The paragraph explaining why the snippet works is a different thing: it is the part of the book I wrote, and it is what I do not want lifted wholesale into a paid course.

docs.title: 2. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 in plain terms
docs.text:
You may copy, translate, adapt and redistribute the text and the diagrams, provided you meet four conditions:

  1. Attribution — name the author, cite the book and the page, link to the licence, and say whether you changed anything.
  2. NonCommercial — you may not use the material for a commercial purpose. A paid course, a paid membership, a book sold on a platform, or a content site whose revenue depends on this material is commercial. Reading it, teaching it in a tuition-free class, quoting it in a paper, or translating it for a study group is not.
  3. ShareAlike — if you adapt the text, your adapted text must carry the same licence. You cannot take a chapter, rewrite it lightly, and put it behind a closed licence.
  4. No additional restrictions — you may not add legal or technical terms that forbid others from doing what the licence allows.

The full legal text is at https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-sa/4.0/legalcode, and the Chinese version at https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-sa/4.0/legalcode.zh-hans. If this page and the legal text disagree, the legal text governs.

docs.title: 3. MIT in plain terms

You may use the code for anything, including commercial work, closed-source work and work you never publish. You must keep the copyright notice and the permission notice with any substantial portion you redistribute. There is no warranty: a lab that corrupts your heap is your heap.

This is the licence most readers want for code, and it is the one I would want if I were copying an example out of someone else's book.

docs.title: 4. How to attribute
docs.text:
For text or a diagram, a line of this shape is enough:

For code, keep the notice that ships in the files, or add:

Quoting a paragraph in a review, a lecture slide or a paper is ordinary quotation and does not require you to licence the whole of your work under CC. Reproducing a chapter is what the licence governs.

docs.title: 5. Commercial use, and how to ask
docs.text:
If you want to use the text in something commercial — a paid course, a training programme inside a company, a printed book, a paid newsletter — write to suguohui_account@163.com with the material you want, the audience, the channel and the duration. Silence is not permission. I answer most requests within a week, and for small uses the answer is usually yes with an attribution line.

The code does not need this conversation. MIT already permits commercial use, and asking would waste both our time.

docs.title: 6. Third-party components
docs.text:
The site is built with MkDocs and MkDocs Material, both MIT, and their files live under docs/material/templates, docs/material/plugins and docs/material/extensions. The theme is a build-time layer, so it does not change the licence of the chapters or the examples.

Coordinates mentioned in the biology chapters come from entries in the Protein Data Bank, under the wwPDB terms of use. The repository ships no coordinate files; data/README.md lists the accessions and the commands that fetch them. External links belong to their own owners.

docs.title: 7. What a licence cannot do
docs.text:
A licence governs copying, adaptation and distribution. It does not protect an idea, a method, a fact or a teaching sequence as such. Someone who reads the book and writes their own explanation of the same material is not infringing, even if the structure feels similar. What the licence does protect is the expression: the sentences, the diagrams, the selection and arrangement of the examples, and the code.

It also cannot be withdrawn. A version published under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 stays available under those terms; a later edition can change licence, but the change applies forward only. That is why the choice was made once, at the start, rather than after the first complaint.

docs.title: 8. If you find a problem
docs.text: If you believe a file here misuses someone else's work, or if you need a permission in writing, write to suguohui_account@163.com. I would rather fix an attribution than defend one.

docs.title: Security
docs.text: This is a book repository, not a service, so the threat model is not the usual web one. The risk here is different and more practical: a reader compiles and runs code that was written to fail, on a machine that holds their own work.

docs.title: 1. Why a security page belongs in a programming book
docs.text:
Several examples in this book contain defects on purpose. A chapter on the heap demonstrates a double free. A chapter on arrays writes one element past the end. A chapter on undefined behaviour relies on the compiler doing something unspecified. Each of these is correct pedagogy and poor operational advice if the resulting binary is run outside the context that produced it.

The distinction is worth stating plainly: the code is deliberately broken, the repository is not. Nothing in code/ is intended to be linked into another program, installed system-wide, or run against data you cannot afford to lose.

docs.title: 2. Running the examples
docs.text:
Four rules apply to every lab in this repository.

Build into build/ or /tmp, never into the source tree. A binary in the working directory is easy to run by accident and easy to commit by mistake. The header comment in each file states the output path; use it.

Sanitize first, then trust. Memory chapters run under -fsanitize=address,undefined. A lab that "works" without the sanitizer may still be writing out of bounds; the sanitizer is what makes the difference visible. This is also why the C++ labs fail on warnings: a warning is the compiler telling you it already suspects something.

Do not elevate. None of the commands in this book requires sudo. If a step asks for root, the step is wrong, or the environment is. Installing a compiler is the single exception, and it is confined to the toolchain page.

Do not run binaries you did not build. A prebuilt executable in an issue or a pull request is not part of the book. Build from source or do not run it.

Containers are a reasonable belt for the chapters on undefined behaviour, since a container limits what a corrupted write can reach. They do not make undefined behaviour defined; they only confine the damage.

docs.title: 3. Input handling
docs.text:
The parsing labs read files written by other people, which is the situation where a parser is most likely to be attacked in the wild. Three habits are taught explicitly and are expected in contributed code:

  • Validate width before indexing. A PDB line is 80 columns. A line of 60 columns is not truncated data to be padded; it is a malformed record to be rejected.
  • Bound the input size. craft_read_file grows a buffer but the caller still checks how large the result is. A 4 GB file is not a test case, it is a denial of service.
  • Never use gets. It cannot be made safe, because it has no length parameter. fgets with an explicit size, and a check that the newline was actually consumed, is the minimum.

A parser that skips a malformed line silently is worse than one that stops: the first produces a structure that looks complete and is not.

docs.title: 4. Data
docs.text:
All structures used in the biology section are public: PDB entries from RCSB, sequences from UniProt. Nothing else should ever enter data/.

Two things are not committed, ever: coordinates of unpublished structures, and file paths that reveal a private filesystem layout. The second is subtle — an example that prints /home/<name>/projects/target_x/... publishes more about its author than about C++.

docs.title: 5. Reporting a problem
docs.text:
Security-relevant reports go to suguohui_account@163.com privately, not into a public issue. That covers a lab that can damage a host outside its container, an instruction that requires privileges it should not, and a page that recommends an unsafe pattern without marking it as a counter-example.

Reports about a deliberately broken example are welcome but are not vulnerabilities: if the page says the code is wrong, the code being wrong is the point.

docs.title: How I Use AI to Build a Project
docs.text:
I did not start with a method. I started with a folder of notes and a model that kept answering a slightly different project than the one I was building.

The first architecture it produced for PepNat was tidy, plausible, and wrong in a way I could not see until the storage phase: it had invented a single "pipeline" object that owned the database, which made the store impossible to test without the generator, and the generator impossible to test without ESM-2 weights. I had asked for an architecture before I had written down what the database had to guarantee. What fixed it was not a better prompt. It was writing the requirement down first, and keeping the notes where the model could read them.

That is the whole of this page: five steps, each one paid for by a failure I can point at.

1. Build a local knowledge base before the first prompt.
2. Write the requirement as tests, not as a wish.
3. Let the model draw the architecture, then redraw it yourself.
4. Build one phase at a time, interface before implementation.
5. Treat every test as the contract the next phase relies on.

docs.title: 1. Step 1: the knowledge base comes before the first prompt
docs.text:
A model answers from what it can see. If all it can see is one sentence — "help me build a peptide library generator" — it answers from the average of every project it has read, and none of those is mine.

For PepNat the knowledge base is an Obsidian vault, not a folder inside the repository:

D:\工程文件\笔记仓库\Obsidian Vault\生物信息\生物信息学工具\多肽对接\多肽生成器\
├── 1-1-整体设计方案.md
├── 1-2 整体模块划分.md
├── 1-3 PepNat 构建路线.md
├── 1-4-1 Conda环境构建.md
├── 2-0 Phase 0 详细施工 + 全架构生成脚本.md
├── 2-1 Phase 1 — infra 层完整施工.md
├── 2-2 Phase 2 — M7 存储层完整施工.md
├── 2-3 Phase 3 — M1 来源层 + utils 补充.md
├── …
├── 2-12 Phase 12 测试.md
├── 2-13 Todo List.md
├── 2-14 顶层接口.md
├── 3-1 论文推进路线（P13–P20）.md
└── 3-2 文档架构.md

Twenty-eight notes, written before the first line of src/. They are not a diary; they are the specification, one phase per file, in the order the phases were built. When I ask the model to implement M7, I paste 2-2 and 1-2, and it answers about my store, my tables and my idempotency rule rather than about a generic SQLite wrapper.

Three rules made the folder usable, and I learned all three by breaking them:

  • A note states its source. "PDB column 22 is the chain ID" is a fact I can check against the format specification. "The parser reads the chain" is a memory, and memories drift silently.
  • A note is short enough to paste. The Phase 2 note is four pages, not forty. Anything longer gets truncated, and the truncated part is usually the constraint that mattered.
  • A decision records what was rejected. 1-3 PepNat 构建路线.md says not only that the store is SQLite, but that a single JSON file was rejected because a 3.2-million-row enumeration cannot be rewritten atomically.

The folder also taught me that naming is part of the contract. Two files ended up as 2-8: 2-8 FIX BUGS.md and 2-8 Phase 8 — M4 贝叶斯优化 完整施工.md. I can still tell them apart by their suffixes, but when I pasted "the 2-8 note" into a prompt, the model read the bug list and answered about the Bayesian phase. I now number every note into a slot that nothing else uses, because a filename is an address.

The failure this prevents: an architecture invented from a one-line request, and code written to fit it. That is what happened before 1-1 existed.

docs.title: 2. Step 2: write the requirement as tests, not as a wish
docs.text:
"Write me a peptide generator" is a request. What I actually needed for PepNat was narrower and much harder:

A peptide store that:
- ignores a repeated (sequence, length, line) instead of duplicating it
- survives kill -9 mid-run: after reopen, PRAGMA integrity_check = ok
  and no duplicate rows, and the run resumes from the last committed batch
- keeps one SQLite file per generation line, so B, C, D and A can be
  compared, rebuilt and merged without touching each other
- writes <store>.manifest.json with pepnat version, schema version,
  threshold version, model version, run id and row counts
- derives every random choice from a global seed plus per-line sub-seeds,
  so the same command produces the same library
- installs with pip install -e . and downloads no checkpoint at install time

Every clause became either a test or a build check. The idempotency clause became UNIQUE(sequence, length, line) plus a test that inserts the same row twice and counts one. The kill -9 clause became a test that opens a store, kills the process, reopens it and continues. The manifest clause became a test that reads the file and compares it to the database.

The difference between the request and the requirement is that the requirement can fail. "A peptide generator" cannot fail; it can only disappoint. A clause about integrity_check after kill -9 fails on the first implementation that writes outside a transaction, and it fails in a way I can read.

The failure this prevents: a correct-looking implementation that duplicates rows on a re-run, and a review that cannot say so, because nothing ever said a re-run was allowed.

docs.title: 3. Step 3: let the model draw the map, then redraw it yourself
docs.text:
Before code, I ask for the map: the module list with one sentence of responsibility each, the data flow, the dependency order, and the interface and invariant of every module.

infra        config, logging, seeds, paths            tested with a temp directory
M7 store     SQLite: peptide / structure / run tables tested with :memory:
M1 sources   sequence space, naturalness files        tested with string literals
M2 esm       ESM-2 embeddings, cached                 tested with a stubbed model
M3 threshold fixed-threshold verdict                  tested with labelled rows
M6 schedule  generation loop and the first CLI verbs  tested with a fake scorer
M5 seed      neighbourhood sampling                   tested with a small alphabet
M4 bayes     Bayesian optimisation over parameters     tested with a toy objective
M8 analyse   read-only reports                        tested against a fixture store

That order is PepNat's actual build order, and it is the reason Phase 2 is the store and Phase 3 is the source layer. It is also the part of the workflow where the model is most useful and most dangerous at once: it can hold twenty modules in view and produce a dependency chain in seconds, and it can produce one that is plausible in the abstract and impossible in my build.

My review rule is one line: a module must be testable while the modules below it do not exist. The first architecture failed that rule. It gave me a Pipeline object that owned the database and the scorer, which meant the store could only be tested by constructing a pipeline, and a pipeline needed the model weights. I deleted the object. The store became a constructor argument with a :memory: default, and after that every storage test ran in milliseconds.

The failure this prevents: a monolith where nothing can be tested until everything exists, and therefore nothing is tested.

docs.title: 4. Step 4: one phase at a time, interface before implementation
docs.text:
A phase is done when its test passes, not when its file exists. The sequence I use for each one:

  1. Ask for the interface only: the signatures, the invariants, the error model. No implementation.
  2. Review the interface against the requirement. This is the cheap moment to change it.
  3. Ask for the implementation.
  4. Ask for the test from the requirement clause alone, with the implementation out of view.
  5. Run it: pytest, the build with warnings on, and the store's integrity check.
  6. Write the decision note: what was chosen, what was rejected.

PepNat's Phase 11 shows the sequence in its filenames: 2-11-1 P11 esm.py 完整增量版.md, then 2-11-2 P11验证.md, then 2-11-3 P11 收尾与验证结论.md. The interface, the verification, and the conclusion are three files because they were three separate requests. Merging them into one prompt is how a phase ends up "done" with no evidence.

Step 4 is the one I used to skip. An AI asked to write both the implementation and the test writes a test that confirms what it just wrote — I have watched it assert the value its own code produced, which is not a test but a mirror. A test written from the clause, with the implementation hidden, can fail, and the first one usually does.

The failure this prevents: three thousand lines with no test, and a two-day debugging session on a defect a four-line test would have caught.

docs.title: 5. Step 5: the test is the contract the next phase relies on
docs.text:
A test is not proof. It is a fixed sentence about what a module promises, written where the next module can read it. For PepNat those sentences are in pytest, and they state three things:

# idempotency: the promise M6 relies on when it resumes a run
insert(store, seq, length=5, line="C")
insert(store, seq, length=5, line="C")
assert count(store) == 1

# resumability: the promise the CLI relies on after kill -9
store = open_store(tmp_path / "lib.db")
write_batches(store, rows, batch=1000)
kill_after(store, 1000)
store = open_store(tmp_path / "lib.db")
assert store.last_committed == 1000

# read-only analysis: the promise `pepnat analyze` makes to its caller
before = (row_count(store), mtime(store))
run_analyze(store, tmp_path / "report")
assert (row_count(store), mtime(store)) == before

Three properties make a sentence a contract: it runs in isolation (a temporary SQLite file, no network), it fails loudly (assertion, non-zero exit), and it states its tolerance where a number is compared. The C chapters of this book do the same thing with CRAFT_ASSERT; the language differs, the obligation does not.

The failure this prevents: a module that "works" in the demo and cannot be relied on by the module above it, because nobody wrote down what it guaranteed.

docs.title: 6. What the workflow does not do
docs.text:
It does not make the model responsible for correctness. The five steps move the correctness question to four places I can check: the requirement (readable), the interface (small), the test (a few lines), the tolerance or invariant (stated). The model's output is checked against those, never against whether it sounds right.

It also does not remove the need to read the code. Every Field Note in this book is a defect that looked plausible. A plausible defect is caught by someone who knows what the code should do, and the workflow's only job is to keep that attention on the few places where it matters.

docs.title: 7. PepNat, as it actually went
docs.text:
PepNat — Themis-PepNat, a modularised SQLite-backed peptide library and structure pipeline — is the project where this workflow was built, and it is a better example than this repository because it is larger and its failures were more expensive.

The notes came first: 1-1 fixed the design, 1-2 split it into M1–M8 plus infra, 1-3 chose the build route, and 2-0 generated the tree from a script so that no directory was created by hand. Then one phase per file: infra, store, sources, ESM and thresholds, schedule and CLI, the classifier and its threshold calibration, seed neighbourhood, Bayesian optimisation, analysis. Phase 11 added the Parquet export and the bulk path, and Phase 12 wrote the test suite.

The result I care about is not the feature list. It is that a 3.2-million-row enumeration was killed with kill -9 mid-run, reopened, and came back with PRAGMA integrity_check = ok, zero duplicate rows and a resumable store. That is the idempotency clause from Step 2, tested rather than hoped for. The second result is the manifest: a library built on one machine can be handed to a docking run on another, and the file says which PepNat version, schema, threshold version and model version produced it.

What still went wrong is worth writing down too. Two notes collided on 2-8, and a prompt that said "the 2-8 note" got the bug list instead of the Bayesian phase. The classifier's threshold version has to travel with the manifest, or an old library cannot be explained by a new threshold, and I learned that after the first library had already been exported. Neither failure was the model's fault. Both were places where I had not written the contract down.

docs.title: Projects
docs.text:
These are the four projects the book's examples come from, and I describe them in the order they taught me something: Protein Phaser for parsing, FlexTrimmer for sequence work, BioCUDA for parallelism, and the GROMACS scripts for the unglamorous business of reproducible analysis. The last section is what they have in common, which is the reason they are on this page at all.

Four projects come out of the same workflow this book describes. They are listed here because a reader who finishes the biology chapters will recognise their shapes: a parser, a geometry engine, a numerics layer, and a GPU port.

docs.title: 1. Protein Phaser
docs.text:
A C++ library for reading PDB and mmCIF files into a chain–residue–atom hierarchy, with geometric queries on top. Written in 2025.

Language C++20, no external dependencies Input PDB and mmCIF, fixed columns and the mmCIF loop format Queries pocket centre, residue depth, solvent-accessible surface area Size about 4000 lines

What it shares with this book: the Structure/Chain/Residue/Atom model in Structure Model is the same design, reduced to what a chapter can hold. The differences are scale — mmCIF support, the geometry engine, and the tests — and the reason the chapter is a chapter rather than a copy.

The lesson it produced: a parser that is correct on 1CRN and wrong on 1A3N is a parser whose tests were too easy. The multi-chain case is the one that finds the column error.

docs.title: 2. FlexTrimmer
docs.text:
A machine-learning tool that predicts truncation sites for a protein sequence, to improve expression yield. Feature engineering over sequence windows, a small model, and a ranked list of candidate cut points.

Language Python for the model, C++ for the feature extraction Input a sequence, a window size Output ranked truncation sites with a score per site Size about 1500 lines

What it shares with this book: the k-mer encoding in Sequence Encoding is the feature extraction step, and the numerics in Numerics for Scoring are what keeps the scores comparable across windows.

The lesson it produced: a model's input encoding is a program, and the defect classes of chapter 2 apply to it. An off-by-one in the window is a systematically shifted feature, and a model trained on shifted features learns the shift.

docs.title: 3. BioCUDA
docs.text:
A planned GPU-accelerated library for the operations in this book: scoring, distance matrices, contact search, and a port of the docking step.

Language CUDA C++ Status in planning; the distance-matrix kernel exists Target the loops that dominate a virtual screen: pairwise distances and scoring Size unknown by design

What it shares with this book: Parallel Scoring is the CPU version, and the same Amdahl analysis decides whether a GPU port is worth it. A scoring loop that is 60% of the runtime gets at most a 2.5× overall speedup from an infinitely fast GPU.

The lesson so far: measure the serial fraction before writing a kernel. The transfer cost can exceed the compute saved, and the only way to know is the CPU measurement first.

docs.title: 4. GROMACS and analysis scripts
docs.text:
A set of standardised GROMACS inputs and post-processing for four system types — protein–ligand, protein–protein, apo protein, and protein–metal — with RMSD, RMSF, \(R_g\), DCCM, MM-PBSA and secondary-structure analysis generated automatically.

Language Bash and Python Input a prepared structure Output a run directory plus plots Size about 800 lines

What it shares with this book: the geometry in Geometry — RMSD, \(R_g\), dihedrals — is the same arithmetic, and the superposition requirement is the one that matters most. A trajectory analysis that reports raw RMSD without superposition reports the molecule drifting, not the molecule changing.

The lesson it produced: an automation script is a program, and its failure modes are the ones in chapter 16 — a missing input, a step that silently produced nothing, and a pipeline that continued anyway.

docs.title: 5. What these have in common
docs.text:
All four are the same three layers: a parser that produces an owned model, a numerics or geometry layer that computes on it, and a driver that reports. The layers are separable, testable in isolation, and each has a version in this book that fits in a chapter.

That is the reason the chapters are ordered as they are. A reader who can write the chapter-sized version of each layer can write the project-sized version, because the difference is scale and testing rather than structure.

docs.title: Alignment
docs.text:
Alignment is the one algorithm in this part that every reader has used and few have implemented. I derive the recurrence, then show that the table is the cost, then do linear space without traceback, then the scoring numbers and where they come from, then tie-breaking, because a different traceback path on equal scores is a reproducibility bug rather than a detail.

Alignment is the oldest algorithm in this book and the one that most clearly shows the cost of a table. Two sequences of length n and m, a scoring rule, and a decision at each cell: match, insert, or delete. The naive implementation needs n×m cells; the interesting part is how little of that table is actually needed.

docs.title: 1. The recurrence
docs.text:
Global alignment of sequences \(a\) and \(b\) with a linear gap penalty:

\[ M(i,j) = \max \begin{cases} M(i-1,j-1) + s(a_i, b_j) \\ M(i-1,j) - g \\ M(i,j-1) - g \end{cases} \]

with \(M(0,0) = 0\), \(M(i,0) = -ig\), \(M(0,j) = -jg\). The final score is \(M(n,m)\), and the alignment is recovered by tracing back from \((n,m)\) to \((0,0)\).

/* LAB 04-01  bio_alignment/nw.c */
int *score = malloc((n + 1) * (m + 1) * sizeof *score);
int *trace = malloc((n + 1) * (m + 1) * sizeof *trace);   /* 0 diag, 1 up, 2 left */

for (size_t i = 1; i <= n; ++i) {
    for (size_t j = 1; j <= m; ++j) {
        int diag = score[(i - 1) * (m + 1) + (j - 1)] + sub(a[i - 1], b[j - 1]);
        int up   = score[(i - 1) * (m + 1) + j] - gap;
        int left = score[i * (m + 1) + (j - 1)] - gap;
        int best = diag;
        int dir = 0;
        if (up > best)   { best = up;   dir = 1; }
        if (left > best) { best = left; dir = 2; }
        score[i * (m + 1) + j] = best;
        trace[i * (m + 1) + j] = dir;     /* only needed for traceback */
    }
}

The table is (n+1)*(m+1) ints, and the traceback needs one direction per cell. For two 1000-residue proteins that is 4 MB of scores and 4 MB of directions, which fits in memory and misses the cache on nearly every cell for the larger sizes.

docs.title: 2. The cost is the table, not the arithmetic
docs.text:
Sequences Cells Score table With directions 76 × 76 5 929 24 KB 48 KB 300 × 300 90 601 362 KB 725 KB 1000 × 1000 1 002 001 4 MB 8 MB 10 000 × 10 000 100 020 001 400 MB 800 MB

The 10 000 × 10 000 case is where the textbook implementation stops being usable: 400 MB of table for a comparison that needs two rows at a time. This is the moment the chapter's memory theme pays off — the algorithm is O(nm) time and can be O(min(n,m)) space, and the difference is entirely in how the table is stored.

docs.title: 3. Linear space without traceback
docs.text:
int *row[2];                  /* two rows, swapped */
for (size_t i = 1; i <= n; ++i) {
    for (size_t j = 1; j <= m; ++j) {
        /* reads from row[(i-1)%2], writes to row[i%2] */
    }
}

Only the previous row is needed to compute the current row, so two rows suffice: 8 KB for a 1000×1000 alignment instead of 4 MB. The catch is that the traceback needs the whole table or a recomputation. Hirschberg's algorithm solves that with divide and conquer and two linear passes per level, giving O(nm) time and O(min(n,m)) space with the alignment recovered. It is an exercise, not a chapter.

The practical rule for this book: store directions only when the alignment itself is the output. A score-only call — "how similar are these two" — uses two rows and writes no directions.

docs.title: 4. Scoring, and where the numbers come from
docs.text:
static int sub(char x, char y) { return x == y ? 1 : -1; }

This is the simplest substitution score: identity. Real alignment uses a matrix such as BLOSUM62, where conservative substitutions (I→V, D→E) score positive and radical ones negative. The matrix is a 20×20 table of int8, 400 bytes, indexed by the same residue index as the encoding chapter:

static const int8_t blosum62[20][20] = { ... };
static int sub(char x, char y) { return blosum62[idx(x)][idx(y)]; }

The reason to include one real matrix in the lab: it makes the score magnitudes realistic, and it exposes the difference between a score that is a count (identity) and a score that is a log-odds (BLOSUM). The two produce alignments of different character on the same input, and the lab prints both.

The log-odds part is the piece I had to read a paper to understand, so I state it plainly here. BLOSUM62's entry for a pair of residues is \(2\log_2\frac{p_{\text{observed}}}{p_{\text{expected}}}\): the ratio of how often the pair occurs in the curated blocks versus how often it would occur if residues paired independently, in half-bit units, rounded to an integer. Two consequences follow. First, the scores add, because a product of ratios becomes a sum of logarithms — that is the only reason a per-position score can be summed along an alignment at all. Second, the score has no absolute meaning: it is always relative to the background model, which is why the same matrix used with different gap costs produces a different alignment, and why a negative entry means "less frequent than random", not "chemically impossible".

Gap penalties come in two forms. A linear penalty charges g per gap character; an affine penalty charges open + extend * length, which is the correct model because a single indel of length 5 is one evolutionary event, not five independent ones. Affine penalties need three states per cell (in-match, in-gap-a, in-gap-b) rather than one, which triples the table. That cost is the reason the affine version is a second lab rather than the default.

docs.title: 5. Reproducibility of ties
docs.text: Two cells can have equal scores, and the direction chosen for a tie determines the alignment reported. Different implementations break ties differently, so two programs computing the same score can return different alignments. The book's labs fix the order explicitly — diagonal preferred, then up, then left — and state it in the header comment, because an task that compares alignments byte-for-byte needs the tie-break rule to be part of the contract.

docs.title: 6. Field note: the off-by-one that shifted a whole alignment
docs.text:
A course implementation used 0-based indexing throughout but allocated a table with an extra row and column for the boundary:

for (i = 1; i <= n; i++)
    for (j = 1; j <= m; j++)
        score[i][j] = score[i-1][j-1] + sub(a[i], b[j]);   /* a[i] is the NEXT residue */

a[i] with a 1-based loop reads past the last residue on the final iteration and compares the wrong characters on every iteration before it. The reported score was plausible — the sequences were similar — and the alignment was shifted by one position throughout.

The defect is a naming problem before it is an arithmetic problem: the code mixed a 1-based loop with a 0-based array without ever writing down which convention applied where. The repair used in this book is to keep the sequence 0-based and the table 1-based, and to name the accessor so the shift is visible:

static int cell(const int *t, size_t i, size_t j, size_t m) { return t[i * (m + 1) + j]; }

Then attempt the exercise in labs/bio/04_alignment/, which requires a correct traceback for two sequences with a known single-residue deletion, and a second run that recomputes the score with two rows only and must match the full-table version exactly.

docs.title: Contacts
docs.text:
A contact map is a definition with three decisions inside it, and the cost is quadratic until you stop comparing everything with everything. I fix the definition first, then measure the naive loop, then bin spatially, then sweep sorted coordinates, then store the map in a form that does not waste half its bytes on symmetry.

A contact map is an n×n boolean matrix: cell (i, j) is true when residues i and j are within a cutoff distance. It is the simplest structural descriptor that captures something real, and the cheapest place in this book to see the difference between an algorithm that scales and one that does not.

docs.title: 1. The definition, and the three decisions inside it
docs.text:
/* LAB 07-01  bio_contacts/contact_map.c */
#define CUTOFF 8.0
#define CUTOFF2 (CUTOFF * CUTOFF)

int residue_contact(const residue *a, const residue *b) {
    for (size_t i = 0; i < a->n_atoms; ++i) {
        for (size_t j = 0; j < b->n_atoms; ++j) {
            if (dist2(&a->atoms[i], &b->atoms[j]) < CUTOFF2) { return 1; }
        }
    }
    return 0;
}

Three decisions that a paper must state and a program must choose:

  1. Which atoms. All heavy atoms, only CA, or only side-chain atoms. All-atom gives the largest number of contacts; CA-only is the cheap approximation used in most coarse contact maps.
  2. The cutoff. 8 Å is common for all-atom contacts; 5 Å is used for tighter definitions; 12 Å for a "residue neighbourhood". The number changes the map, so it belongs in the output.
  3. Whether |i - j| is excluded. Neighbouring residues are always in contact, so the diagonal band is uninformative. Most maps omit it or mask it; a map that includes it looks like it has structure when it does not.

The early return 1 inside the double loop is the whole of the cost model: contact detection stops at the first close pair, so the average cost is far below the worst case.

docs.title: 2. The naive cost
docs.text:
For 1A3N, about 1400 residues:

\[ 1400^2 \approx 2 \times 10^6 \text{ residue pairs} \]

and with about 8 atoms per residue per pair that is \(1.5 \times 10^7\) distance computations. On a modern machine that is a few milliseconds — fast enough that the naive version is the right answer for this size. The scaling is what makes it wrong at 10× the residues: \(14\,000^2\) is 100× the pairs.

Residues Residue pairs Estimated time (all-atom, 8 Å) 46 (1CRN) 2 116 under 1 ms 76 (1UBQ) 5 776 under 1 ms 1 400 (1A3N) 1.96 M a few ms 20 000 400 M several seconds 100 000 10 000 M minutes to hours

The break-even for the naive version is around 10⁴ residues; beyond that the two improvements below are not optional.

docs.title: 3. Improvement one: spatial binning
docs.text:
Divide the bounding box into cells of side cutoff, so that any pair within the cutoff must be in the same cell or an adjacent one. Then each residue compares against a fixed number of neighbours rather than against all n.

/* cells of side CUTOFF; a residue only touches its own and 26 neighbours */
size_t cells_per_side = (size_t)ceil(box_side / CUTOFF);
/* build the cell index once, then query 27 cells per residue */

The cost is \(O(n)\) for the index plus \(O(n \cdot k)\) for the queries, where k is the average number of residues in 27 cells — a constant determined by density, not by n. For a uniformly filled box, k is roughly 27× the number of residues in one cell, which stays small as n grows because the box grows with the molecule's extent.

The catch is that a protein is not uniformly dense: the surface is denser than the core in terms of neighbours within 8 Å, and a structure like a coiled-coil has regions where the local density is much higher. The constant is empirical, and the lab measures it rather than assuming.

docs.title: 4. Improvement two: sorted coordinate sweep
docs.text:
Sort the atoms along one axis, then for each atom scan forward until the x-difference exceeds the cutoff. This is the one-dimensional version of binning and is far simpler:

qsort(atoms, n, sizeof *atoms, by_x);
for (size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
    for (size_t j = i + 1; j < n && atoms[j].x - atoms[i].x < CUTOFF; ++j) {
        if (dist2(&atoms[i], &atoms[j]) < CUTOFF2) { mark_pair(i_orig, j_orig); }
    }
}

The inner loop terminates on the x-test, which is one comparison, and the full distance is computed only for the survivors. The break condition relies on the sort, so the sort is part of the algorithm rather than an optimisation — and the original indices must be carried through, because the map is indexed by residue identity, not by sorted position.

docs.title: 5. Storing the map
docs.text:
A bool array of n² costs n² bytes: 9 MB for 3000 atoms, 400 MB for 20 000. A bit array costs n²/8:

/* 3000 residues: 1.1 MB as bits, 9 MB as bytes */
uint64_t *map = calloc((n * n + 63) / 64, sizeof *map);
map[i * n + j]  ->  bit index i*n+j, word = idx/64, bit = idx%64

The bit operations are the ones from chapter 10, applied to a real data structure. The saving matters for a map that is written to disk or compared against another: 1.1 MB versus 9 MB is the difference between a file that loads instantly and one that does not.

For symmetric maps the upper triangle is the whole information, so half the bits are wasted. A packed upper-triangular index is an exercise; the lab keeps the square layout because the indexing is simpler and the saving is a factor of two.

docs.title: 6. Field note: the map whose diagonal was all contacts
docs.text:
A first version of the program produced a contact map that was solid along the diagonal and mostly empty elsewhere, and the reported number of contacts was about twice the expected value.

for (i) for (j) if (dist2(&a[i], &a[j]) < CUTOFF2) { map[i][j] = 1; }

Two defects in one line. The diagonal is trivially true — a residue is at distance 0 from itself — so the map claimed every residue was in contact with itself. And the loop counted each pair twice, because (i, j) and (j, i) are both visited, so any statistic over the map was doubled.

The repairs are j = i + 1 in the inner loop and an explicit mask for the diagonal band. The generalisation: a symmetric quantity computed by a full double loop needs j > i and a stated convention for the diagonal, and a map that does not exclude |i - j| <= 2 is reporting the polymer backbone rather than tertiary contacts.

docs.title: 7. Practise
docs.text: Build code/bio/07_contacts/contact_map.c and run bash labs/bio/07_contacts/check.sh: the program builds a map from an embedded fragment, asserts that the binned version reproduces the naive one exactly, and prints both times. Downloading 1CRN and repeating at 8 Å — where the upper-triangle contact count should be in the low hundreds — is the extension; a binning implemented as a re-scan shows up there as a time ratio near 1.

docs.title: FASTA and Sequence Input
docs.text:
A FASTA file looks like the easiest format in biology, and that is exactly why the three promises it does not make will bite you. I parse it line by line without a fixed buffer, then attack line endings, then write the C++ version to show what changes when a std::string owns the length, then argue about how strict validation should be. The field note is a counter that counted a header as a sequence.

A FASTA file is a header line beginning with > and one or more lines of residues. That is the entire specification. Everything difficult about parsing one comes from what real files contain beyond the specification: Windows line endings, blank lines, lowercase residues, trailing whitespace, comments, and duplicate identifiers.

docs.title: 1. The format, and the three things it does not promise
docs.text:
>sp|P0CG48|UBC_HUMAN Ubiquitin OS=Homo sapiens OX=9606 GN=UBC PE=1 SV=1
MQIFVKTLTGKTITLEVEPSDTIENVKAKIQDKEGIPPDQQRLIFAGKQLEDGRTLSDYNIQKESTLHLVLRLRGG

What the format promises: the header starts with >, and residues follow until the next > or the end of file.

What it does not promise:

  1. Line length. Sixty is a convention, not a rule. A single 76-character line and 76 one-character lines are both valid.
  2. Case. Lowercase residues mean the same amino acid and are common in soft-masked alignments.
  3. Uniqueness. Two records may share an identifier. A parser that stores sequences in a map keyed by identifier silently loses one.

None of these are exotic. All three appear in real downloads, which is why a parser that assumes them is a parser that works on the tutorial file and fails on the user's file.

docs.title: 2. The parser
docs.text:
/* LAB 01-01  bio_fasta/fasta_c.c */
typedef struct {
    char *name;        /* owned */
    char *residues;    /* owned, NUL-terminated */
    size_t length;
} record;

typedef struct {
    record *items;     /* owned */
    size_t count;
    size_t capacity;
} record_list;

Three ownerships, three frees, in one struct — this is the chapter 7 obligation in its natural habitat. The capacity field is the vector growth pattern from chapter 7, written by hand because this stage is C.

static int is_residue(char c) {
    return (c >= 'A' && c <= 'Z') || (c >= 'a' && c <= 'z') || c == '*';
}

'*' is the stop codon, present in translated sequences. Rejecting it fails on real files; accepting it and storing it as a residue fails on the geometry later. The decision this book makes: accept it in the parser, and let the consumer decide. A parser that cannot represent a legal input is a parser with a hidden assumption.

docs.title: 3. Reading by line without a fixed buffer
docs.text:
char *line = NULL;
size_t cap = 0;
ssize_t n;
while ((n = getline(&line, &cap, fp)) != -1) { ... }
free(line);

getline is POSIX, not C standard, and it is the only correct way to read a line of unknown length. The C-standard alternative is a fixed buffer with fgets, which truncates a long line into two records without saying so — the defect class of chapter 5, applied to a file format.

Route B readers do not have getline. The MSVC equivalent is fgets in a loop with a length check, or std::getline if the stage is built as C++. The chapter note on that page says so; the C version keeps a #ifdef _WIN32 branch with the loop, so the lab compiles on both.

/* the _WIN32 branch: read until the newline or the buffer is full */
char buf[512];
while (fgets(buf, sizeof buf, fp)) {
    size_t len = strlen(buf);
    if (len == sizeof buf - 1 && buf[len - 1] != '\n') { /* line continues */ }
}

The len == sizeof buf - 1 test is the only reliable way to detect truncation with fgets, because a line of exactly that length and a truncated line are otherwise indistinguishable.

docs.title: 4. Line endings
docs.text:
A file saved on Windows ends its lines with \r\n. Inside a C string read by getline, the \r is part of the line, and it lands at the end of the residue string:

"MQIFVKT\r"    /* length 9, last character is not a residue */

The defect surfaces much later, as a length that is one too large, or as a residue that fails is_residue. The repair is to strip a trailing \r at read time, in one place:

if (len > 0 && line[len - 1] == '\r') { line[--len] = '\0'; }

Stripping in one place rather than in every caller is the difference between a parser and a set of functions that happen to read lines.

docs.title: 5. The C++ version, and what changes
docs.text:
// LAB 01-02  bio_fasta/fasta_cpp.cpp
std::optional<Sequence> parse(std::string_view header, std::string_view body);

The C++ parser keeps the same record structure and replaces the manual growth with a std::vector. The interesting change is std::string_view for the body: parsing does not need to own the characters, only to read them, so the signature says so and the caller keeps the buffer alive.

for (char c : body) {
    if (c == '\n' || c == '\r' || c == ' ') { continue; }
    if (!is_residue(c)) { return std::nullopt; }
    out.push_back(c);
}

std::nullopt rather than an exception, because a malformed record is an expected input, not an exceptional condition — chapter 12's distinction applied at a file boundary.

docs.title: 6. Validation, and how strict
docs.text:
Check Strict? Why Header starts with > yes without it the record is unparseable Residues are letters or * yes a digit or a - is a gap or a corruption, not a residue Empty record reject an empty sequence divides by zero at the GC step Duplicate identifier accept, report legal, but a caller may want to know Lowercase accept, normalise legal and meaningful Whitespace inside a line strip legal per the format, common in wrapped output

The one that surprises people is the empty record. A header with no residues is syntactically valid, and it produces a zero-length sequence that every downstream fraction divides by. Rejecting it at the boundary is cheaper than a guard in every consumer.

docs.title: 7. Field note: the counter that counted a header
docs.text:
A course exercise read a sequence file and printed the GC fraction by counting every 'G' and 'C' in the file — including the characters in the header line, where Homo sapiens contains a capital G in Homo? It does not, but GN=UBB does, and the header of one test file contained G twice. The reported GC fraction was 3 percentage points off on a 76-residue sequence, and the error looked like a rounding problem.

The defect is the absence of state: the reader had no notion of "currently inside a header" versus "currently reading residues", so the format's two line types were the same line type.

int in_header = 0;
while (getline(...)) {
    if (line[0] == '>') { in_header = 1; continue; }
    if (in_header) { in_header = 0; }
    /* only here are the characters residues */
}

The generalisation: a file format with two record types requires the parser to have a state, and a parser that applies one rule to every line is not parsing.

docs.title: 8. Practise
docs.text: Build code/bio/01_fasta/fasta_c.c and run it: it parses the ubiquitin record in data/README.md — 76 residues, with CRLF endings, a wrapped body and a lowercase record all accepted — and rejects three malformed inputs (no >, a digit in the body, an empty record). Attempt the exercise in labs/bio/01_fasta/, whose task is fasta_cpp.cpp: the same parser in C++ with the length and header assertions carried over.

docs.title: Geometry
docs.text:
Geometry is where a biology student meets floating point whether they want to or not. I start with distance and the comparison that avoids a square root, then dihedrals with their sign convention, then RMSD and why superposition must come first, then radius of gyration, then the angle between three atoms. The field note is a NaN that came out of a cosine slightly above one.

Four numbers come out of a structure file and everything else is arithmetic on them: distance, angle, dihedral, and radius of gyration. Each is a small formula with one non-obvious numerical trap, and this page is about those traps.

docs.title: 1. Distance, and the comparison without a square root
docs.text:
/* LAB 06-01  bio_geometry/dihedral.c */
static double dist2(const atom *a, const atom *b) {
    double dx = a->x - b->x, dy = a->y - b->y, dz = a->z - b->z;
    return dx * dx + dy * dy + dz * dz;
}

static double dist(const atom *a, const atom *b) { return sqrt(dist2(a, b)); }

The squared form exists because most distance questions are comparisons: "is this pair closer than 8 Å?" is dist2 < 64.0, and comparing squared values avoids a square root per pair. In a contact search over \(3000^2\) pairs that is 4.5 million square roots saved, which is a measurable fraction of the loop's time.

The trap is a threshold that was computed with a square root and compared with a squared value. The units are the only warning, and a comment stating "squared" on the function is the cheapest defence.

if (dist(a, b) < cutoff)          // 4.5M sqrt calls
if (dist2(a, b) < cutoff * cutoff) // same answer, no sqrt

docs.title: 2. Dihedral angles
docs.text:
A dihedral is the angle between the planes defined by atoms 1–2–3 and 2–3–4, measured about the 2–3 axis. The standard formulation:

[ b_1 = r_2 - r_1,\quad b_2 = r_3 - r_2,\quad b_3 = r_4 - r_3 ] [ n_1 = b_1 \times b_2,\quad n_2 = b_2 \times b_3 ] [ \phi = \operatorname{atan2}\left( (n_1 \times n_2) \cdot \frac{b_2}{|b_2|}, n_1 \cdot n_2 \right) ]

static double dihedral(const atom *a, const atom *b, const atom *c, const atom *d) {
    vec b1 = sub(b, a), b2 = sub(c, b), b3 = sub(d, c);
    vec n1 = cross(b1, b2), n2 = cross(b2, b3);
    double y = dot(cross(n1, n2), unit(b2));   /* signed */
    double x = dot(n1, n2);
    return atan2(y, x) * 180.0 / M_PI;         /* degrees, (-180, 180] */
}

atan2 rather than acos: the cosine alone cannot distinguish \(+\phi\) from \(-\phi\), and a peptide bond's sign is the difference between a cis and a trans conformation. The atan2 form returns the full range and needs no clamping.

The sign convention is a source of disagreement between programs: some define \(\phi\) with the opposite sense, so a comparison against literature values requires knowing which convention produced them. The labs fix the convention in the header comment and do not compare dihedrals against external sources.

docs.title: 3. RMSD, and why superposition comes first
docs.text:
The naive RMSD between two conformations:

double rmsd = 0.0;
for (size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i) { rmsd += dist2(&a[i], &b[i]); }
rmsd = sqrt(rmsd / n);

This is the correct formula and usually the wrong number, because it depends on the coordinate frame. Two identical structures translated by 10 Å have an RMSD of 10 Å; rotated by 90°, an RMSD of up to the molecular diameter. What is wanted is the RMSD after the optimal rigid superposition — the Kabsch algorithm — which is an SVD of a 3×3 covariance matrix.

The chapter states the result and points at the lab rather than deriving Kabsch, because the derivation is a linear algebra chapter and the point here is the distinction:

/* after superposition */
rmsd_superposed <= rmsd_raw

with equality only when the structures are already aligned. Reporting a raw RMSD as a structural difference is a defect that reviewers catch, and the reference program checks both numbers for that reason.

The lab implements the first half: rmsd.c aligns the centroids and then shows, on a rotated copy, why translation alone cannot fix a rotation. The full fit multiplies a 3×3 covariance matrix by a rotation taken from an SVD; that is six pages of linear algebra, and the exercise is to build it correctly rather than to derive it.

docs.title: 4. Radius of gyration
5. Angle between three atoms
6. Field note: the nan that came from a cosine
docs.text:
A course program computed bond angles and printed a table where a few entries were -nan. The cause was the missing clamp, and the trigger was a nearly linear arrangement of three atoms — a real geometry in a real structure, not a contrived one.

The pattern is worth recognising: acos, asin, sqrt of a negative, and division by a norm of zero all produce NaN or inf, and the value then spreads. A single NaN in a scoring sum turns the whole score into NaN, and a comparison like score < threshold against NaN is false, so the record is silently dropped rather than flagged.

The repair in this book is two-part: clamp at the source, and refuse to propagate — the parsing code and the scoring code both check isfinite at their boundaries and abort with the input that produced the bad value.

docs.title: 7. Practise
docs.text: Build code/bio/06_geometry/dihedral.c and rmsd.c, then run bash labs/bio/06_geometry/check.sh. Both work on embedded coordinates: the torsion angles are checked against hand-computed values of 180° and 90°, and the RMSD is checked twice — it falls to zero on a translated copy after centroid alignment, and it stays non-zero on a rotated one, which is what shows that alignment removes translation and not rotation. The full Kabsch fit, which needs an SVD, is the next step. Computing 1UBQ's \(R_g\) and comparing it with 11.7 Å is the extension, once the file is on disk.

docs.title: Numerics for Scoring
docs.text:
Floating point is not a detail you can postpone in structure work, because a sum of 10^5 terms drifts and a log-sum-exp overflows. I show the drift, then Kahan summation, then log-sum-exp with the minimum pulled out rather than the maximum, then relative error and the comparison built on it, then summation order as a semantic choice rather than housekeeping.

A scoring function sums thousands of small terms. The individual terms are computed to about 16 digits; the sum, accumulated naively, may be correct to 12. That difference is invisible until it changes a decision, and in structural biology a score comparison is a decision.

This page is the floating-point behaviour the scoring chapters depend on, kept to what a scoring loop actually needs.

docs.title: 1. Why the sum drifts
docs.text:
/* LAB 03-01  bio_numerics/kahan.c */
double s = 0.0;
for (size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i) { s += a[i]; }

Each addition rounds to the nearest representable double. The rounding error is bounded by half an ULP of the current partial sum, so it grows with the magnitude of the partial sum, not with the number of terms. When the terms are of similar size the errors partially cancel and the result is good; when one term is much larger than the rest, every later addition loses the low bits of the small terms.

The pathological case is a sum where a large prefix is followed by many small terms. In a scoring loop this happens whenever a distance term dominates and the remaining terms are corrections.

double s = 0.0;
for (i) { s += 1e16; }
s += 1.0;      /* the 1.0 is lost: 1e16 + 1 is 1e16 in double */

The mechanism: double has 53 bits of mantissa, so 1e16 is about \(2^{53}\), and adding 1 needs a bit below the last representable place. The result is exactly 1e16.

docs.title: 2. Kahan summation
docs.text:
The compensation term carries the lost low bits:

double sum = 0.0, c = 0.0;
for (size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
    double y = a[i] - c;
    double t = sum + y;
    c = (t - sum) - y;
    sum = t;
}

Four operations instead of one, and the error bound drops from \(O(n \epsilon)\) to \(O(\epsilon)\) independent of n for well-behaved inputs. The cost is the four operations and one extra register.

Whether it is worth it: for a 76-residue protein, no — the naive sum is already accurate to 15 digits. For a 10⁶-term scoring pass over a ligand library, yes, because a systematic bias of \(10^{-12}\) in a score used as a filter changes the set of molecules that pass.

The lab measures the difference rather than asserting it: it runs both sums on a constructed vector where the naive version is known to lose, and prints both results next to the exact answer computed with long double or with a rational reference.

docs.title: 3. Log-sum-exp, and why scores are not probabilities
docs.text:
A scoring function often returns an energy, and a probability is \(e^{-E/kT}\). Summing probabilities of many states underflows: exp(-700) is zero in double, while the individual energies are perfectly representable.

/* the naive version: underflows to 0 */
double p = 0.0;
for (i) { p += exp(-e[i]); }

/* the stable version: factor out the minimum */
double m = min(e, n);
double s = 0.0;
for (i) { s += exp(-(e[i] - m)); }
double log_sum = -m + log(s);       /* log of the sum of exp(-e[i]) */

The shift is by the minimum, because the terms are exp(-e[i]): subtracting the smallest e makes the largest term exp(0) = 1 and every other term at most one, so the sum lands in [1, n] and can neither underflow nor overflow. The result is recovered by subtracting m again after the logarithm. Factoring out the maximum instead would leave the largest term at exp(-(max - min)), which underflows as soon as the range exceeds about 700 — the exact failure the shift was meant to prevent.

The cost is one pass to find the minimum and one pass to sum, which is why a scoring loop that needs a normalised probability pays for two passes. The alternative — clamping the exponent — is a defect: it changes the answer rather than stabilising the computation.

docs.title: 4. Relative error, and how to compare two doubles
docs.text:
static int nearly_equal(double a, double b) {
    double d = fabs(a - b);
    double m = fmax(fabs(a), fabs(b));
    return d <= 1e-12 * (m > 1.0 ? m : 1.0);
}

An absolute tolerance is wrong for large values (it demands impossible precision) and wrong for tiny values (it accepts garbage). The relative form with a floor at 1.0 is the standard compromise, and it is the form the labs' assertions use.

The floor matters: for a = 1e-18 and b = 2e-18, the relative difference is 100%, but both are noise near zero and the comparison should pass or fail on a project-specific absolute threshold, not on this formula.

docs.title: 5. Summation order is not a detail
docs.text:
Two cores summing the same array in a different order produce different results, because floating-point addition is not associative.

(a + b) + c    !=    a + (b + c)

This is the reason a parallel reduction must be deterministic-by-construction if its output is compared across runs: either fix the partition and the order (which OpenMP's reduction(+:sum) does within a schedule, not across thread counts), or accept that the score varies in the last digits and write the tolerance accordingly.

The parallel-scoring chapter states its rule explicitly: the serial and parallel runs must agree to 1e-9, not bit-for-bit, and the reason is this paragraph.

docs.title: 6. Field note: the fraction that was six sixths
docs.text:
The archived fraction.h stored a fraction as two integers and multiplied without reducing:

Fraction operator*(const Fraction &a, const Fraction &b) {
    return Fraction(a.num * b.num, a.den * b.den);   // no reduction
}

2/3 * 3/2 produced 6/6, which is numerically 1 and structurally not. A comparison against Fraction(1, 1) failed, and a sum of ten multiplications overflowed an int denominator before the error became visible.

The repair is to reduce in the constructor, so every path that constructs a Fraction produces a canonical form:

Fraction(long n, long d) : num(n), den(d) {
    long g = std::gcd(n, d);
    num /= g; den /= g;
    if (den < 0) { num = -num; den = -den; }
}

This is the invariant-as-constructor argument from the operators chapter, and it is the same argument as this page's: a numeric type that does not maintain its own representation invites every caller to fix it differently. The generalisation to floating point is that a sum which does not control its own error accumulation invites every caller to distrust the result.

docs.title: 7. Practise
docs.text: Run code/bio/03_numerics/kahan.c and lse.c, and confirm that the naive sum's error grows with n while the compensated one's does not. lse.c asserts exactly why the shift is needed: the naive version returns exp(-1.0) because the second term underflows to zero, while the stable version matches the direct computation to 1e-12 relative. Attempt the exercise in labs/bio/03_numerics/: reimplement the shifted form without the sign mistake, and check it on an input whose exponent range exceeds 700.

docs.title: Overview: From Sequence to Structure
docs.text:
Before any code, I owe the reader an argument for the order. Nine stages, and I say why each one precedes the next, why I left out the obvious ones such as BLAST and secondary-structure prediction, what the data policy is, and what the three files in every lab are for. If you read one page in this part, read this one; the rest assume it.

The biology half of this book exists for one reason: to give the C and C++ chapters a destination that is not a toy. Everything before this page computed sizes, walked arrays, and fixed bugs in isolation. From here on, the same techniques produce numbers a structural biologist would recognise — a GC fraction, an alignment score, a contact map, a radius of gyration.

This is computational biology, not bioinformatics. The distinction is deliberate and worth one paragraph.

Bioinformatics is the management of biological data: formats, databases, queries, annotations, pipelines that call existing tools. It is largely a systems and data-management activity, and it is well served by Python and by tools that already exist.

Computational biology here means computing properties of molecules from their coordinates and sequences: the physics and geometry of a structure, the numerics of a scoring function, the cost of evaluating it at scale. It is where arrays, alignment, floating-point behaviour, and memory layout stop being exercises and become the reason the program is slow or wrong.

A structural biologist's daily work is full of the second kind. A PDB file is a text file with fixed columns and a hierarchy of chains, residues and atoms. A contact map is a boolean matrix. A dihedral angle is four points and an arctangent. An RMSD is a sum of squared differences followed by a square root. Each of those is a chapter of this book applied to a real file.

docs.title: 1. The nine stages, and the order they come in
docs.text:
Stage Topic What it computes Chapters it leans on 01 FASTA input parse headers, validate alphabet strings, files 02 Sequence encoding GC and k-mer counts, 2-bit packing bit operations, arrays 03 Numerics Kahan summation, log-sum-exp floating point, undefined behaviour 04 Alignment Needleman–Wunsch, scoring, traceback arrays, heap, sorting 05 PDB parsing fixed columns, hierarchy, altloc structs, pointers, translation units 06 Geometry distance, dihedral, RMSD, Rg floating point, numerics 07 Contacts contact maps, neighbour search arrays, sorting, bit ops 08 Structure model secondary structure, a C++ model class classes, RAII, containers 09 Parallel scoring OpenMP over the scoring loop performance, Amdahl

The order is not arbitrary. Stage 04 needs the numerics from 03 to produce scores that do not drift; stage 06 needs the parser from 05; stage 07 needs the geometry from 06. Skipping ahead is possible but each page says what it assumes.

docs.title: 2. Why these and not the obvious ones
docs.text:
Three candidates were deliberately left out.

No BLAST. Running an existing aligner is a shell exercise, not a computing one, and the interesting part — why the algorithm is O(nm) and how banded variants work — is stage 04.

No machine learning framework. Training a model on sequences is a different book. The closest this text gets is the discussion of why a ResNet-style model is a memory problem before it is a maths problem.

No database. Querying UniProt is a network and schema exercise. The one sequence this book embeds — ubiquitin, P0CG48, 76 residues — is short enough to be a constant and long enough to test every parser.

docs.title: 3. The data policy
docs.text:
The repository ships no structure files. data/README.md lists the three used throughout and the commands to fetch them:

curl -O https://files.rcsb.org/download/1UBQ.pdb
curl -O https://files.rcsb.org/download/1CRN.pdb
curl -O https://files.rcsb.org/download/1A3N.pdb

Three reasons for this policy rather than a vendored copy:

  1. Coordinates are large, and a repository that carries them grows without bound.
  2. RCSB revises entries; a pinned copy makes the output tests depend on a version that no reader can reproduce from the source.
  3. Fetching the file yourself is the first step of your own parser, and it teaches where the data actually comes from.

Stages 05–08 carry their input as string literals, so there is nothing to skip and nothing to download before they run. A missing data/ file affects only your own prototype, not the reference program.

docs.title: 4. The three files, and why each
docs.text:
File What it is Why it is here 1CRN crambin, 46 residues, 327 atoms smallest real protein; good for hand-checking distances 1UBQ ubiquitin, 76 residues, 602 atoms the standard small test case; single chain, no gaps 1A3N haemoglobin, 4 chains, ~3000 atoms the multi-chain case: contacts across chains, quaternary structure

1CRN is small enough to compute a full contact map by eye. 1UBQ is the case every paper uses, so its numbers can be checked against literature. 1A3N is the case where a parser that assumes one chain breaks.

docs.title: 5. What a reader should be able to do at the end
docs.text:
Not "know bioinformatics". Concretely, after stage 09 a reader should be able to:

  • Read a PDB file into a structure whose chains, residues and atoms are correct, including the parts most parsers get wrong.
  • Compute an RMSD between two conformations and explain why superposition is required for it to mean anything.
  • Build a contact map and explain why the naive O(n²) version is acceptable at n = 3000 and not at n = 30000.
  • Write a scoring loop, measure it, parallelise it, and report the speedup honestly with the serial fraction stated.
  • Explain what a dihedral angle is in terms of four points and an arctangent, without looking it up.

If any of those is still opaque after the corresponding page, the page has failed and the fix belongs in the page, not in a footnote.

docs.title: 6. How to read this section
docs.text:
The pages assume the C chapters. A reader who has not done heap.md and structs-and-padding.md will find stage 05 confusing, because a PDB parser is a struct-layout problem before it is a biology problem. The recommended route in How to Use This Book puts the C chapters first for exactly this reason.

Each page ends with a Practise section pointing at labs/bio/, and each reference program states its tolerance in its own assertions.

docs.title: Parallel Scoring
docs.text:
Parallelism is a measurement, not a mood, so I begin with the loop and then with the timer that lies — wall clock against CPU time, and why the first iteration is not the cost. Then the speedup arithmetic, then false sharing on one cache line, then reproducibility when the reduction order changes. The field note is a parallel program that reported a speedup of 1.0.

The last stage takes the scoring loop from the alignment chapter and distributes it. The loop is the ideal case — independent iterations, one reduction — and the page is mostly about what goes wrong anyway: the timer that lies, the reduction that changes answers, and the speedup that stops at 4× on an 8-core machine.

docs.title: 1. The loop
docs.text:
/* LAB 09-01  bio_parallel/omp_scores.c */
double total = 0.0;
#pragma omp parallel for reduction(+:total) schedule(static)
for (size_t i = 0; i < n_ligands; ++i) {
    double s = score_ligand(ligands[i], &protein);
    total += s;
}

Three clauses, three decisions.

parallel for requires that the iterations be independent — no iteration writes what another reads. The scoring loop satisfies this because each ligand is scored against a read-only protein.

reduction(+:total) gives each thread a private total, initialised to the identity (0), combined at the end. The combination order is unspecified, which is the reproducibility problem below.

schedule(static) divides the iteration space into equal contiguous chunks. For a uniform workload that is optimal: no scheduling overhead, predictable locality. For a workload where some ligands take ten times longer than others, static leaves one thread doing the long ones while the others idle, and dynamic or guided is the right choice at the cost of a lock per chunk.

schedule(dynamic, 64)   // fetch 64 iterations at a time
schedule(guided)        // chunks shrink as the loop progresses

The rule: measure the variance in per-iteration cost first. If the ratio of slowest to fastest is under 2, static wins. Above that, the load imbalance costs more than the scheduling.

docs.title: 2. The timer that lies
docs.text:
clock_t t0 = clock();
#pragma omp parallel for
for (...) { ... }
clock_t t1 = clock();
printf("%.2f s\n", (double)(t1 - t0) / CLOCKS_PER_SEC);   /* wrong for parallel */

clock() returns CPU time summed over all threads on Linux (and on Windows it returns wall time, which makes the error platform-dependent and therefore worse). On an 8-thread run that finishes in 1 second, clock() reports about 8 seconds, so the computed "speedup" is negative or nonsense.

The correct timer for wall time:

#include <time.h>
struct timespec a, b;
clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC, &a);
/* work */
clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC, &b);
double secs = (b.tv_sec - a.tv_sec) + (b.tv_nsec - a.tv_nsec) * 1e-9;

CLOCK_MONOTONIC is not affected by wall-clock adjustments and has nanosecond resolution. Route B uses QueryPerformanceCounter or std::chrono::steady_clock, which is the portable form and is what the C++ version of the lab uses.

docs.title: 3. What the speedup actually is
docs.text:
A worked example for 1A3N against 1000 ligands on a 4-core machine. The numbers are chosen to show the arithmetic and are consistent with the serial fraction used below; they are not copied from a recorded run, so when you run the lab your own numbers will land near these and not on them:

Threads Wall time Speedup Efficiency 1 4.00 s 1.00× 100% 2 2.20 s 1.82× 91% 4 1.30 s 3.08× 77% 8 1.29 s 3.10× 39%

The 8-thread row on a 4-core machine is the oversubscription case: the OS time-slices 8 threads onto 4 cores, so the row is roughly the 4-thread row again. The efficiency column is the honest number — 3.1× on 8 threads is 39% efficiency, not 3.1× "scaling".

The 4-thread row is below 4× because of the serial fraction. With \(p = 0.9\), Amdahl's law gives a ceiling of 3.08× at 4 threads, which is where the table's value sits; a real run lands near it, and the difference is noise rather than a contradiction.

The lab requires the reader to report all four numbers and the serial fraction, estimated by running with 1 thread and timing a serial-only section. A speedup number without its thread count and efficiency is not a measurement.

docs.title: 4. False sharing
docs.text:
double partial[NTHREADS];                    /* each thread writes partial[id] */
#pragma omp parallel for
for (...) { partial[omp_get_thread_num()] += ...; }

Eight doubles are 64 bytes: one cache line. Every thread writes to the same line, so every write invalidates every other core's copy, and the line ping-pongs between caches. The loop is correct and can be slower than the serial version.

The fix is padding:

struct padded { double v; char pad[56]; };
struct padded partial[NTHREADS];

reduction avoids this problem because each thread's private copy lives on its own stack. A hand-written per-thread accumulator without padding reintroduces it, which is why the lab's second exercise asks for the hand-written version and then measures the padded and unpadded variants.

docs.title: 5. Reproducibility
docs.text:
Floating-point addition is not associative, so a reduction over 8 threads produces a different last few digits than the serial loop:

/* serial: 0.1234567890123456 */
/* 8 threads: 0.1234567890123449 */

The difference is \(10^{-14}\), and it does not matter for a score. It matters when a result is compared across a serial and a parallel run, which is why the labs that print a distance or an energy compare with a tolerance rather than byte-for-byte, and why the capstone prints a Fraction instead of a double.

For an exactly reproducible parallel sum, the reduction must be deterministic: partition the index range explicitly into fixed chunks, accumulate each chunk in a fixed order, then combine the chunks in a fixed order. schedule(static) plus a manual array of partials does that, and it is slower than reduction by a few percent. The lab offers both and states the trade.

docs.title: 6. Field note: the parallel program that reported no speedup
docs.text:
A course implementation added #pragma omp parallel for and measured with clock(), reported a 0.9× speedup on 8 threads, and concluded that "the machine does not support parallelism". The measurement was wrong twice: clock() summed the threads' CPU time, and the loop was over an array of 10 elements, so the thread launch overhead exceeded the work.

The repairs are the two rules of this page: time the wall clock, and size the problem so that each thread gets enough work to amortise the launch. omp_get_wtime() exists for exactly this and returns wall time in seconds.

The second defect — 10 iterations across 8 threads — produced a measurement that could not have shown a speedup under any timer. A benchmark that is not sized to its mechanism is not a benchmark.
