docs.title: PDB Format
docs.text:
PDB is a fixed-column format pretending to be whitespace-separated, and every parser that splits on spaces is a future bug. I mark the columns of one record, then show the split failing, then read coordinates, then build the hierarchy of model, chain, residue, atom, then decide what to do with HETATM. Everything is a struct because a 30 MB file is not a place for per-atom allocation.

The Protein Data Bank format is a fixed-column text format from 1971. Every field has a column range, not a delimiter. This is the single most important fact about the format, and it is the reason most parsers of it are subtly wrong.

docs.title: 1. A record, with columns marked
docs.text:
1         2         3         4         5         6         7         8
12345678901234567890123456789012345678901234567890123456789012345678901234567890
ATOM      1  N   MET A   1      27.340  24.430   2.614  1.00  9.19           N
Field Columns Content record name 1–6 ATOM or HETATM serial 7–11 atom serial number atom name 13–16 N, CA, with the element right-aligned altLoc 17 alternate conformation indicator residue name 18–20 MET chain ID 22 A residue sequence 23–26 1 insertion code 27 or A x, y, z 31–38, 39–46, 47–54 %8.3f occupancy 55–60 %6.2f temperature factor 61–66 %6.2f element 77–78 N, C

The columns are the contract. A file may contain spaces inside a field, and the fields are separated by nothing in particular — so tokenising on whitespace is wrong in a way that usually works.

docs.title: 2. Why whitespace splitting fails
docs.text:
char *tok = strtok(line, " \t");

Three failures, all real:

  1. The atom name field has leading spaces by design. N and CA are both four columns, and the alignment encodes whether the element is one or two letters. Splitting drops that information, so a parser cannot distinguish a calcium atom CA from an alpha carbon CA without guessing from the residue name.
  2. A blank chain ID collapses the token stream. With no chain, columns 22 is a space, and splitting produces one fewer token than the parser's field table expects — every subsequent field shifts.
  3. Residue names with spaces (A for a nucleic acid) and negative occupancies break the assumption further.

The format's designers chose fixed columns precisely so that a blank field is still a field.

docs.title: 3. Reading the coordinates
docs.text:
/* LAB 05-01  bio_pdb/pdb_dump.c */
double x, y, z;
/* the substring, not the whole line */
char xs[9] = {0}, ys[9] = {0}, zs[9] = {0};
memcpy(xs, line + 30, 8);
memcpy(ys, line + 38, 8);
memcpy(zs, line + 46, 8);
x = atof(xs); y = atof(ys); z = atof(zs);

%8.3f guarantees three decimal places and at most eight columns; atof on the copied substring handles the sign and the decimal point. sscanf(line + 30, "%8lf%8lf%8lf", &x, &y, &z) is also correct and avoids the copy, because the field width limits the conversion — the width is the part that matters, not the copy.

sscanf(line + 30, "%8lf", &x);      // correct: width-limited
sscanf(line, "%*31s %lf", &x);      // wrong: relies on whitespace

The wrong form works on well-formed files and fails on any file where a coordinate has a leading space and the previous field is short.

docs.title: 4. The hierarchy
docs.text:
Structure
└── Chain (A, B, C, ...)
    └── Residue (identified by sequence number + insertion code)
        └── Atom (identified by name + altLoc)

The residue identity is (chain, resSeq, iCode), not resSeq. Two residues in the same chain can share a sequence number when an insertion code distinguishes them, which happens in real structures. A key that uses only resSeq merges them.

The atom identity is (name, altLoc). Alternate conformations are labelled A, B, ... in column 17, and a structure with two conformations has two atoms named CA in the same residue. A parser that keeps the first one and ignores the rest is a parser that silently drops half the model.

typedef struct {
    char name[5];
    char altloc;
    char element[3];
    double x, y, z;
    float occupancy, bfactor;
} atom;

typedef struct {
    char name[4];
    char icode;
    int seq;
    atom *atoms;
    size_t n_atoms, cap;
} residue;

The altloc field is one char and costs nothing; omitting it costs the ability to represent a legal file.

docs.title: 5. ATOM versus HETATM, and what to keep
docs.text:
ATOM records are polymer atoms; HETATM are ligands, waters, and modified residues. A structure viewer usually shows both; a contact map usually wants only the polymer. The distinction must be stored, not applied at parse time, because different consumers want different subsets.

TER marks the end of a chain in older files; END marks the end of the model. Files with multiple models (MODEL/ENDMDL) exist — an NMR ensemble has twenty — and the parser must either read only the first model or index the rest explicitly.

docs.title: 6. Size, and why everything is a struct
docs.text:
sizeof(atom)      /* 64 bytes: 5 + 1 + 3 + padding + 3 doubles + 2 floats */

1UBQ has 602 atoms, so the atom array is 38 KB — smaller than the file it came from, and comfortably in L2. 1A3N has about 3000 atoms, 190 KB. Neither is a memory problem, which is why the parser can afford one struct per atom and the coordinates can be double rather than float.

The struct is 64 bytes because of alignment: five chars plus padding to reach the first double at offset 8, and the two floats padded to the end. Chapter 6's layout rules apply directly, and a parser that reorders the members to {double x, y, z; float occupancy, bfactor; char name[5]; char altloc; char element[3];} gets 48 bytes — same data, 25% less memory, and a different cache behaviour on the iteration that touches only coordinates.

docs.title: 7. Field note: the parser that read the wrong column
docs.text:
A course program parsed atom records like this:

sscanf(line, "%6s%5d %4s %3s %c%4d %8lf%8lf%8lf",
       rec, &serial, atom_name, res_name, &chain, &res_seq, &x, &y, &z);

It worked on 1CRN and failed on 1A3N. The cause: the format's spaces between fields are not guaranteed to be single, and %4s for the atom name consumes N correctly but for CA consumes CA and leaves the space to be eaten by the next specifier — which happens to be fine. The failure came one field earlier: %3s for the residue name matched MET and then %c read the space in column 21 rather than the chain in column 22, because the format has a two-column gap between residue name (18–20) and chain (22) that the sscanf format string did not account for.

The chain came out as ' ' for every residue, so all four chains of haemoglobin merged into one, and the quaternary contacts were computed within a single merged chain.

The repair is the one this chapter keeps repeating: parse by column offset, and let the field widths enforce the widths. A format defined by columns cannot be parsed by delimiters, and a sscanf format that does not encode the gaps is a delimiter parser in disguise.

docs.title: Sequence Encoding
docs.text:
Counting is the first real algorithm in this part, and I use it to introduce the idea that an encoding is a decision about memory. Plain characters, then composition, then k-mers, then 2-bit packing with its four-symbol limit, then a table that puts the three side by side. The bug at the end is an index that went negative, which is what happens when you trust an unsigned length.

Once a sequence is in memory as characters, every question about it is a counting question, and the cost of a counting question depends almost entirely on how the characters are laid out. This page compares three encodings that trade memory against speed against clarity.

docs.title: 1. Counting, the simple version
docs.text:
/* LAB 02-01  bio_encoding/gc_kmer.c */
size_t counts[26] = {0};
for (size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
    int idx = to_index(seq[i]);          /* 0..25 */
    if (idx >= 0) { ++counts[idx]; }
}

One array access per residue, and the array is 208 bytes — it stays in L1 for the whole loop. This is the right answer for residue composition, and it is fast enough that the encoding question does not arise.

static int to_index(char c) {
    if (c >= 'A' && c <= 'Z') { return c - 'A'; }
    if (c >= 'a' && c <= 'z') { return c - 'a'; }
    return -1;
}

The -1 is the whole of the validation. A parser that normalises case before this point makes the second branch unnecessary, and one that does not needs it. The defect this guards against is idx = c - 'A' computed on a lowercase character, which yields 32 for 'a' and writes eight elements past the end of a 26-element array — a stack buffer overflow that ASan catches immediately and that no amount of correct arithmetic hides.

docs.title: 2. Composition and GC fraction
docs.text:
size_t gc = counts['G' - 'A'] + counts['C' - 'A'];
size_t at = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < 20; ++i) { at += counts[residue_letter(i) - 'A']; }
double fraction = (double)gc / (double)at;

Two decisions in three lines.

The denominator is the count of residues, not the length of the sequence. A sequence containing * or an ambiguous code (X, B, Z) has a length larger than its residue count, and dividing by the length reports a GC fraction that is too small. The difference is small per sequence and systematic across a genome.

The numerator counts G and C only. Whether S (G or C) counts as GC is a convention question, and the convention must be stated in the code's comment rather than left to the reader.

(double)gc / (double)at casts both operands. Casting only the numerator also works, because the division promotes, but casting both makes the intent visible and prevents the integer-division defect from reappearing when someone edits the line.

docs.title: 3. k-mer counting
docs.text:
A k-mer is a substring of length k. For k = 3 there are 4³ = 64 possible DNA 3-mers and 20³ = 8000 possible protein 3-mers.

size_t kmer[64] = {0};        /* DNA, k = 3 */
for (size_t i = 0; i + 3 <= n; ++i) {
    int code = 16 * base_code(seq[i]) + 4 * base_code(seq[i + 1]) + base_code(seq[i + 2]);
    ++kmer[code];
}

The code is base-4 arithmetic: A=0, C=1, G=2, T=3 gives a unique index for every 3-mer, computed with two shifts and two additions. This is the same masking idea as chapter 10's bit fields, expressed in base 4.

The table is 512 bytes and in L1, so each iteration is one load and one store. The alternative — building a char[4] key and hashing it — costs a hash computation, a bucket walk, and a cache miss per k-mer, and is an order of magnitude slower for no benefit.

docs.title: 4. 2-bit packing
docs.text:
A DNA sequence of length n needs 2n bits: four bases, two bits each. For a 3 Gbp genome that is 750 MB instead of 3 GB, and for a 1 Mbp gene it is 250 KB instead of 1 MB.

/* LAB 02-02  bio_encoding/two_bit.c */
typedef struct {
    uint64_t *words;
    size_t n_bases;
} packed_seq;

static void set_base(packed_seq *s, size_t i, uint8_t code) {
    size_t w = i / 32, b = (i % 32) * 2;
    s->words[w] = (s->words[w] & ~(3ULL << b)) | ((uint64_t)code << b);
}

static uint8_t get_base(const packed_seq *s, size_t i) {
    size_t w = i / 32, b = (i % 32) * 2;
    return (uint8_t)((s->words[w] >> b) & 3ULL);
}

~(3ULL << b) clears the two bits before ORing the new value: read-modify-write, one shift, one mask, one or. Missing the clear turns set into an OR that can only add bits, which is the defect this lab is written to catch — set a base to G after A and read it back as G, then set it back to A and read G again.

The packing is worth it only when the sequence is large or is stored many times. For a single 76-residue protein it costs more in shifts than it saves in memory. The chapter's claim is not that packing is always better; it is that the trade is arithmetic and should be made deliberately.

docs.title: 5. The three encodings side by side
docs.text:
Encoding Memory per residue Access cost Where it wins char 1 byte one load parsing, everything except storage char + count table 1 byte + 208 B one load, one increment composition, k-mers 2-bit packed 0.25 byte two shifts, mask, load storage, transmission, cache

The count table is not an encoding of the sequence; it is a summary. Both are needed, for different questions, and a program that keeps only the summary cannot answer a question about position.

docs.title: 6. Field note: the index that went negative
docs.text:
The archived absCal.c computed an absolute value as:

int absF(int x) {
    if (x < 0) { return -x; }
    return x - 1;
}

For a non-negative input the function subtracts one. The function is named for absolute value and implements |x| for negatives and x - 1 for non-negatives — a branch that was probably a return x with a stray edit, and which no test caught because the only caller passed negative numbers.

The parallel in this chapter is the index computation: both are a one-character deviation in a branch that looks plausible. The defence is the same in both cases — a test with inputs on both sides of the branch, and a name that states the contract. absF promises |x|; the test that would have caught it is assert(absF(5) == 5).

docs.title: Structure Model
docs.text:
A structure is an ownership graph before it is a data structure, and the page is about who frees what. I draw the graph, then load with an error path that returns instead of exiting, then the queries a caller actually makes, then what the C++ version buys — destructors, mostly — then the guard that only guarded half the cases.

The C parser in stage 05 produced arrays and pointers. This stage produces the same data as an object graph, because the operations a reader actually wants — select a chain, find a residue, iterate over atoms — are all queries that a set of parallel arrays makes awkward and a hierarchy makes natural.

docs.title: 1. The ownership graph
docs.text:
Structure  owns  std::vector<Chain>
Chain      owns  std::vector<Residue>
Residue    owns  std::vector<Atom>
Atom       owns  nothing (plain data)

// LAB 08-01  bio_model/model.cpp
struct Atom {
    std::string name;
    char altloc{};
    char element[3]{};
    double x{}, y{}, z{};
    float occupancy{}, bfactor{};
};

class Residue {
public:
    char chain{};
    int seq{};
    char icode{};
    std::string name;
    std::vector<Atom> atoms;
};

class Chain {
public:
    char id{};
    std::vector<Residue> residues;
};

class Structure {
public:
    std::vector<Chain> chains;
    static std::optional<Structure> load(std::istream &in);
    std::size_t atom_count() const;
    const Residue *find(char chain, int seq, char icode) const;
};

Every level owns its children, so destruction is automatic and there is no free anywhere. The graph is a tree of vectors, which means the memory is contiguous at each level: a chain's residues are one block, a residue's atoms are one block. That is better for iteration than a linked structure and worse for insertion, which is the right trade for a file parsed once.

Atom holds a std::string name — five bytes of content in a 32-byte object on a 64-bit system. That is 27 bytes wasted per atom, 3000 atoms, 80 KB. The alternative is a char name[5], which costs the ability to compare with == but saves nothing else; for a structure of this size it is not worth the change. For a 100 000-atom model the decision flips.

docs.title: 2. Loading, and where the error goes
docs.text:
std::optional<Structure> Structure::load(std::istream &in) {
    Structure s;
    std::string line;
    while (std::getline(in, line)) {
        if (line.size() < 54) { continue; }              // too short to be ATOM
        if (line.compare(0, 6, "ATOM  ") != 0 &&
            line.compare(0, 6, "HETATM") != 0) { continue; }
        Atom a;
        a.name = trim(line.substr(12, 4));
        a.altloc = line[16];
        a.x = std::stod(line.substr(30, 8));
        a.y = std::stod(line.substr(38, 8));
        a.z = std::stod(line.substr(46, 8));
        s.attach(line[21], std::stoi(line.substr(22, 4)), line[26], a);
    }
    if (s.chains.empty()) { return std::nullopt; }
    return s;
}

substr with a column offset and a width is the C++ form of the fixed-column read, and it is the same discipline as the C page: the offset and the width come from the format table, not from a delimiter.

std::stod throws on malformed input, which is the wrong behaviour for a parser reading an untrusted file: one bad coordinate should reject the file, not unwind. The lab's version wraps the conversions in a try block at the load boundary and converts to std::nullopt, which is the explicit translation from "the library's error model" to "this parser's error model".

attach does the hierarchy work: find or create the chain, find or create the residue keyed by (seq, icode), then append the atom. In a vector-based graph this is a linear search per atom, which is O(1) amortised in practice because consecutive atoms belong to the same residue and the search starts at the end.

void Structure::attach(char chain_id, int seq, char icode, Atom a) {
    if (chains.empty() || chains.back().id != chain_id) { chains.push_back(Chain{chain_id}); }
    auto &c = chains.back();
    if (c.residues.empty() || c.residues.back().seq != seq || c.residues.back().icode != icode) {
        c.residues.push_back(Residue{chain_id, seq, icode, ""});
    }
    c.residues.back().atoms.push_back(std::move(a));
}

The assumption — atoms arrive grouped by chain and residue, in order — is a property of the PDB format and is stated in the comment. A parser that assumed it without stating it would be wrong for a file that interleaves chains, which some files do. The exercise is to feed the same structure in interleaved order and require the model to come out identical, which forces a real lookup rather than a back() check.

docs.title: 3. Queries
docs.text:
const Residue *Structure::find(char chain, int seq, char icode) const;
std::size_t Structure::atom_count() const;      // sum over chains and residues

The find is O(chains + residues) with the linear scan. For repeated lookups the lab adds an index:

std::unordered_map<key, const Residue *> index_;   // key is (chain, seq, icode) packed

The pointer is valid as long as the structure is not modified — which the model guarantees by keeping chains private after load and exposing only const access. This is the RAII argument applied to a query: the index borrows, the structure owns, and the borrow cannot outlive the owner because the owner cannot change.

docs.title: 4. What the C++ version buys
docs.text:
C version (stage 05) C++ model (stage 08) Allocation one malloc per level, cap fields automatic, growth amortised Destruction three free functions, called by the caller destructors Error path return code checked at every call one optional at the boundary Iteration index arithmetic on parallel arrays range-for over vectors Copy hand-written deep copy or none implicit, deep, correct

The last row is the one that matters most: a C structure with three owned pointers has no correct implicit copy, so every caller must either avoid copying or write a deep copy. The C++ version's default copy is deep and correct without being written.

docs.title: 5. Field note: the guard that was only half a guard
docs.text:
The archived CPU.h began:

#ifndef CPU_H
#pragma once
class CPU { ... };
#endif

There is no #define CPU_H. The guard therefore never becomes active, and #pragma once is doing all the work — which it does correctly on GCC, Clang and MSVC. The problem appears the day the file is included through a path that the compiler considers distinct (a symlink, a case-insensitive filesystem with two spellings, a build system that copies headers), because #pragma once is keyed on the file identity and the guard is keyed on the macro.

The file worked for a year, and the defect was one line: #define CPU_H after the #ifndef. The generalisation: a guard is a three-line construct and an incomplete one is worse than none, because it looks like protection. The repository's headers use both the macro and #pragma once; a one-line grep for #ifndef without a matching #define is what catches the half-written guard, and it belongs in review rather than in check.sh, because a header that no lab includes is still a header.

The same file had person.h with the constructor body inside the class — the defect the CMake chapter describes — so the project had two headers with two different incomplete mechanisms and neither was sufficient.

Then attempt the exercise in labs/bio/08_structure_model/, which requires the parser to produce identical results for a chain-interleaved file and a chain-ordered file, and to hold a residue index that stays valid through a full pass.

docs.title: Arrays and Layout
docs.text:
Two dimensions are a convenience, not a type: the memory is one row after another, and every surprise in this chapter comes from someone forgetting the arithmetic that maps an index pair to an offset. I go from one dimension to two, then to the parameter that silently loses a dimension, then to the write one past the end, and only then to the fixes — variable-length arrays, a struct that carries the row width, and an in-place transpose that shows why the loop bounds matter.

An array is the simplest object in C and the one whose layout is most often assumed rather than measured. This chapter measures it: one dimension, then two, then the parameter form that silently loses the second dimension.

docs.title: 1. One dimension, contiguously
docs.text:
int a[4] = {10, 20, 30, 40};
printf("%zu\n", sizeof a);              /* 16 */
printf("%td\n", &a[1] - &a[0]);         /* 1, in elements */

The four int objects are adjacent, with no gaps, because sizeof(int) is a multiple of alignof(int). Adjacency is guaranteed by the standard, and it is what makes pointer arithmetic over an array meaningful: a[i] is defined as *(a + i).

The one-past-the-end rule from the previous chapter has a second use here. a + 4 is a valid pointer value, which is why the idiomatic loop uses end rather than an index:

for (int *p = a; p != a + 4; ++p) { /* ... */ }

An index loop has the same semantics and one more opportunity to get the bound wrong. Neither form is faster after optimisation; the pointer form is chosen in this book because it makes the sentinel explicit.

docs.title: 2. Two dimensions are one dimension with arithmetic
docs.text:
int m[3][4] is not a matrix object. It is an array of three objects, each of which is an array of four int. The layout is row-major: the four elements of row 0, then the four of row 1, then row 2, with nothing between them.

offset of m[i][j] = i * 4 + j        (in elements)
address           = base + (i * 4 + j) * sizeof(int)

That formula is the entire content of two-dimensional indexing. It also explains why the column count must be known to compute an address: without it, i * 4 has no meaning.

/* LAB 04-01  arrays_layout/01_row_major_walk.c */
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void) {
    int m[2][3] = {{1, 2, 3}, {4, 5, 6}};
    for (int i = 0; i < 2; ++i) {
        for (int j = 0; j < 3; ++j) {
            printf("m[%d][%d]=%d  addr=%p\n", i, j, m[i][j], (void *)&m[i][j]);
        }
    }
    printf("row stride = %zu bytes\n", sizeof m[0]);
    return 0;
}

The printed addresses advance by 4 bytes within a row and by 12 bytes between rows — sizeof m[0], not sizeof(int). That number is the row stride, and it is the one to memorise: a row is an object, and the stride is its size.

docs.title: 3. The parameter that loses a dimension
docs.text:
void correct(int m[][3], int rows);     /* column count preserved */
void broken(int m[2][3]);               /* rewritten to int (*)[3] ... still fine */
void wrong(int **m);                    /* a completely different object */

void correct(int m[][3]) decays to int (*m)[3]: a pointer to an array of three int. Pointer arithmetic on it advances by 12 bytes, which is exactly one row. This is correct and it is why the column count appears in the parameter list.

void wrong(int **m) expects a pointer to a pointer. A int[2][3] array is not that: it is a contiguous block, and m[1] in the callee would read the second int of row 0 as if it were a pointer, then dereference it. The type system does not catch this; the resulting crash is several frames away from the call.

The rule: the inner dimension travels with the type, the outer dimension does not. Pass rows separately.

docs.title: 4. Out of bounds, and what actually happens
docs.text:
Array bounds are not checked. The standard defines the behaviour of an access outside the object as undefined, which in practice means one of four outcomes depending on what is adjacent in memory: the write lands in padding and nothing observable changes; it lands in another local and corrupts it; it lands on the return address and the function returns somewhere else; it lands on a guard page and the process dies.

/* LAB 04-02  arrays_layout/02_bounds_probe.c */
int m[2][3];
m[0][4] = 99;    /* still inside the array object: it is m[1][1] */
m[2][0] = 99;    /* outside the object: undefined */

The first line is the one worth pausing on. m[0][4] is out of bounds for row 0 but inside the overall object, and row-major arithmetic makes it exactly m[1][1]. Nothing complains, because nothing is wrong from the memory model's point of view — only from the programmer's, who intended a row.

The second line is a genuine out-of-bounds write, and AddressSanitizer reports it with the object's bounds:

ERROR: AddressSanitizer: stack-buffer-overflow on address 0x...
WRITE of size 4 at 0x... thread T0
    #0 0x... in unsafe_write .../code/c/04_arrays_layout/02_bounds_probe.c:26
    #1 0x... in main         .../code/c/04_arrays_layout/02_bounds_probe.c:42

The first frame names the function that performed the write and the exact line — a[LEN] = 0; — while the second names the call that allowed it. That pair is why every memory chapter in this book runs under a sanitizer: the report converts an undefined outcome into a named one, with a line number you can open.

docs.title: 5. Variable-length arrays
docs.text:
C99 permits an array whose length is a run-time value:

void scale(int n, double factor[n]) { /* ... */ }

The object lives in the caller's frame, so a large n is a stack overflow rather than a failed allocation. C11 makes the feature optional, MSVC does not implement it, and C++ does not have it at all. The book uses it exactly once, in a chapter that also shows the heap alternative, and the note on the page says so. For anything whose size is not known at compile time, the pattern that travels is malloc plus a length parameter.

docs.title: 6. Fixed-size rows as a type
docs.text:
The useful compromise between a raw pointer and a variable-length array is a pointer to a fixed-width row, because it keeps the stride in the type:

void print_row(const double (*row)[3]) {
    printf("%f %f %f\n", (*row)[0], (*row)[1], (*row)[2]);
}

The biology section uses exactly this form for coordinates: a position is a three-element array, and a chain of positions is a contiguous block whose stride is 3 * sizeof(double). Passing const double (*)[3] means the callee cannot accidentally treat the block as a flat array of double and lose the grouping.

docs.title: 7. Transposing in place
docs.text:
A square matrix can be transposed without a second buffer by swapping above and below the diagonal:

/* LAB 04-03  arrays_layout/03_transpose_inplace.c */
static void transpose(int n, int m[n][n]) {
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
        for (int j = i + 1; j < n; ++j) {
            int t = m[i][j];
            m[i][j] = m[j][i];
            m[j][i] = t;
        }
    }
}

The loop starts at j = i + 1, not j = 0. Starting at zero swaps each pair twice and returns the original matrix — a defect that is invisible for symmetric input and obvious for any other. 03_transpose_inplace.c asserts on an asymmetric case for that reason.

For a rectangular matrix the in-place swap is not possible, and the choice becomes row-major versus column-major traversal. The chapter on performance returns to this: walking a 1000 × 1000 matrix in the wrong order costs a cache miss per element, and the transpose itself is the standard fix.

docs.title: Bit-Level Programming
docs.text:
Bit work is where the type system and the hardware disagree most often, so I start with masks and fields and keep everything unsigned until the boundary. popcount comes in three versions because the difference between them is a measurement, not a preference, and the two-bit packing section is the same idea applied to a biological sequence. Bit order is stated as an assumption rather than left implicit, and the shift rules are the ones I have seen fail in code review.

Bit operations are the one part of C where the language's model of an integer as a bag of bits becomes explicit. They are also the part that the biology section leans on hardest: a nucleotide alphabet has four letters, which is exactly two bits, and packing a sequence into a word is the difference between 4 GB and 1 GB of memory for a genome-scale library.

docs.title: 1. Masks and fields
docs.text:
Extracting a field from a packed word is two operations: shift down to the low end, then mask off everything above the field.

/* LAB 10-01  bitops/01_mask_fields.c */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdint.h>

int main(void) {
    uint32_t word = 0xABCD1234u;
    unsigned low  = word & 0xFFu;              /* 0x34 */
    unsigned next = (word >> 8) & 0xFFu;       /* 0x12 */
    unsigned high = (word >> 24) & 0xFFu;      /* 0xAB */
    printf("%02X %02X %02X\n", low, next, high);
    return 0;
}

Writing a field is the mirror image: clear the field with an inverted mask, then OR in the shifted value.

word = (word & ~(0xFFu << 8)) | ((value & 0xFFu) << 8);

The value & 0xFFu before the shift is not decoration. Without it, a value larger than 255 carries bits into the neighbouring field, and the corruption is silent because the OR succeeds.

docs.title: 2. Unsigned is the type for bit work
docs.text:
Shifting and masking on signed integers runs into the rules from the previous chapter: left-shifting into the sign bit is UB, and right-shifting a negative value is implementation-defined. The fix is to do all bit work in uint32_t or uint64_t and cast only at the boundary.

uint32_t read_be_u32(const uint8_t *p) {
    return ((uint32_t)p[0] << 24) | ((uint32_t)p[1] << 16) |
           ((uint32_t)p[2] << 8)  |  (uint32_t)p[3];
}

That function is the portable way to read a big-endian word. Note the casts before the shifts: p[0] promotes to int, and (p[0]) << 24 with a byte above 127 shifts a value into the sign bit. Casting to uint32_t first makes the operation defined.

docs.title: 3. popcount, three ways
docs.text:
Counting set bits is the standard micro-benchmark for bit tricks, and the three implementations differ by a factor of about thirty.

/* LAB 10-02  bitops/02_popcount.c */
static unsigned count_naive(uint32_t v) {
    unsigned n = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < 32; ++i) { n += (v >> i) & 1u; }
    return n;
}

static unsigned count_kernighan(uint32_t v) {
    unsigned n = 0;
    while (v != 0u) { v &= v - 1u; ++n; }     /* clears the lowest set bit */
    return n;
}

Kernighan's loop runs once per set bit rather than once per bit position, so a sparse word is fast and a dense one is not. For a word with all 32 bits set it performs 32 iterations of a cheaper body; for a word with one bit set, one iteration.

Modern compilers recognise both idioms and may emit a single popcnt instruction when the target supports it (-mpopcnt on x86-64). The measurement in the lab compares naive, Kernighan, and __builtin_popcount, and the third is usually fastest because it is the instruction.

docs.title: 4. Packing a nucleotide sequence
docs.text:
The alphabet is A, C, G, T; the encoding is two bits per base; sixteen bases fit in one uint32_t.

/* LAB 10-03  bitops/03_two_bit_code.c */
static uint32_t pack16(const char *seq) {
    uint32_t word = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < 16; ++i) {
        uint32_t code = base_code(seq[i]);          /* 0..3 */
        word |= code << (2 * (15 - i));             /* first base in the high bits */
    }
    return word;
}

Two decisions are embedded in that loop and both matter later. Placing the first base in the high bits makes the packed word print in sequence order when read left to right, which is what makes debugging bearable. Encoding A as 0 rather than 1 makes a word of all A equal to zero, which makes a zeroed buffer a valid sequence rather than a sentinel.

The unpacking function is the inverse, and the pair is what the encoding chapter of the biology section benchmarks: 3 billion bases in one byte-per-base representation is 3 GB, and in two-bit packing it is 750 MB — which is the difference between a library that fits in memory and one that does not.

docs.title: 5. Bit order: the assumption to state
docs.text:
The loop above assumes that base i of the sequence is stored in bits 2(15−i), i.e. the first base is the most significant pair. That is a choice, and every file format that stores packed sequence makes the same choice or the opposite one. Nothing in C determines it; the code declares it, and the parser must agree.

The failure mode when the two disagree is not a crash. It is a decoded sequence that is reversed or shuffled, which looks like a biology problem and is a documentation problem. This is why 03_two_bit_code.c carries a round-trip assertion: pack, unpack, compare to the original string.

docs.title: 6. Shifts that are defined
docs.text: Expression Defined? Note 1u << 31 Yes The top bit of an unsigned word 1 << 31 No Signed, so it overflows x >> 3 for negative x Implementation-defined GCC and MSVC both do arithmetic shift x << 32 on uint32_t No Shift count must be < width (uint32_t)x << 31 Yes Cast first, then shift

docs.title: 7. Field note: the mask that forgot the range
docs.text:
An early version of the packing routine wrote the base code without masking the input:

word |= (code << shift);       /* code came from a table lookup */

The table was indexed by the character, and an unexpected character — a N for an unknown base — landed outside the table and produced a code of 4. Shifting 4 into a two-bit field carried into the neighbouring base, so a single ambiguous base silently corrupted two residues of the packed sequence.

The repair was two lines: map unknown characters to a separate N bitmask outside the packed word, and mask every code with & 3u before shifting. The general lesson is that a packed word has no bounds checking of its own; the width of the field exists only in the mask, and a missing mask is a write into the next field.

docs.text:

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
C has no exceptions, so error handling is a design decision made in public: which layer reports, which layer translates, and which layer decides. I start with three layers rather than one, then errno and what it is not, then the goto cleanup pattern that makes partial construction safe. Return-code conventions come next, because a convention nobody wrote down is a convention nobody follows, and the gdb section exists because a failure that crashes and a failure that returns a wrong value are read differently.

C has no exceptions, so every failure travels as a value. The quality of a program is largely the quality of that travel: whether the failure is detectable, whether it carries a reason, whether the cleanup happens, and whether the caller is forced to acknowledge it.

docs.title: 1. Three layers, not one
docs.text:
Mixing these up is the most common error-handling defect:

Layer Mechanism Cost when it fires Correct use Programmer error assert abort An invariant that must hold if the code is correct Expected failure return code a branch A file that is missing, a parse that fails Impossible state abort() / __builtin_unreachable abort A switch arm that cannot be reached

An assert on user input is a category error: it converts a malformed file into a crash, which is exactly what the security page argues against. A return code on an invariant is also a category error, because the branches pile up and are never tested.

#include "craft_assert.h"

CRAFT_ASSERT(index >= 0 && index < n);   /* internal invariant */

In release builds assert may compile to nothing (if NDEBUG is defined), so an assert must never guard a side effect. The macro above is used in the labs precisely because it is always active: the checks in a lab are part of the lab.

docs.title: 2. errno, and what it is not
docs.text:
errno is a thread-local integer that library functions set on failure. It is not cleared on success, so it is only meaningful immediately after a call that reported failure.

/* LAB 16-01  error_handling/01_errno_chain.c */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <errno.h>
#include <string.h>

int main(void) {
    FILE *fp = fopen("missing.txt", "r");
    if (fp == NULL) {
        int saved = errno;                       /* copy before anything else */
        fprintf(stderr, "fopen failed: %s\n", strerror(saved));
        return saved;
    }
    fclose(fp);
    return 0;
}

The copy into saved is not paranoia. Any subsequent library call may overwrite errno, including fprintf itself, so the value must be read before the error message is built. This is the reason the diagnostic is captured first and formatted second.

strerror is not thread-safe on all platforms (strerror_r is the replacement), and it returns a pointer to a static buffer. In a single-threaded program that is fine; in the parallel lab it is not.

docs.title: 3. The goto cleanup pattern
docs.text:
The one place goto is standard practice in C is unwinding a partially constructed resource set:

/* LAB 16-02  error_handling/02_cleanup_goto.c */
int load(const char *path, struct dataset *out) {
    int rc = -1;
    FILE *fp = NULL;
    char *buf = NULL;
    struct record *records = NULL;

    fp = fopen(path, "rb");
    if (fp == NULL) { goto done; }

    buf = craft_read_file(path, NULL);
    if (buf == NULL) { goto done; }

    records = parse_records(buf, &out->count);
    if (records == NULL) { goto done; }

    out->items = records;
    rc = 0;

done:
    free(records);      /* free(NULL) is a no-op */
    free(buf);
    if (fp != NULL) { fclose(fp); }
    return rc;
}

Three properties make this correct. Every acquisition is initialised to NULL or zero, so the cleanup path is valid at every point. The cleanup is written once, not at each failure point. And the success path falls through the same cleanup, so no resource is released in one path and forgotten in another.

The alternative — a cleanup block per failure — duplicates the release order in each branch, and the duplication is where the leaks live.

docs.title: 4. Return-code conventions
docs.text:
Two conventions are common, and mixing them in one codebase is a defect waiting:

/* Convention A: 0 is success, negative is a category */
int rc = parse_file(path);        /* 0 ok, -1 io, -2 format */

/* Convention B: 0 is success, errno value on failure */
int rc = parse_file(path);        /* 0 ok, otherwise an errno value */

This book uses A inside the library (small negative categories, documented per function) and B at the boundary with the C library. A function that returns an errno value must document that the value is meaningful only when the return is nonzero, and must not confuse -1 with EPERM on platforms where they differ.

Whatever the convention, it must be in the header comment. A function whose failure code is undocumented is a function the caller will check wrongly — usually by comparing against 0 and ignoring the value, which loses the reason and the log line that would have explained it.

docs.title: 5. Reading a failure in gdb
docs.text:
Errors that produce a wrong value are found by reading code; errors that crash are found by reading a core. A short session, on a two-function toy (main.c calling load.c) rather than on a file from code/, because the frame layout is the lesson and a toy keeps it short:

(gdb) run
Program received signal SIGSEGV, Segmentation fault.
0x00005555555551a9 in load (path=0x0, out=0x7fffffffdcd0) at load.c:14
14          FILE *fp = fopen(path, "rb");
(gdb) bt
#0  load (path=0x0, out=...) at load.c:14
#1  main () at main.c:9
(gdb) p path
$1 = (const char *) 0x0

The frame line already answers the question: path=0x0. The call site passed NULL, and the function did not check. The fix is one line at the top of load, and the general rule is that every pointer parameter is either documented as non-null or checked.

A crash inside a library function with a plausible argument is usually an earlier corruption: free on an already-freed pointer, or a write past the end of a buffer. The sanitiser chapters exist because the crash site and the defect site are rarely the same.

docs.title: 6. Field note: the error that was reported as success
docs.text:
A batch script called a parsing function, checked if (rc < 0), logged, and continued. The function returned 1 for a malformed record — a positive value, so the check did not fire, and the caller proceeded with a partially filled structure. Downstream, a missing residue was interpreted as a gap, and the geometry step produced a plausible wrong distance.

The contract had said "nonzero on failure". The caller had implemented "negative on failure". Both were internally consistent and mutually incompatible, which is the definition of an undocumented interface.

The repair was to make the contract explicit in the header — Returns 0 on success, a positive error code otherwise — and to change the check to if (rc != 0). The lesson belongs here rather than in a review checklist: a return code is only as good as the sentence that documents it.

docs.title: Files and Streams
docs.text:
I wrote a program that lost its last line for a month, and this chapter is the explanation. Open modes come first because the wrong one truncates the file, then line reading without the feof trap, then block reads, then seeking and what it does to the buffer. Buffering gets its own section because a write that never reached the disk is the failure that survives a successful exit, and the Field Note is exactly that truncation.

A FILE * is a buffered handle, not a file descriptor and not a path. Almost every file defect comes from confusing the three: assuming a read reached the disk, assuming a write failed visibly, or assuming the end of the file is detectable before the next read.

docs.title: 1. Open modes, and the one that surprises
docs.text:
Mode Read Write If exists If missing "r" yes no opens fails "w" no yes truncates creates "a" no append appends creates "r+" yes yes opens fails "rb", "wb" binary variants — — —

"w" truncates on open, before a single byte is written. A program that opens a file for writing, fails partway through, and exits leaves a truncated file and no indication that the original content is gone. The defensive pattern is to write to a temporary name and rename on success, which is what the FASTA writer in the biology section does.

"b" has no effect on POSIX systems; on Windows it suppresses the CRLF translation. The book always uses "rb" and "wb" explicitly, because a PDB file read in text mode on Windows has its line endings rewritten and its column offsets shifted by nothing — which is correct — while a binary trajectory read in text mode is corrupted.

docs.title: 2. Reading lines without the feof trap
docs.text:
/* LAB 12-01  files_streams/01_line_reader.c */
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void) {
    FILE *fp = fopen("sample.txt", "r");
    if (fp == NULL) { return 1; }

    char line[256];
    int count = 0;
    while (fgets(line, sizeof line, fp) != NULL) {
        ++count;
    }
    printf("lines: %d\n", count);
    fclose(fp);
    return 0;
}

The loop condition tests the return value of fgets, not feof(fp). The difference is one extra iteration: feof only becomes true after a read has failed, so while (!feof(fp)) always processes a final empty line. The condition is the classic C file bug, and it is invisible unless the file has a trailing newline or the processing has side effects.

Why the extra iteration happens: fgets reads until the newline, returns the string, and the stream still has not observed EOF. The next call reads zero bytes, sets the EOF flag, and returns NULL — but by then the loop has already run once with stale data if the condition was feof.

Truncation is the other case to handle. When a line is longer than the buffer, fgets returns the first part without a newline. Detecting it is the same check as before:

size_t len = strlen(line);
if (len > 0 && line[len - 1] != '\n' && !feof(fp)) {
    /* the line was truncated: consume or report */
}

docs.title: 3. Reading a block
docs.text:
For binary data, fread is the primitive and its return value is a count of items, not bytes:

double coords[3];
size_t got = fread(coords, sizeof coords[0], 3, fp);
if (got != 3) { /* short read: file ended or an error occurred */ }

A short read is not necessarily an error. If the file legitimately ends mid-record, got is smaller and the caller must decide whether that is a valid truncation or corruption. Checking ferror(fp) distinguishes the two: a nonzero result means the stream itself failed, while feof(fp) means the data simply ran out. The habit is to check both after a short read, not just the count.

docs.title: 4. Seeking, and what it does to the buffer
docs.text:
fseek and ftell manipulate a position measured in bytes, and both flush or discard buffered data as needed. Three rules keep them predictable:

fseek(fp, 0, SEEK_SET);            /* rewind: next read starts at byte 0 */
long pos = ftell(fp);              /* the current byte offset */
fseek(fp, 20L, SEEK_CUR);          /* advance 20 bytes from here */

The offset type is long, which is 4 bytes on Windows even in 64-bit builds; a file over 2 GB cannot be addressed portably with ftell. fgetpos/fsetpos use an opaque type and are the portable alternative. For the coordinate files in this book, which are under 100 MB, long is adequate and the note is a footnote rather than a design constraint.

Seeking in a file opened for writing is more delicate: the standard requires a flush between a write and a seek, and fseek does that implicitly. Mixing fread and fwrite on the same handle without an intervening seek is undefined.

docs.title: 5. Buffering, and the write that never reached the disk
docs.text:
fwrite returns when the data is in the stream's buffer, not on the disk. A program that writes, then calls _exit, loses the buffer. fclose flushes, and fflush flushes explicitly.

if (fwrite(buf, 1, len, fp) != len) { /* handle */ }
if (fflush(fp) != 0) { /* the flush failed: the write is not durable */ }
if (fclose(fp) != 0) { /* the final flush failed */ }

fclose returning nonzero is the case people skip, and it is the one that matters for durability: the data may have been buffered successfully and the final write may still have failed. A writer that ignores the return value reports success for a file that was never written.

The cost of buffering is why the line reader above is fast: it performs one read system call per buffer, not per line. It is also why a program that reads a file, writes to another, and never closes either can produce a target file with content that appears only when the process exits.

docs.title: 6. Error checking, at the right moment
docs.text:
Every stream function can fail, and the failure is reported at the point of the call, not at the point where the data is used. The pattern that works is to check the return of each call in the direction of data flow:

FILE *fp = fopen(path, "rb");
if (fp == NULL) { perror(path); return -1; }

char *buf = craft_read_file(path, &len);   /* helpers in code/include */
...
int failed = (fclose(fp) != 0);
return failed ? -1 : 0;

perror prints the reason from errno with the caller's string as a prefix, which is the least-effort diagnostic and the one to use before a real logging system exists. Chapter 16 turns this into a return-code contract.

docs.title: 7. Field note: the truncation nobody noticed
docs.text:
A parser wrote its result with "w" and a single fwrite, then checked the return value of the write. The write succeeded; the flush inside fclose failed because the disk was full. The program exited zero, and the output file was shorter than expected by exactly the amount that did not fit.

The fix had two parts: check fclose, and write to a temporary file then rename. The second part is what makes the failure atomic — a reader either sees the previous complete file or the new complete file, never a truncated one.

The general lesson belongs to this chapter rather than to error handling: a flushed write is a claim about durability, and only the last call in the chain can make that claim.

docs.title: Continue
docs.text:

  • Error Handling formalises the return-code contract used above.
  • FASTA applies the line reader to a format whose records span two lines.

docs.title: Function Pointers and Callbacks
docs.text:
The type of a function is the part people skip, so I write it out — return type, parameter list, and the parentheses that make the pointer a pointer. Then the comparator, because qsort is where most readers meet a function pointer and where the subtraction overflow lives, then a dispatch table, then a callback that needs context. The cost section is short: an indirect call is a load and a branch, and the branch predictor decides whether you notice.

A function has an address. Storing that address in a variable turns a fixed call into a choice made at run time, which is how C expresses dispatch, comparators, and callbacks without any object system. Two thirds of the C++ section is an elaboration of this idea, so it is worth doing carefully in C first.

docs.title: 1. The type of a function
docs.text:
int add(int a, int b);
int (*op)(int, int) = add;      /* the name decays to a pointer */
printf("%d\n", op(2, 3));

The declaration reads right to left: op is a pointer to a function taking two int and returning int. The parentheses around *op are required because int *op(int, int) would declare a function returning int *, which is a different thing — the ambiguity the previous chapter's table listed.

A typedef removes the noise and is what every real codebase uses:

typedef int (*binary_op)(int, int);
binary_op table[] = { add, sub, mul };

docs.title: 2. Comparators, and the subtraction that overflows
docs.text:
qsort is the standard library's demonstration of a callback:

/* LAB 11-01  callbacks/01_qsort_words.c */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>

static int by_length(const void *a, const void *b) {
    const char *const *sa = a;
    const char *const *sb = b;
    size_t la = strlen(*sa), lb = strlen(*sb);
    return (la > lb) - (la < lb);      /* not la - lb */
}

The comparator returns a negative, zero, or positive value; qsort only uses the sign. Writing la - lb on size_t returns an unsigned value that is never negative after conversion to int, so the comparator only ever reports "greater" or "equal" — and the sort produces a confidently wrong order. The idiomatic (a > b) - (a < b) produces exactly −1, 0, or 1 with no overflow, for any ordered type.

The cast from const void * to const char *const * is the one place where a generic interface forces a type pun. It is legal because qsort passes pointers to the array elements, and the array elements are const char *. The two-level const is not decoration: it says the comparator may not modify the pointers it receives.

docs.title: 3. A dispatch table
docs.text:
A table of function pointers replaces a chain of if on a command string:

/* LAB 11-02  callbacks/02_dispatch_table.c */
typedef int (*command_fn)(const char *arg);

struct command {
    const char *name;
    command_fn  fn;
    const char *help;
};

static const struct command commands[] = {
    {"len",   cmd_len,   "print the length of the argument"},
    {"rev",   cmd_rev,   "print the argument reversed"},
    {"count", cmd_count, "count vowels in the argument"},
};

Lookup is a linear scan over a table that is sorted by name at compile time — or a binary search when the table grows. The advantage over a switch is that the table is data: it can be printed as help, generated, or extended in one place without touching the dispatcher.

The help field is the part that makes this pattern worth teaching. A dispatch table that carries its own documentation can produce --help output without a second list to keep in sync, and the sync failure is otherwise inevitable.

docs.title: 4. Callbacks with context
docs.text:
A bare function pointer cannot carry state. The standard solution is a void * context passed alongside:

typedef void (*visitor_fn)(void *context, const char *key, int value);

static void for_each(const struct map *m, visitor_fn visit, void *context) {
    for (size_t i = 0; i < m->len; ++i) {
        visit(context, m->items[i].key, m->items[i].value);
    }
}

The caller supplies a struct of its own and casts it back inside the callback. This is type-erasure in C: the library does not know what the context is, and the callback does. The alternative — a global variable — works for exactly one callback at a time and fails the moment two are registered, which is the defect that makes this pattern necessary rather than optional.

void * conversion to and from a function pointer is not guaranteed by ISO C, which permits the two to have different representations. POSIX guarantees it for object and function pointers on its platforms, and in practice every mainstream compiler allows it. Code that needs to be strictly conforming stores the function pointer in a union of the two types and documents the assumption.

docs.title: 5. What a function pointer costs
docs.text:
An indirect call cannot be inlined, so the compiler cannot see through it. On a hot loop this costs more than the call itself: the branch predictor has to guess a target that changes, and the call is not vectorised.

The measurement is worth doing once. A loop calling a function pointer that is never reassigned inside the loop is often devirtualised by the compiler — it can prove the target is constant — and then the cost disappears. A loop whose target changes per iteration cannot be, and the difference is typically a factor of two to five on a tight body.

This is the reason the C++ virtual-call chapter measures before and after devirtualisation, and the reason the dispatch table above is acceptable for commands (called once per user action) and unacceptable for an inner loop over atoms.

docs.title: 6. Field note: the comparator that sorted nothing
docs.text:
An early version of a student project passed qsort a comparator that returned a->score - b->score, where score was an int between 0 and 100. That is safe for those values. When the field was later widened to a full range and one record held a negative score, the subtraction overflowed on the negative end, and qsort produced a partially ordered array — sorted enough that a visual check passed, wrong enough that a binary search failed.

The repair was the comparison form above. The lesson is worth generalising: a comparator's contract is a sign, and a subtraction only supplies a sign when the range makes it safe. The contract does not promise a range, so the comparator cannot assume one.

docs.text:

  • STL Algorithms supplies comparators and predicates that do not require a context pointer.

docs.title: The Heap
docs.text:
Heap defects share a property that makes them hard: nothing crashes at the moment of the mistake. I start with the two lifetimes a block has — allocated, then owned — because malloc gives you a block, realloc may move it, and the owner is whoever is willing to free it. The tools come after that, not before, because an ASan report only reads clearly when you already know which of the three errors you are looking at. Fragmentation is one section, not a chapter, because the fix is an arena, not a different allocator.

The stack gives every object a lifetime tied to a function call. The heap exists for the objects that outlive their frame, and it replaces the frame's automatic cleanup with an obligation: every block has exactly one owner, and that owner must free it exactly once.

That sentence is the whole chapter. Everything else is the consequence of violating it.

docs.title: 1. Two allocations, two lifetimes
docs.text:
void stack_object(void)   { int a[4];       }   /* dies at the closing brace */
void heap_object(void)    { int *p = malloc(4 * sizeof *p); }  /* survives until free */

The stack object is reclaimed by a single instruction when the function returns. The heap block is reclaimed only when free is called on the exact pointer that malloc returned. If that call never happens, the block is lost to the process for its entire lifetime — and the process's lifetime is not the function's.

The heap also removes the size limit that the stack imposes. A frame of 8 MB is generous for a 100 × 100 matrix and hopeless for a 10,000 × 10,000 one, which is 800 MB. That is why every structure in the biology section whose count is not known at parse time is heap-allocated.

docs.title: 2. malloc returns a block, not an array
docs.text:
int *p = malloc(n * sizeof *p);
if (p == NULL) { /* allocation failed: return an error, do not proceed */ }

Three details in that line are load-bearing.

sizeof *p rather than sizeof(int): the idiom cannot drift from the pointer's type, and the drift is the defect in the previous chapter's field note.

The multiplication is not checked. n * sizeof *p overflows size_t when n exceeds SIZE_MAX / sizeof *p, and the result is a small allocation followed by writes past its end. The defensive form is a check before the call:

if (n > SIZE_MAX / sizeof *p) { return NULL; }

malloc can return NULL, and every caller must handle it. A program that assumes success works until the machine is under memory pressure, which is exactly when the failure is least welcome.

malloc does not initialise. calloc zeroes, and is the right choice when a zero value is meaningless but harmless; malloc plus explicit initialisation is the right choice when every field will be written anyway.

docs.title: 3. realloc may move the block
docs.text:
/* LAB 07-01  heap/01_growth_trace.c */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

int main(void) {
    size_t cap = 4, len = 0;
    int *data = malloc(cap * sizeof *data);
    if (data == NULL) { return 1; }

    for (int i = 0; i < 12; ++i) {
        if (len == cap) {
            size_t next = cap * 2;
            int *grown = realloc(data, next * sizeof *grown);
            if (grown == NULL) { free(data); return 1; }
            data = grown;
            cap = next;
            printf("realloc -> capacity %zu\n", cap);
        }
        data[len++] = i;
    }

    printf("final: len=%zu cap=%zu\n", len, cap);
    free(data);
    return 0;
}

realloc returns a pointer that may differ from the argument. When the allocator cannot extend the block in place, it copies the contents to a new block and frees the old one. The consequence is the most common heap defect in student code:

data = realloc(data, next);   /* if realloc fails, data is leaked and NULL is lost */

The two-statement form above exists because realloc returning NULL leaves the original block intact. Assigning directly to data overwrites the only pointer to it with NULL, leaking the block and losing the handle at the same time. The temporary is not defensive style; it is the only correct form.

The growth trace also shows the amortised argument: doubling from 4 gives capacities 8, 16, 32, so twelve insertions trigger three reallocations rather than twelve. Growing by a constant instead makes the total cost quadratic, which is the subject of the dynamic-array discussion in the C++ section.

docs.title: 4. Ownership: one block, one owner
docs.text:
There is no reference counting in C and no way to ask the allocator who owns a block. Ownership is a convention the code must enforce, and the convention that works is the simplest one: exactly one pointer is responsible for freeing, every other pointer is a borrow whose lifetime is documented.

struct buffer {
    char  *data;      /* owned */
    size_t len;
};

void buffer_free(struct buffer *b) {
    free(b->data);    /* the one place that frees it */
    b->data = NULL;   /* a second call is now harmless */
    b->len = 0;
}

Setting the pointer to NULL after freeing converts a double free from undefined behaviour into a defined no-op, because free(NULL) is specified to do nothing. It does not fix a dangling pointer held elsewhere — that copy still points at freed memory — but it removes the most common second free, which is the one through the same handle.

docs.title: 5. What the tools report
docs.text:
AddressSanitizer distinguishes three heap errors, and the distinction is worth reading carefully:

ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow     # wrote past the block
ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-use-after-free      # read or wrote after free
ERROR: LeakSanitizer: detected memory leaks       # block never freed

The first two abort at the offending instruction. The third is reported at process exit, because "never freed" is only knowable once nothing else can free it. LeakSanitizer is part of ASan on Linux and runs by default; the report lists the allocation site and the size of each leaked block, which is enough to find the missing free without a debugger.

Valgrind reports the same three categories with more detail and roughly twenty times the slowdown. It is the fallback when ASan cannot run — inside some containers, or when the leak is in a library compiled without instrumentation.

docs.title: 6. Fragmentation, briefly
docs.text:
Freeing blocks in a different order than they were allocated leaves holes. A long-running process that allocates and frees blocks of varying size eventually has plenty of total free memory and no contiguous region large enough for the next request. This is external fragmentation, and no standard C facility addresses it.

The two practical mitigations are pool allocation (one large block carved into fixed-size slots, freed all at once) and arena reset (allocate everything, then discard the whole arena). Both appear in real parsers, including the one behind Protein Phaser: structures are parsed into a single arena and released in one call, so a 30,000-atom file costs one allocation and one free rather than 30,000 of each.

docs.title: 7. Field note: the leak that looked like a design
docs.text:
The mocal.c defect from the previous chapter has a second half that belongs here. After the ten inner blocks were allocated and the outer block freed, the program printed all ten strings correctly. It leaked every byte and looked, from the output, entirely healthy.

That is the shape of most leaks: no symptom, no crash, and a slow growth in resident memory that nobody measures until the process is killed by the OOM reaper. The only reliable detector is the tool, run routinely rather than when a problem is suspected.

The habit worth forming is smaller than the tool: every malloc in a function should have a matching free visible in the same function, or a comment naming the function that will free it. A block whose owner is not identifiable within the function that allocated it is a leak waiting for a branch that returns early.

docs.text:

docs.title: Linked Structures
docs.text:
A linked list is two fields and one invariant, and the invariant is the whole difficulty. I begin with the node and the two operations that matter, then reversal with the invariant written down, because the three-pointer dance is only confusing when the invariant is implicit. Teardown follows the same shape, which is the point; then cycles and the two-speed walk; then a ring buffer, which is the version of the structure that does not allocate per element. The Field Note is a free that broke the list by freeing the wrong node.

A linked list is the smallest structure whose shape is not implied by its type. The nodes are separate heap blocks, the links are pointers, and every operation is a small exercise in ownership. It is also the standard interview question, which means most readers have memorised the reversal loop without ever seeing why it works.

docs.title: 1. The node, and the two operations that matter
docs.text:
struct node {
    int          value;
    struct node *next;
};

Insertion at the front is three lines and cannot fail if the allocation succeeded:

/* LAB 15-01  linked_structures/01_list_reverse.c */
static struct node *push_front(struct node *head, int value) {
    struct node *n = malloc(sizeof *n);
    if (n == NULL) { return head; }        /* caller checks for no change */
    n->value = value;
    n->next = head;
    return n;
}

The function returns the new head rather than modifying the caller's variable, because C has no references. The caller must assign: head = push_front(head, 3);. A caller that forgets the assignment loses the new node, which then leaks — the pointer to it existed only inside the function.

Insertion at the back requires walking to the end, which is O(n) per insertion unless the list keeps a tail pointer. That is the first design decision this chapter makes: a struct list { struct node *head, *tail; } costs eight bytes and turns push_back into O(1).

docs.title: 2. Reversal, with the invariant made visible
docs.text:
static struct node *reverse(struct node *head) {
    struct node *prev = NULL;
    struct node *cur  = head;
    while (cur != NULL) {
        struct node *next = cur->next;   /* save before overwriting */
        cur->next = prev;                /* reverse the link */
        prev = cur;                      /* advance prev */
        cur  = next;                     /* advance cur */
    }
    return prev;
}

Three pointers, four assignments, and one invariant: at the top of each iteration, prev is the fully reversed prefix and cur is the untouched remainder. The next save is not optional; without it, cur->next = prev destroys the only pointer to the rest of the list, and the loop walks into the reversed part, producing a cycle.

The reference program asserts on a five-node list: it pushes 1 to 5, checks the head is 5, reverses once and checks the head is 1 with a length of 5, then reverses again and checks 5 4. The one-node list is the case it does not cover, and it is where implementations that return head instead of prev fail, because after the loop head still points at the node whose next is now NULL — which is correct for one node and wrong for any longer list. Adding that case is the first thing to do after copying the file.

docs.title: 3. Teardown, in the right order
docs.text:
static void free_list(struct node *head) {
    while (head != NULL) {
        struct node *next = head->next;
        free(head);
        head = next;
    }
}

The saved next is the same idea as in the reversal loop: freeing head invalidates head->next, so the next pointer must be copied first. A teardown that writes free(head); head = head->next; reads freed memory, which AddressSanitizer reports as a heap-use-after-free at the second line.

Recursive teardown is also possible and is a trap for long lists: a 100,000-node list recurses 100,000 times and overflows the stack, which is the failure from chapter 2 applied to a data structure.

docs.title: 4. Cycles, and the two-speed walk
docs.text:
A list that accidentally points back into itself has no end, so every traversal loops forever. Detecting it without extra memory uses two pointers advancing at different speeds:

static int has_cycle(const struct node *head) {
    const struct node *slow = head;
    const struct node *fast = head;
    while (fast != NULL && fast->next != NULL) {
        slow = slow->next;
        fast = fast->next->next;
        if (slow == fast) { return 1; }
    }
    return 0;
}

If there is a cycle, the fast pointer enters it first and the slow pointer eventually catches up from behind; if there is none, the fast pointer reaches NULL. The proof is short and worth reading once, because the technique generalises to any "detect repetition in a finite state space" problem.

The cycle itself is usually created by the reversal defect above, or by a node inserted twice. Both are ownership errors: a node with two predecessors is a node that will be freed twice or traversed twice.

docs.title: 5. A ring buffer, without allocation per element
docs.text:
A different shape worth knowing before the C++ containers: a fixed-size array with a head index and a count, wrapping by modulo.

/* LAB 15-02  linked_structures/02_ring_buffer.c */
struct ring {
    int   data[8];
    size_t head;
    size_t count;
};

static int ring_push(struct ring *r, int v) {
    if (r->count == 8) { return -1; }               /* full */
    r->data[(r->head + r->count) % 8] = v;
    ++r->count;
    return 0;
}

static int ring_pop(struct ring *r, int *out) {
    if (r->count == 0) { return -1; }               /* empty */
    *out = r->data[r->head];
    r->head = (r->head + 1) % 8;
    --r->count;
    return 0;
}

The modulo is the only subtle part. Writing (head + count) % 8 rather than head + count avoids growing the index without bound, and the count distinguishes full from empty — without it, head == tail means both, which is the classic ambiguity in a naive ring.

The ring buffer is the right structure when the size is bounded and known, which is the case for the sliding windows in the biology section: a contact-map builder keeps the last k residues in a ring rather than allocating a deque.

docs.title: 6. Field note: the free that broke the list
docs.text:
An early implementation freed the list in a loop that read the next pointer after freeing the current node:

while (p != NULL) {
    free(p);
    p = p->next;        /* reads freed memory */
}

On the developer's machine this usually worked, because the allocator had not yet reused the block and the first eight bytes still held the old next value. Under AddressSanitizer it failed immediately; under a different allocator it corrupted a random node and crashed later.

The repair is the two-line form above. The lesson is broader than the fix: a use-after-free that happens to work is more dangerous than one that crashes, because it survives long enough to be copied into other code.

docs.title: Objects in Memory
docs.text:
I start with a value that looks like a typo: sizeof('a') is 4 on a C compiler and 1 in C++. That single number is the shortest proof that the object model, not the syntax, is what you are learning. From there I measure widths, then two's complement, then endianness, and only then alignment, because each section depends on the previous measurement rather than on a definition. By the end you should be able to predict a struct's size before printing it.

A C program does not manipulate values. It manipulates regions of memory that have been given a name, a width and an alignment, and the value is whatever those bytes happen to spell. Every later chapter depends on this picture: the stack is a region, the heap is a region, a struct is a region with a layout, a pointer is an integer holding an address inside some region.

The chapter opens with an anomaly that most readers have already seen without noticing.

docs.title: 1. sizeof('a') is not 1
docs.text:
printf("%zu\n", sizeof('a'));

In C this prints 4. In C++ the same expression prints 1. Nothing is broken: in C, a character literal has type int, not char, because the language promotes it before any operator sees it. In C++, a character literal has type char. The two languages disagree about the width of the smallest thing you can write.

This is the first lesson of the section, and it is not about characters. It is about the difference between the value a literal denotes and the object the compiler creates for it. Asking "how big is 'a'" is the wrong question; the right question is "what type did the compiler give this expression, and how many bytes does that type occupy on this target".

docs.title: 2. The widths, measured
docs.text:
The only trustworthy source for widths is the compiler on the target machine. Anything else is a table someone copied from a book written for a different platform.

/* LAB 01-01  objects_in_memory/01_sizeof_table.c */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdint.h>
#include <stddef.h>

int main(void) {
    printf("char        %zu\n", sizeof(char));
    printf("short       %zu\n", sizeof(short));
    printf("int         %zu\n", sizeof(int));
    printf("long        %zu\n", sizeof(long));
    printf("long long   %zu\n", sizeof(long long));
    printf("float       %zu\n", sizeof(float));
    printf("double      %zu\n", sizeof(double));
    printf("pointer     %zu\n", sizeof(void *));
    printf("size_t      %zu\n", sizeof(size_t));
    printf("'a'         %zu\n", sizeof('a'));
    return 0;
}

On x86-64 Linux with GCC the output is:

char        1
short       2
int         4
long        8
long long   8
float       4
double      8
pointer     8
size_t      8
'a'         4

On x86-64 Windows with MSVC the first four lines are identical and the fifth is the one that moves: long is 4 bytes, not 8. That difference is not a bug in either compiler. The C standard fixes only that sizeof(char) == 1 and that sizeof(short) <= sizeof(int) <= sizeof(long) <= sizeof(long long); everything else is the platform's choice. This is why the book uses int32_t and int64_t in the biology chapters, where a coordinate serialized on one machine is read on another.

sizeof is an operator, not a function call. Its result is size_t, an unsigned type, which is the reason printf("%zu", ...) is used above and printf("%d") would be a conversion warning — one the first chapter already taught you to read.

docs.title: 3. Two's complement, and the value that has no negation
docs.text:
Signed integers are stored in two's complement: the top bit carries a negative weight, and the rest carry positive weights. For a 32-bit int, the representable range is −2 147 483 648 to 2 147 483 647. The negative end has one more value than the positive end, and that asymmetry is the source of a defect that has shipped in production code more than once.

int x = INT_MIN;
int y = -x;          /* undefined behaviour */

-x cannot be represented, because the positive counterpart of INT_MIN does not exist. The standard does not define what the machine should do, so the compiler may assume the negation never happens — and with optimisation enabled, it will assume exactly that. The signed overflow lab in chapter 9 demonstrates the consequence: the branch that was meant to guard the negation gets deleted, because a program in which x == INT_MIN is a program the compiler has decided cannot occur.

Unsigned types have no such hole. They wrap, by definition: UINT_MAX + 1u == 0u. That is why unsigned arithmetic is used for hashing and for bit manipulation, and why it is the wrong type for a loop bound that might go below zero.

docs.title: 4. Endianness
docs.text:
A multi-byte value has to be laid out in some order. Two orders dominate: least-significant byte first (little-endian, x86 and ARM in their usual modes), and most-significant first (big-endian, some network and embedded formats). The order is a property of the platform, and C gives you no portable way to ask — only a way to test at run time.

/* LAB 01-02  objects_in_memory/02_endianness_probe.c */
union {
    uint32_t word;
    uint8_t  bytes[4];
} probe = { .word = 0x01020304u };

printf("%02x %02x %02x %02x\n",
       probe.bytes[0], probe.bytes[1], probe.bytes[2], probe.bytes[3]);

On a little-endian machine this prints 04 03 02 01; on a big-endian machine, 01 02 03 04. The union works because its members share the same storage: writing word and reading bytes is the standard-blessed way to inspect the representation without violating aliasing rules.

This matters the moment a file format is involved. A PDB file stores coordinates as text, so byte order is irrelevant there; a binary trajectory or a serialized matrix does not, and reading it with the wrong order produces numbers that are plausible and wrong by a factor of 16 million. Chapter 12 returns to this with fread.

docs.title: 5. Alignment, and why a struct is larger than its fields
docs.text:
Objects are not packed at arbitrary addresses. Each type has an alignment requirement — the addresses it may legally occupy must be multiples of that number — because the hardware fetches memory in aligned chunks, and some architectures fault on misaligned access. alignof(int) is 4 on x86-64, alignof(double) is 8.

Consequences follow immediately:

struct pair { char c; int i; };
printf("%zu\n", sizeof(struct pair));   /* 8, not 5 */

The char occupies byte 0, three bytes of padding follow so that i starts at offset 4, and i occupies 4 through 7. The struct is 8 bytes. The padding is not waste in the sense of a leak — it is what makes the field reachable in one aligned load. Chapter 6 takes this apart with offsetof and shows how field order changes the total.

The rule worth remembering now: sizeof describes the object including its padding, and memset on a struct is only safe because the padding bytes are also part of the object.

docs.title: 6. What this buys
docs.text:
Three practical outcomes, before moving on.

A translation unit that prints the table above tells you more about the target than any specification. Keep the habit: when a width matters, print it.

sizeof on an expression reveals the type the compiler actually gave it, which is often not the type you wrote. sizeof('a') is the smallest example; sizeof(arr) versus sizeof(ptr) in chapter 4 is the one that breaks real code.

Representation is not value. A float holding 0.1 does not contain one tenth; it contains the nearest binary fraction, and the difference is why chapter 3 of the biology section spends a page on Kahan summation.

docs.text:
