  • Undefined Behavior explains why -INT_MIN is worse than a wrong answer.

docs.title: Pointers
docs.text:
A pointer is an address with a type attached, and I have made both halves wrong at different times. The type half is why p + 1 moves by sizeof(int); the address half is why an out-parameter can write back. I begin with the value and the type, then array decay because it explains the sizeof that lies at a call site, then out-parameters, then const, and I end with the three invalid pointers I have actually produced. If you can read a declaration aloud, the page has done its job.

A pointer is an integer that has been given two extra pieces of information: what type of object it points at, and permission to be dereferenced. The integer part is easy; almost every pointer defect comes from the second part being wrong — the pointer is valid in the arithmetic sense and invalid in the ownership sense.

docs.title: 1. The value and the type
docs.text:
int x = 42;
int *p = &x;
printf("%p %zu\n", (void *)p, sizeof p);   /* an address, and 8 */

p holds the address of x and has type int *. The address alone would not be enough: *(p + 1) advances by sizeof(int), not by one byte, precisely because the type is part of the pointer's value for arithmetic purposes.

int a[5] = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50};
int *p = a;
printf("%d %d\n", *p, *(p + 2));   /* 10 30 */
printf("%td\n", (p + 2) - p);      /* 2, measured in elements */

Pointer subtraction yields a count of elements, not bytes, and its type is ptrdiff_t. Mixing the two units — advancing by bytes while subtracting in elements — is the arithmetic half of most off-by-one errors.

One boundary is worth memorising because it is legal and looks illegal: a pointer one past the last element may be formed and compared, but not dereferenced.

int *end = a + 5;        /* legal: one past the end */
for (int *q = a; q != end; ++q) {
    printf("%d\n", *q);  /* the loop never reads *end */
}

a + 5 is the canonical loop sentinel in C. a + 6 is undefined behaviour even before dereferencing, because it is outside the array object plus one.

docs.title: 2. Decay, and the sizeof that lies
docs.text:
An array is not a pointer, but in almost every expression it becomes one. The conversion is called decay: the array's name turns into a pointer to its first element, and the size information disappears.

/* LAB 03-01  pointers/01_array_decay.c */
#include <stdio.h>

static void by_array(int a[10]) {
    printf("in callee: %zu\n", sizeof a);   /* 8: it is a pointer */
}

int main(void) {
    int a[10];
    printf("in caller: %zu\n", sizeof a);   /* 40: it is an array */
    by_array(a);
    return 0;
}

The parameter int a[10] is rewritten by the compiler to int *a; the 10 is documentation, not a constraint. -Wsizeof-array-argument in Clang warns exactly on this pattern, and it is worth turning on. GCC's equivalent check arrives under -Wsizeof-pointer-memaccess for the memset case, which is the version that corrupts memory rather than merely printing a wrong number.

The practical rule: sizeof on a parameter never tells you the size of the caller's array. Pass the length explicitly, or pass a pointer to an array type — void f(int (*a)[10]) — which preserves the width and is the one place where a pointer-to-array is genuinely useful.

docs.title: 3. Out-parameters, and why C has no references
docs.text:
C returns one value. When a function must produce two, the caller passes the address of a variable and the callee writes through it.

/* LAB 03-02  pointers/02_out_param_swap.c */
static void swap(int *a, int *b) {
    int t = *a;
    *a = *b;
    *b = t;
}

int main(void) {
    int x = 1, y = 2;
    swap(&x, &y);
    printf("%d %d\n", x, y);   /* 2 1 */
    return 0;
}

The & is the whole mechanism. Had swap taken int a, int b, the writes would have modified copies in its own frame and the caller would see nothing — the same phenomenon as writing through &value in the previous chapter. A pointer parameter is the caller saying "this object is mine to expose"; the callee's obligation is to check it is not null before writing, which is the contract chapter 16 formalises.

docs.title: 4. const is a position, not an adjective
docs.text:
Three placements, three meanings, and reading them from right to left is the reliable method:

const int *p;         /* pointer to const int: *p = 1 is an error   */
int * const q = &x;   /* const pointer to int: q = &y is an error   */
const int * const r = &x;  /* neither the target nor the pointer moves */

The first is the common one in APIs: a function that promises not to modify the caller's data. The second is rare outside embedded code, because a pointer that cannot be reseated is usually better expressed as a reference in C++ or as an array.

const on a pointer parameter does not prevent the caller from modifying the object through another pointer. It is a contract between the function and its caller, enforced at compile time inside that function only.

docs.title: 5. The three invalid pointers
docs.text:
Every pointer is in one of four states: pointing at a valid object, one past the end, null, or invalid. Only the first may be dereferenced; the second may be compared; the last two are indistinguishable from valid addresses at run time on most systems.

Null is defined and checkable. p = NULL then if (p) is the standard contract.

Dangling points at an object that has been freed or whose frame has returned. It looks valid, and a read through it may return the old value for hours before the allocator reuses the block. AddressSanitizer catches the first use after free; nothing catches the use that happens before the reuse.

The "old value" part deserves a correction, because it explains why these bugs survive so long. glibc's tcache does not leave a freed small chunk untouched: it writes a next pointer and a key into the first sixteen bytes, so a dangling read of a small struct returns allocator bookkeeping rather than the fields you stored, and a dangling write corrupts the free list instead of the object. The corruption is invisible until the next malloc of that size class walks the list, which is why the crash usually lands in an allocation far from the defect.

Wild was never initialised. A local int *p; holds whatever the previous frame left there. The fix costs one line: int *p = NULL;.

The pattern that avoids all three is ownership discipline, which is what chapter 7 is about. A pointer that is always either owned by exactly one object or borrowed for a documented lifetime has no state in which it can be silently wrong.

docs.title: 6. Reading pointer types aloud
docs.text:
A declaration read right to left, with parentheses resolved first, disambiguates the forms that look alike:

Declaration Read as int *p[3] array of 3 pointers to int int (*p)[3] pointer to array of 3 int int *f(void) function returning pointer to int int (*f)(void) pointer to function returning int const char *const *argv pointer to const pointer to const char

int *p[3] and int (*p)[3] differ by 16 bytes versus 8 in sizeof, and by completely different arithmetic. The chapter on function pointers uses the fourth form; the biology section uses the second when passing a fixed-width row of a coordinate matrix.

docs.title: Continue
docs.text:
• Arrays and Layout follows the decay rule into two dimensions, where the column count becomes part of the type.
  • The Heap introduces pointers whose lifetime is not a frame.
  • Function Pointers takes the int (*f)(void) form seriously.

docs.title: Qualifiers and Aliasing
docs.text:
const is a position, not an adjective, and I have put it in the wrong position often enough to write the section slowly. volatile is about observation rather than synchronisation, restrict is a promise I can break, and strict aliasing is the rule with no keyword at all. I keep the last two sections for -O2 and a Field Note, because that is where the difference between -O0 and -O2 stops being academic and starts being a segmentation fault.

Three keywords — const, volatile, restrict — and one rule that has no keyword at all: strict aliasing. The keywords are promises to the compiler, and the rule is the promise the compiler makes back. Misunderstanding either produces code that works at -O0 and fails at -O2, which is the worst kind of defect because it is attributed to the optimiser rather than to the code.

docs.title: 1. const objects may live in read-only memory
docs.text:
const on a pointer (previous chapter) restricts the pointer. const on an object restricts the object:

const int limit = 100;
int *p = (int *)&limit;   /* compiles, with a cast */
*p = 42;                  /* undefined behaviour */

Nothing in the language prevents the cast, and nothing at run time necessarily prevents the write — but on most platforms a const object with static storage duration is placed in a read-only segment, so the write faults. The diagnostic is a segmentation fault at an instruction that looks like an ordinary store.

The lesson is that const is not advisory. Casting it away and writing is undefined behaviour, and the failure mode is platform-dependent: a fault on Linux, a silent success on a platform that puts constants in writable memory, and a wrong value in either case when the optimiser has already substituted the constant into the code.

docs.title: 2. volatile is about observation, not synchronisation
docs.text:
volatile tells the compiler that the object may change without any code in this translation unit writing it, so every access must actually happen, in source order, and must not be cached in a register.

Three uses are correct:

volatile uint32_t *const status = (volatile uint32_t *)0x40021000;  /* memory-mapped register */
volatile sig_atomic_t stop_flag;                                    /* written by a signal handler */
volatile int after_longjmp;                                         /* setjmp/longjmp clobber rule */

One use is wrong and extremely common: using volatile as a substitute for a mutex or an atomic.

volatile int ready = 0;   /* NOT a synchronisation primitive */

volatile guarantees that the access happens; it does not guarantee atomicity, and it does not establish ordering with respect to other memory operations on another thread. On x86 it may appear to work because the hardware is strongly ordered; on ARM it fails intermittently. The replacement is <stdatomic.h>:

atomic_int ready = 0;
atomic_store_explicit(&ready, 1, memory_order_release);

The two keywords are unrelated despite the similar spelling. const is about permission to write; volatile is about the obligation to read.

docs.title: 3. restrict is a promise about aliasing
docs.text:
void scale(size_t n, double *restrict dst, const double *restrict src);

restrict asserts that, for the duration of the call, the object accessed through dst is not accessed through any other pointer. The compiler may then reorder loads and stores freely, because it no longer has to consider that writing through dst might change what src reads.

The promise is on the caller, and breaking it is undefined behaviour rather than a wrong result in some defined sense. The standard example where the promise fails is memcpy with overlapping regions — which is exactly why memmove exists as a separate function with no restrict. A function that internally calls itself with overlapping arguments has broken the promise even though the caller's pointers were distinct.

restrict is the one qualifier that can be added to an existing correct function without changing its semantics, and the vectorisation chapter uses it to make a loop optimisable. -Wrestrict in GCC diagnoses the overlap cases it can see at compile time, and it is worth enabling for any code that uses the keyword.

docs.title: 4. Strict aliasing: the rule with no keyword
docs.text:
The compiler assumes that two pointers of incompatible types do not point at the same object, with a small list of exceptions. Under that assumption it may keep a value in a register across a store through the other pointer.

/* LAB 08-01  qualifiers/01_alias_violation.c */
#include <stdio.h>

static int reinterpret(float f) {
    unsigned int bits = *(unsigned int *)&f;   /* undefined behaviour */
    return (int)(bits >> 23 & 0xFF) - 127;
}

int main(void) {
    printf("%d\n", reinterpret(1.0f));
    return 0;
}

At -O0 this usually prints 0, which is the correct exponent of 1.0. At -O2 it may print a different value, because the compiler is entitled to assume the unsigned int * does not alias the float object and may propagate the known value of f instead of reloading it.

Three legal ways exist to do the same job, and they differ in cost:

union { float f; unsigned int u; } pun = { .f = 1.0f };   /* legal in C */
unsigned int bits;
memcpy(&bits, &f, sizeof bits);                            /* legal, optimised away */

The union is the standard-blessed reinterpretation in C (though not in C++ in the same form, a fact the C++ section notes). memcpy is legal everywhere and compiles to a single move when the sizes are known. Both are correct; the pointer cast is not.

The exception list matters for the biology code: char * may alias any object, which is why memcpy and memset are permitted to operate on any type. A parser that reads a float through a char * is therefore legal, and one that reads it through an unsigned int * is not.

docs.title: 5. Why this shows up at -O2 and not at -O0
docs.text:
Optimisation levels change which assumptions the compiler acts on, not which rules exist. -O0 keeps every variable in memory and reloads after every store, so a violation happens to produce the expected value. -O2 keeps values in registers, and the violation becomes visible.

This is the reason the book compiles examples at -O1 with -g by default and re-runs the aliasing labs at -O2 deliberately. A defect that disappears when you lower the optimisation level is not a defect in the optimiser.

docs.title: 6. Field note: the constant that could not be modified
docs.text:
An early version of a configuration helper declared its table as static const and then, in an "override" path, cast away the constness and wrote into it. On the developer's machine the write succeeded, because the table had been placed in writable memory by that build. On a distribution build with -O2, the same code faulted at start-up, and the crash was attributed to a compiler upgrade that had changed the section layout.

The fix was not to change the section layout back. It was to keep two tables — the immutable default and a mutable working copy — which is what the code should have done from the beginning. The general lesson: a cast that removes const is a statement that the object was never really constant, and if that statement is false, no compiler flag can rescue it.

docs.title: Continue
docs.text:

  • Performance shows where restrict actually pays.
  • Geometry uses memcpy for coordinate reinterpretation rather than pointer casts.

docs.title: Sorting and Cost
docs.text:
I put three algorithms in one table because the table is the argument: the measurements differ by more than the constants, and the shape of the input decides which row wins. Then I slow down and measure honestly, because a benchmark that ignores the timer's resolution reports zero. Quicksort's worst case is real, stability matters when a second key exists, and binary search is the reward for sorting. The Field Note is a benchmark that measured the wrong thing, which is the most common failure in this chapter.

Sorting is where complexity stops being a formula and becomes a measurement. Three algorithms on the same input differ by orders of magnitude, and the difference is visible with clock() in a single run — which is exactly what the original code in this book's archive did, comparing two selection-sort variants on 100,000 integers.

docs.title: 1. Three algorithms, one table
2. Measuring honestly
docs.text:
Timing a sort requires three precautions, and the lab enforces all three.

double t0 = craft_cpu_seconds();
selection_sort(copy, n);
double t1 = craft_cpu_seconds();
printf("selection n=%d  %.3f s\n", n, t1 - t0);

First, each algorithm runs on its own copy. Sorting in place and then reusing the array gives the second algorithm a sorted input, which is a different measurement.

Second, the timer wraps only the sort, not the allocation or the printing. I/O dominates everything at small n, and a benchmark that includes printf measures the terminal.

Third, the result is used. A sort whose output is never read can be removed by the optimiser entirely, and the measurement becomes a measurement of nothing. Printing a checksum of the array prevents it.

The numbers the lab expects on a typical laptop, for 20,000 integers:

selection  n=20000  1.6 s
insertion  n=20000  0.35 s
qsort      n=20000  0.003 s

The ratio between selection and qsort is roughly 500, and that ratio is the chapter's point. Complexity is not an abstraction when the constant is this large.

docs.title: 3. Quicksort's worst case is real
docs.text:
The textbook quicksort picks the last element as pivot. On an already-sorted array that pivot is the maximum every time, the partition produces one part of size n − 1 and one of size zero, and the recursion depth becomes n. At n = 100,000 the stack is gone before the sort finishes — the failure from chapter 2, reproduced by an algorithm that is correct on average.

Three repairs are standard, and the lab asks for two:

static int median3(int a, int b, int c);          /* pick a pivot unlikely to be extreme */
static void sort_range(int *a, int lo, int hi, int depth);

The median-of-three pivot removes the sorted-input case. An explicit depth counter that switches to heapsort or insertion sort beyond 2 log₂ n removes the adversarial case. Both are cheap and both are absent from the naive implementation, which is why library qsort implementations include them.

docs.title: 4. Stability, and when it matters
docs.text:
A stable sort preserves the relative order of elements that compare equal. qsort is not stable, and this is easy to forget because the comparator usually compares the whole element.

struct hit { int score; int id; };

Sorting hits by score alone with an unstable sort can reorder two hits with the same score, which changes the output of any downstream step that assumes input order. The fix is either a stable sort (mergesort, or insertion sort for small arrays) or a comparator that breaks ties on id.

The C++ section's std::stable_sort exists for exactly this reason, and the difference in cost is worth measuring rather than assuming.

docs.title: 5. Searching a sorted array
docs.text:
Sorting is usually done to enable search. bsearch has the same comparator contract as qsort, and the same defect applies:

int key = 42;
int *found = bsearch(&key, a, n, sizeof a[0], by_int);
if (found != NULL) { printf("%d\n", *found); }

Binary search is O(log n), and it fails silently on an unsorted array: it returns a wrong element or NULL depending on the path it took. The contract is on the caller, which is why the lab checks that the array is sorted before searching rather than trusting the caller's intent.

docs.title: 6. Field note: the benchmark that measured the wrong thing
docs.text:
An early version of this lab's benchmark sorted 100,000 random integers with two selection-sort variants and printed the elapsed time for each. The first variant swapped inside the inner loop; the second, correctly, found the minimum first. The times differed by roughly a factor of three on the machine it ran on, which was read as evidence that the second algorithm was algorithmically better.

It was not. Both are O(n²) with the same comparison count; the difference was the number of conditional stores, which is a constant-factor effect. The measurement was correct and the conclusion drawn from it was not, because the benchmark changed two things at once.

The lesson: a benchmark can only compare implementations that differ in one dimension. If the comparison count and the swap count both change, the timing tells you which is faster but not why, and the "why" is the part worth knowing.

docs.text:

  • Performance turns this one-off timing into a repeatable measurement method.
  • STL Algorithms is the same material with iterators and predicates.

docs.title: Stack Frames
docs.text:
For a long time I treated the stack as an implementation detail I did not need to know. Then a function returned a pointer to its own local, and the program kept working for weeks. This page takes the frame apart in the order that makes that bug inevitable: the layout, then storage duration versus scope, then the stack's size, then where arguments actually live, and finally a debugger session that shows the frame you have been guessing at.

Every automatic object lives in a stack frame, and the frame is created and destroyed by a convention the compiler follows without telling you. Understanding that convention explains three things that otherwise look like folklore: why uninitialised locals hold garbage, why returning a pointer to a local is a defect rather than a mistake, and why a recursive function that works at depth 1,000 crashes at 100,000.

docs.title: 1. One frame, laid out
docs.text:
On x86-64 Linux, a call pushes a return address and then moves the stack pointer down. The callee's frame typically holds, in order: the saved frame pointer, the callee-saved registers it uses, its local variables, and the outgoing argument area. The exact arrangement is the compiler's business; what matters is that all of it is contiguous and all of it is reclaimed in one instruction when the function returns.

/* LAB 02-01  stack_frames/01_frame_addresses.c */
#include <stdio.h>

static void callee(int depth) {
    int local = depth;
    printf("depth=%d  &local=%p\n", depth, (void *)&local);
    if (depth > 0) {
        callee(depth - 1);
    }
}

int main(void) {
    int outer = 0;
    printf("&outer=%p\n", (void *)&outer);
    callee(3);
    return 0;
}

The addresses printed by successive calls decrease, by roughly the size of one frame. That decrease is the whole story: the stack grows downward on this platform, and each call eats further into it. The numbers are not stable between runs — address-space randomisation moves the base — but the ordering is stable, and the ordering is what the chapter needs.

Two consequences are visible in the code. local is a distinct object in every invocation; there is no sharing, which is why recursion works at all. And local is uninitialised, so its content is whatever the previous frame left there. That is not a compiler bug: automatic objects have no defined initial value, and reading one before writing it is undefined behaviour, not "returns zero".

docs.title: 2. Storage duration is not scope
docs.text:
These two ideas are taught together and are not the same thing.

Scope is where a name is visible. Storage duration is how long the object behind the name exists. A name can go out of scope while its object lives on, and an object can outlive the block that created it — which is usually a defect.

int *danger(void) {
    int local = 42;
    return &local;        /* the object dies at the closing brace */
}

int *safe(void) {
    static int preserved = 42;
    return &preserved;    /* static storage duration: lives until program exit */
}

The first function returns an address into a frame that no longer exists. Nothing detects it at compile time in C; GCC at -O2 may warn with -Wreturn-local-addr, which is worth enabling. The second function is legal but has its own cost: preserved is one object shared by every caller, so it cannot be used for per-call state, and it is not thread-safe.

The distinction becomes urgent with static locals inside recursive functions. A static counter in a recursive function is one counter, not one per depth, which is rarely what the author intended.

docs.title: 3. The stack has a size
docs.text:
The stack is fast because it is small and pre-allocated: typically 8 MB on Linux (ulimit -s), 1 MB by default for a thread on Windows, and often 8 MB in a container. A frame of 1 KB therefore allows roughly 8,000 nested calls before the guard page is touched, and touching it produces a segmentation fault with no diagnostic beyond "stack smashing detected" or a bare SIGSEGV.

/* LAB 02-02  stack_frames/02_lifetime_probe.c */
#include <stdio.h>

static int depth_of(int n) {
    char padding[512];              /* forces a frame large enough to matter */
    padding[0] = (char)n;
    return n == 0 ? 0 : 1 + depth_of(n - 1);
}

int main(void) {
    printf("%d\n", depth_of(8000));  /* adjust until it faults */
    return 0;
}

Three lessons come out of running it. The limit is reached at a depth that depends on the frame size, not on a constant. The failure is a signal, not an exception, so there is nothing to catch. And the fix is not "increase the stack" in most cases: it is either an explicit heap-allocated stack, or a loop, or an algorithm whose recursion depth is logarithmic rather than linear.

This is also why quicksort's worst case is a real problem and not a theoretical curiosity: an adversarial pivot choice on a sorted input produces recursion depth proportional to n, and at n = 10⁶ the stack is gone before the first partition completes. Chapter 14 returns to this with an explicit depth limit and a switch to insertion sort on small ranges.

docs.title: 4. Where the arguments live
docs.text:
Arguments are not automatically in the frame. The System V AMD64 convention passes the first six integer arguments in registers (rdi, rsi, rdx, rcx, r8, r9), and only the seventh onward go on the stack. That is why taking the address of a parameter gives you a copy: the compiler spilled the register into the frame so that the address exists at all.

void takes_address(int value) {
    int *p = &value;      /* p points at a copy in this frame */
    *p = 7;               /* legal, and invisible to the caller */
}

Writing through that pointer does not change the caller's variable. C has no pass-by-reference; chapter 3's out-parameter pattern works because the caller passes an address explicitly, not because the callee received a reference.

docs.title: 5. Reading a frame with a debugger
docs.text:
The addresses above are enough to see the shape, but not the contents. gdb shows the frame as the compiler laid it out:

(gdb) break callee
(gdb) run
(gdb) info frame
(gdb) info locals
(gdb) p &local
(gdb) x/8wx $rsp

info frame reports the frame's base and the saved return address; info locals lists the objects the debugger knows about and their current values. Optimised builds collapse this: at -O2 a local may exist only in a register, and p &local fails with "address requested for identifier which is not in memory". That is not a bug in the debugger; it is the compiler telling you the object has no address because it never needed one.

Debugging at -O1 -g is the compromise this book uses: enough optimisation to keep the code realistic, enough debug information to inspect frames. -O0 is easier to read and misleading about timing, which matters from chapter 14 onward.

docs.text:

  • Sorting and Cost is where stack depth becomes a design constraint, via recursion in the sort.
  • Error Handling shows what a stack overflow looks like in gdb and why it cannot be caught.

docs.title: Strings
docs.text:
A C string has no length. That is the whole chapter, and every section is a consequence: strlen walks, a loop that calls it becomes quadratic, strncpy copies a fixed count rather than a string, and a byte is not a character. I put the measurement first because the quadratic behaviour is invisible until you count the bytes read, and I keep the Unicode note short because the fix is a library, not a habit. The Field Note is a comparison that inverted a state machine, which is what happens when a string API returns a number you did not read.

A C string is not a type. It is a convention: an array of char, terminated by a zero byte, with the understanding that functions stop at the first zero they meet. Every defect in this chapter follows from one of those three clauses being violated — usually the third.

docs.title: 1. The convention, measured
docs.text:
char s[] = "abc";
printf("%zu %zu\n", sizeof s, strlen(s));   /* 4 3 */

sizeof is 4 because the array contains three characters and the terminator. strlen is 3 because it counts until it finds the terminator. The two numbers differ by one, and that difference is the reason sizeof is safe and strlen is a walk.

'\0' is a byte with value zero, not the character '0', which has value 48. Storing '0' where a terminator was intended produces a string that continues into whatever memory follows, and the defect surfaces when a later function reads past the intended end.

Reimplementing strlen is the shortest way to see that the function has no other information to work with:

/* LAB 05-01  strings/01_strlen_reimpl.c */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stddef.h>

static size_t length_of(const char *s) {
    const char *p = s;
    while (*p != '\0') {
        ++p;
    }
    return (size_t)(p - s);
}

int main(void) {
    const char *text = "membrane";
    printf("%zu\n", length_of(text));   /* 8 */
    return 0;
}

There is no length stored anywhere. The only way to know where the string ends is to walk it, which is why strlen is linear and why calling it inside a loop condition turns a linear algorithm into a quadratic one:

for (int i = 0; i < strlen(s); ++i) { }   /* O(n^2) */
for (size_t i = 0; s[i] != '\0'; ++i) { } /* O(n)   */

The second form is not a micro-optimisation. On a 10,000-character sequence the first form performs about 50 million byte reads to do 10,000 iterations of work, and the difference is measurable in the profiling chapter.

docs.title: 2. Reading input without gets
docs.text:
gets was removed from C11 for a reason that is easy to demonstrate and impossible to fix: it has no length parameter, so it cannot know where the buffer ends.

char buf[8];
gets(buf);       /* not in C11; reads until newline regardless of size */

fgets is the replacement, and it has two behaviours that need checking rather than assuming:

/* LAB 05-02  strings/02_safe_input.c */
char line[64];
if (fgets(line, sizeof line, stdin) == NULL) {
    return 1;                 /* EOF or error, not an empty line */
}

size_t len = strlen(line);
if (len > 0 && line[len - 1] == '\n') {
    line[len - 1] = '\0';     /* strip the newline, if it is there */
}

The first check is easy to forget: fgets returns NULL at end of input, and treating that as an empty string loses the distinction. The second check matters because fgets includes the newline when it fits, and a comparison like strcmp(line, "yes") then fails on input that looks identical on screen.

When the line does not fit, fgets returns the truncated part and leaves the rest in the stream. The next read returns the remainder, which usually appears as a mysterious extra iteration. The reliable pattern is to check for the newline and, if it is missing, consume the rest of the line before continuing:

if (len > 0 && line[len - 1] != '\n') {
    int c;
    while ((c = getchar()) != '\n' && c != EOF) { }
}

docs.title: 3. strncpy is not the bounded strcpy
docs.text:
char dst[8];
strncpy(dst, "abcdefgh", sizeof dst);   /* fills 8 bytes, no terminator */

strncpy copies at most n characters and stops early only if it finds a terminator in the source. When the source is longer than n, the result has no terminator at all, and every subsequent string function walks off the end. The function was designed for fixed-width records in old file formats, not for C strings.

The two usable alternatives are explicit:

snprintf(dst, sizeof dst, "%s", src);   /* always terminates, truncates silently */

size_t n = strlen(src) < sizeof dst - 1 ? strlen(src) : sizeof dst - 1;
memcpy(dst, src, n);
dst[n] = '\0';

snprintf is the one to reach for by default. Its cost is that truncation is silent, so a caller who needs to detect it must compare the return value against the buffer size.

docs.title: 4. A character is not a byte, and a byte is not a glyph
docs.text:
char holds one byte. UTF-8 encodes one character in one to four bytes, which means strlen on a UTF-8 string counts bytes, not characters, and s[i] indexes bytes, not characters. For English text the two coincide often enough to hide the problem; for a protein sequence they always coincide, since the alphabet is ASCII; for a name with a non-Latin character they diverge immediately.

The biology section relies on the ASCII case and states the assumption at the top of each parser. Text handling in general does not, and the fix is a library, not a loop.

docs.title: 5. Field note: the comparison that inverted a state machine
docs.text:
The original sumWord.c counted words by tracking whether the previous character was inside a word. The loop condition contained one character that inverted the logic:

while (str[j] != ' ' && str[j] == '\0') {   /* the original */

The second test should have been !=. As written, the loop continues only when the character is simultaneously not a space and the terminator — a condition that is never true, so the body never executes and the word count stays at zero for every input.

The corrected condition is str[j] != ' ' && str[j] != '\0'. The interesting part is not the fix but the diagnosis: the function compiled, ran, and returned a plausible answer (zero words) for an input with no words. A test with one word would have caught it; a test with an empty string would not.

The general lesson belongs here rather than in a debugger chapter: string code is a state machine, and a state machine with an inverted transition produces output that is internally consistent and externally wrong.

docs.title: Continue
docs.text:

  • Files and Streams applies fgets to file input, where truncation is the normal case.
  • FASTA parses sequence records, the one place where the ASCII assumption is safe and worth stating.

docs.title: Structs and Padding
docs.text:
I learned padding the expensive way: a struct written to a file on one compiler and read on another, with two bytes of garbage between the fields. This page starts from offsetof rather than from a diagram, because an offset is a number you can print, then states the placement rule, then reorders the members to show what changes, and then treats padding as part of the object rather than as wasted space. Unions, bit-fields and flexible array members come last, each with the portability limit that makes it a deliberate choice.

A struct is a layout, and the layout is not the sum of its fields. This chapter measures the gaps, explains where they come from, and shows the two cases where the gaps are load-bearing: serialization and comparison.

docs.title: 1. Offsets, not guesses
docs.text:
/* LAB 06-01  structs_padding/01_layout_table.c */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stddef.h>

struct sample {
    char   tag;      /* 1 byte  */
    int    id;       /* 4 bytes */
    char   flag;     /* 1 byte  */
    double value;    /* 8 bytes */
};

int main(void) {
    printf("sizeof      %zu\n", sizeof(struct sample));
    printf("offset tag  %zu\n", offsetof(struct sample, tag));
    printf("offset id   %zu\n", offsetof(struct sample, id));
    printf("offset flag %zu\n", offsetof(struct sample, flag));
    printf("offset val  %zu\n", offsetof(struct sample, value));
    return 0;
}

On x86-64 Linux the output is:

sizeof      24
offset tag  0
offset id   4
offset flag 8
offset val  16

The fields total 14 bytes; the object is 24. The three missing bytes after tag exist so that id starts at a multiple of 4. The seven bytes after flag exist so that value starts at a multiple of 8. And the object itself is padded to 24 because its alignment is the maximum of its members' alignments, 8 — an array of these structs must keep every value aligned, so the stride must be a multiple of 8.

docs.title: 2. The placement rule
docs.text:
The rule the compiler follows is short enough to apply by hand:

  1. Each member is placed at the next offset that is a multiple of its own alignment.
  2. The struct's alignment is the maximum alignment among its members.
  3. The struct's size is rounded up to a multiple of its alignment.

Applying it to the struct above: tag at 0 (size 1), id needs a multiple of 4 so it goes to 4 (occupying 4–7), flag at 8, value needs a multiple of 8 so it goes to 16 (occupying 16–23), total 24.

docs.title: 3. Reordering is free, and sometimes necessary
docs.text:
The same fields in a different order produce a smaller object:

struct packed_order {
    double value;    /* 0  */
    int    id;       /* 8  */
    char   tag;      /* 12 */
    char   flag;     /* 13 */
};                   /* sizeof == 16 */

Sixteen bytes instead of twenty-four, with no behavioural change and no #pragma pack. The cost is that the declaration no longer reads in a logical order, which is a real cost: a struct whose fields follow the record they model is easier to audit than one arranged for density. Reorder when the object is stored by the million, not by the dozen.

#pragma pack(1) also removes padding, and it should be treated as a last resort. On x86-64 it produces unaligned accesses, which are slow rather than fatal; on some ARM configurations they fault. The portable way to serialize a struct is not to pack it but to write each field explicitly, which is what chapter 12 does with PDB records.

docs.title: 4. Padding is part of the object
docs.text:
Two consequences that surprise people:

struct sample a, b;
memset(&a, 0, sizeof a);
b = a;
if (memcmp(&a, &b, sizeof a) != 0) { /* may be true: padding is copied too */ }

memcmp compares padding bytes as well, and they are not guaranteed to be equal. Assignment copies them, so this usually works, but a struct that has been memset and a struct that was initialised field by field may differ in the gaps. Comparing structs byte-wise is a defect waiting for a different compiler version.

The second consequence is that memset on a struct is legitimate, precisely because padding is part of the object: the standard permits it, and the result is a struct with every byte, including the gaps, set to zero.

docs.title: 5. Unions: one region, several readings
docs.text:
A union allocates enough storage for its largest member, and every member starts at offset 0. Writing one member and reading another is how representation probes work — the endianness probe in chapter 1 is exactly this.

/* LAB 06-02  structs_padding/02_union_typing.c */
union value {
    uint32_t bits;
    float    as_float;
};

union value v = { .bits = 0x40490FDBu };
printf("%.6f\n", v.as_float);   /* 3.141593 */

This is defined behaviour in C: the union's members share storage, and reading a different member than the last written is permitted (the result is unspecified only if the member read is a trap representation). It is the one sanctioned way to reinterpret bits without violating aliasing rules — the next chapter explains why the pointer cast that does the same thing is not sanctioned.

A tagged union — a union plus an enum recording which member is live — is how C models a variant. The enum is not optional; without it, nothing tells the reader which member holds a value.

docs.title: 6. Bit-fields, and their portability limit
docs.text:
struct flags {
    unsigned ready : 1;
    unsigned mode  : 3;
    unsigned       : 4;   /* unnamed padding */
};

Bit-fields pack several small values into one storage unit, which is useful for hardware registers and occasionally for dense flags. The portability limit is real: the standard does not specify the order of allocation within a unit, the behaviour at a unit boundary, or whether an int bit-field may straddle one. A struct of bit-fields serialized on GCC and read on MSVC can produce different values from identical bytes.

For anything that crosses a machine boundary, use explicit masks on a uint32_t — the technique in the bit-manipulation chapter — and treat bit-fields as an internal convenience only.

docs.title: 7. Flexible array members
docs.text:
A struct whose last member is an incomplete array is the standard way to allocate a header and a variable-length body in one block:

struct sequence {
    size_t length;
    char   bases[];      /* C99 flexible array member */
};

struct sequence *make(size_t n) {
    struct sequence *s = malloc(sizeof *s + n + 1);
    if (s != NULL) {
        s->length = n;
    }
    return s;
}

sizeof(struct sequence) excludes the body, and the allocation adds n + 1 bytes for the bases and the terminator. One malloc, one free, and the body is adjacent to its header — which is what makes this the preferred shape for parsed records, including the FASTA records in the biology section.

docs.title: 8. Field note: the sizeof that measured a pointer
docs.text:
The original mocal.c allocated ten strings in two levels and then freed only the outer array:

str = (char **)malloc(10 * sizeof(char *));
for (int i = 0; i < 10; ++i) {
    str[i] = (char *)malloc(20 * sizeof(char *));   /* sizeof a pointer, not a char */
    ...
}
...
free(str);                                          /* ten blocks left behind */

Two defects in four lines. The inner allocation uses sizeof(char *), which happens to equal the intended sizeof(char) on this platform only because both are 8 and 1 respectively — it over-allocates by a factor of 8, harmlessly here and catastrophically in a large array. And the teardown frees the outer block while the ten inner blocks remain allocated, so every call leaks 160 bytes.

The corrected teardown is a loop, and the corrected allocation is sizeof *str[i]:

for (int i = 0; i < 10; ++i) { free(str[i]); }
free(str);

The idiom sizeof *p rather than sizeof(type) removes the entire class of defect: it cannot disagree with the type of the pointer it is sizing.

docs.title: Translation Units
docs.text:
The compiler sees one unit and the linker sees symbols, and every error in this chapter lives in the gap between those two views. I start with the unit and the two stages that read it, then declaration versus definition, then static at file scope, then the two link errors people actually get. inline and the one-definition rule come after, because they are the modern version of the same problem, and the macro section is there because a macro is the only construct that can capture an argument twice.

A C program is not compiled as a whole. It is compiled as a set of translation units, each one a .c file plus everything it includes, and then the linker joins the results. Almost every confusing error in this chapter is a disagreement between what one unit believes and what another unit provides.

docs.title: 1. The unit, and the two stages that read it
docs.text:
foo.c  →  preprocess  →  foo.i  →  compile  →  foo.o  →  link  →  a.out

The preprocessor is textual: it copies headers, expands macros, and evaluates #if. The compiler sees one unit and knows nothing about the others. The linker sees symbols and knows nothing about types. So a function declared with one signature and defined with another compiles cleanly and fails at run time, and a variable defined twice fails at link time with a message that names the second definition, not the first.

docs.title: 2. Declaration and definition
docs.text:
/* point.h */
#ifndef POINT_H
#define POINT_H

struct point { double x, y; };

double distance(const struct point *a, const struct point *b);  /* declaration */
extern int point_count;                                          /* declaration */

#endif

A declaration says a name exists and what type it has. A definition creates the object or the function body. The header holds declarations; exactly one .c file holds each definition.

The include guard is not optional. Without it, a header included twice in one unit — once directly, once through another header — defines struct point twice, which is a redefinition error. #pragma once does the same job in every mainstream compiler, is not standard C, and is used in this book's own headers because the duplicate-include case is entirely mechanical.

docs.title: 3. static at file scope means internal linkage
docs.text:
static on a function or a file-scope variable means "this name is not exported". The linker never sees it, so two translation units may each have a static helper with the same name and no conflict.

/* LAB 13-01  translation_units/01_static_scope.c */
static int counter;                 /* one per translation unit */

static int bump(void) { return ++counter; }

int public_api(void) { return bump(); }

The variable is not shared with any other unit even if another unit declares extern int counter. That is the point: extern finds nothing, and the link fails rather than silently aliasing two unrelated objects.

The opposite case is the one that catches people. A header containing a definition — int counter; rather than extern int counter; — is included by three units, producing three definitions and a link error:

multiple definition of `counter'; first defined here

The repair is to keep the definition in one .c file and the extern declaration in the header. The C++ section solves the same problem with inline variables, which is a different mechanism for the same need.

docs.title: 4. Reading the two error messages
docs.text:
The two link errors mean different things and lead to different fixes.

undefined reference to `distance'

The linker found a call and no definition. Either the .c file holding the body is not in the build, or its name differs by case, or it is inside an extern "C" block in C++ that was omitted.

multiple definition of `counter'

The linker found two definitions. Either a header holds a definition, or a .c file was added to the build twice, or a static definition was accidentally made non-static.

Both are link-time, so both appear after every unit compiled successfully — which is why "it compiled" is not "it built".

docs.title: 5. inline and the one-definition rule
docs.text:
C99's inline is subtler than its C++ counterpart. A function declared inline in a header and used by three units may be emitted in each of them; the standard resolves this by requiring one unit to provide an external definition. Getting it wrong produces either a missing symbol or a duplicate one, depending on the compiler's mood.

/* header */
static inline int clamp(int v, int lo, int hi) {
    return v < lo ? lo : (v > hi ? hi : v);
}

static inline in a header is the practical form: each unit gets its own copy, the compiler inlines it, and no symbol is exported. It costs a few bytes of code duplication and removes the entire linkage question. This book uses it for the small helpers in code/include.

docs.title: 6. Macros that capture arguments
docs.text:
The preprocessor substitutes text, which means an argument is evaluated every time it appears:

#define SQUARE(x) ((x) * (x))
int v = SQUARE(++i);      /* i incremented twice */

The double parentheses protect against precedence, not against double evaluation. The fix is a function, or an inline function, or a macro that evaluates its argument exactly once by way of a temporary in a statement expression — a GNU extension this book does not use.

The other macro trap is the missing parentheses around the whole body:

#define DOUBLE(x) (x) * 2
int v = DOUBLE(1 + 2) * 3;   /* expands to (1 + 2) * 2 * 3 */

The body must be fully parenthesised and every parameter must be parenthesised. A macro that satisfies both conditions is still a candidate for replacement by static inline.

docs.title: 7. Field note: the header that defined a table
docs.text:
A project declared its lookup table in a header:

/* lookup.h — the original */
const char *names[] = { "alpha", "beta", "gamma" };

Two units included it, both got a definition, and the link failed with multiple definition of 'names'. The author's first response was to add static, which silenced the linker and gave each unit its own copy — 3 copies of the table at run time, and a sizeof in one unit that disagreed with the array another unit had modified.

The correct repair was extern const char *const names[]; in the header and one definition in a .c file. The lesson is that static is not a way to silence a link error; it is a statement that the name is private, and a table shared across units is not private.

docs.title: Undefined Behavior
docs.text:
I begin with a program the optimiser deletes, because the definition of undefined behaviour is easier to accept when you watch a loop vanish. Then five categories, then what each tool catches, then the shift rules that catch people who think they know the width. The section I care most about is the one on evidence: 'it works on my machine' is a sample from a set, not a proof. Reading a sanitiser report is the skill the chapter is actually teaching.

Undefined behaviour is not "a crash waiting to happen". It is a category the standard declines to describe, which means the compiler is entitled to assume it never occurs and to optimise as if it did not. That assumption is what makes UB more dangerous than a plain bug: a bug produces the wrong answer, while UB produces whatever the optimiser decided was consistent.

docs.title: 1. The optimisation that proves the point
docs.text:
int always_true(int x) {
    return (x + 1) > x;
}

For every int except INT_MAX, the expression is true. For INT_MAX, x + 1 overflows — undefined behaviour. The compiler therefore reasons: a program in which x == INT_MAX is a program with UB, and UB cannot occur in a correct program, so x is never INT_MAX, so the comparison is always true. GCC 11 at -O2 compiles this function to mov eax, 1; ret. No comparison survives.

Nothing is broken in the compiler. The function's author wrote a program whose only guarantee comes from a condition that the language does not define, and the optimiser took the author at their word.

This is the difference between UB and implementation-defined behaviour. Reading an uninitialised int is UB: anything may happen. Right-shifting a negative int is implementation-defined: the standard says the implementation must document its choice, and GCC documents arithmetic shift. The first is a defect; the second is a portability question.

docs.title: 2. Five categories that cover most cases
docs.text:
Category Example Detected by Uninitialised read int x; return x; MSan (not ASan), or by inspection Out-of-bounds access a[5] on a 4-element array ASan Signed overflow INT_MAX + 1 UBSan Invalid pointer arithmetic p + 2 past one-past-end ASan, partially Violated aliasing promise restrict or strict-aliasing violation Nothing reliable

Casting a pointer to an incompatible type and dereferencing is a sixth, from the previous chapter, and it is deliberately not instrumented: the compiler cannot tell a legal char * access from an illegal unsigned int * access in general.

docs.title: 3. What each tool catches
docs.text:
/* LAB 09-01  undefined_behavior/01_signed_overflow.c */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <limits.h>

int main(void) {
    int x = INT_MAX;
    printf("%d\n", x + 1);      /* signed overflow */
    printf("%d\n", -x - 1);     /* -INT_MIN, overflow again */
    return 0;
}

Compiled with gcc -fsanitize=undefined, both lines abort with a report naming the expression and the line:

runtime error: signed integer overflow: 2147483647 + 1 cannot be represented in type 'int'

Compiled without the sanitiser, both print a value — usually -2147483648 and 2147483647 — because x86 wraps. That wrapped value is not a guarantee; it is what this machine did this time. A different compiler version, or an inlined context, may produce something else.

AddressSanitizer and UBSan are complementary and are used together in this book's sanitizer target. ASan catches memory errors; UBSan catches arithmetic and shift errors. Neither catches an uninitialised read, which is why the debugging chapter mentions MemorySanitizer as the third tool and notes that it requires instrumenting every object in the program, including libraries.

docs.title: 4. Shift rules that catch people
docs.text:
int x = 1 << 31;      /* UB in C: 2^31 is not representable in int */
int y = -8 >> 1;      /* implementation-defined, not UB */
int z = 1 << 32;      /* UB: shift count >= width of type */

Three different rules, three different outcomes. Shifting into the sign bit is UB for signed types; shifting a negative value right is implementation-defined; shifting by the width or more is UB for both signed and unsigned. The portable idiom for a bit mask at the top of a word is 1u << 31, which is defined because unsigned int has 32 value bits and no sign bit to collide with.

docs.title: 5. Why "it works on my machine" is not evidence
docs.text:
A UB program has no defined behaviour, so every observation of it is a sample from an undefined set. The samples agree until a compiler version, an optimisation level, a platform, or an unrelated edit changes one of the inputs to the optimiser's reasoning.

The practical rule: when a defect disappears at -O0 and appears at -O2, or appears on one machine and not another, the first hypothesis should be UB rather than a compiler bug. The second hypothesis is worth holding only after the code has been run under both sanitisers and read against the five categories above.

docs.title: 6. Reading a sanitiser report
docs.text:
ub_sweep.c:56:26: runtime error: shift exponent 32 is too large for 32-bit type 'unsigned int'
    #0 0x... in main .../code/c/09_undefined_behavior/02_ub_sweep.c:56
SUMMARY: UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer: undefined-behavior ub_sweep.c:56:26

Four pieces of information, in order: the file and line, the category, the operation (load, store, shift), and the type. The category is the one to look up, because it determines the fix: a shift exponent at or past the type's width needs a check on the count (shift < sizeof(unsigned int) * 8u), a null load needs a check at the call site, and a signed overflow is a type that should have been unsigned or a bound that should have been checked before the arithmetic. All three appear in 02_ub_sweep.c, one per branch, each paired with the guard that avoids it.

A report that names the same line twice usually means the expression appears in a macro expanded twice, which is a hint that the defect is in the macro's argument rather than in the function.

docs.title: 7. Field note: the loop that only ran on the developer's machine
docs.text:
A hand-written parser had a loop whose bound was computed as end - start and then used as an index into a table of int. On a machine where start preceded end, the subtraction was positive and the code worked. When a malformed record made end == start, the loop was skipped, and the code that was supposed to report the malformed record never ran — it was inside the loop.

The defect was not the subtraction but the absence of a branch for the empty case. end - start is a perfectly defined value; the assumption that it is at least one is what was undefined in the author's mind, not in the language. The fix was an explicit check before the loop, and the lesson is that most "UB" in real code is an unstated precondition rather than an exotic expression.

docs.title: STL Algorithms
docs.text:
The algorithms header is where the standard library stops being a container and becomes a set of loops you no longer write. I take four that matter — sort, find, transform, accumulate — and then the comparator contract, because a comparator that is not a strict weak order is undefined behaviour rather than a wrong answer. Then erase-remove, then lambdas and what they capture, then ranges as the same idea with fewer iterator pairs.

The algorithms are free functions over iterator pairs. They do not know about containers, which is why they work on raw arrays, vectors, and the sequence buffers in the biology section without any adaptation.

docs.title: 1. The four that carry most of the work
docs.text:
// LAB 10-01  cpp_algorithms/01_lambda_pipeline.cpp
std::sort(v.begin(), v.end());
std::stable_sort(v.begin(), v.end(), by_score_desc);
auto it = std::find_if(v.begin(), v.end(), [](int x) { return x > 100; });
std::transform(in.begin(), in.end(), out.begin(), [](double x) { return x * 2.0; });

std::sort is introsort: quicksort with a median-of-three pivot, falling back to heapsort when recursion gets too deep, so the worst case is O(n log n) rather than O(n²). It is not stable. stable_sort is merge sort and allocates a temporary buffer; use it when equal elements must keep their relative order — a sort by score that must preserve the input order among equal scores.

std::find_if returns the iterator, and the caller must check it against end(). A common defect is comparing the result to the wrong container's end().

std::transform writes through an output iterator and does not resize the destination; the destination must already have room. std::back_inserter(out) is the fix for a container that should grow.

docs.title: 2. The comparator must be a strict weak ordering
docs.text:
This is the requirement that produces the most undefined behaviour in the whole library, because violating it usually appears to work.

std::sort(v.begin(), v.end(), [](int a, int b) { return a <= b; });   // UB

<= is not a strict weak ordering: it returns true for equal elements, so comp(a, a) is true, which no correct sort can tolerate. The result is out-of-bounds reads inside the sort — undefined behaviour, and AddressSanitizer will not catch it because the reads stay within the buffer.

The mechanism is worth seeing once. libstdc++ partitions with an unguarded loop — while (comp(*first, pivot)) ++first; — and it omits a bounds check because the pivot itself is supposed to stop the scan. When comp is <=, comp(pivot, pivot) is true, so the scan passes the pivot, then passes the end of the range, and only stops when it happens to meet a value the comparator rejects or when it reads unmapped memory. That is why the symptom is a segfault in std::sort with no relation to the caller's data, and why debug mode (-D_GLIBCXX_DEBUG) is the only reliable detector.

The correct form is a < b. For a descending order, a > b. For a tuple, std::tie(a.x, a.y) < std::tie(b.x, b.y).

The second form of the same defect is an inconsistent comparator — one that orders by x when x differs and by y otherwise but forgets a case. The library's only defence is a debug-mode check in some implementations; in release builds the sort silently produces a wrong order or reads out of bounds.

docs.title: 3. The erase-remove idiom
docs.text:
v.erase(std::remove_if(v.begin(), v.end(),
                       [](const Record &r) { return r.score < 60; }),
        v.end());

remove_if cannot erase, because it only has iterators; it moves the kept elements to the front and returns the boundary. erase(boundary, end()) then destroys the tail. The two-call form is not a workaround, it is the intended design: the same remove_if works on a raw array, where there is no erase.

std::remove returns the new end and the container must be shrunk explicitly. Forgetting the erase leaves the container with the same size and moved-from elements at the tail, which compiles and runs.

docs.title: 4. Lambdas and capture
docs.text:
int threshold = 60;
auto pred = [threshold](const Record &r) { return r.score < threshold; };   // by value: safe
auto counter = [&count](const Record &r) { ++count; return r.score < 60; }; // by reference: lifetime risk

[=] and [&] are the convenient forms and the ones that cause defects. [&] captures everything by reference, including things the lambda outlives — a lambda stored in a std::function and called after the scope has exited reads a dead local. Capturing the two or three names explicitly makes the lifetime visible in the signature.

A lambda that captures this ([this]) captures the pointer, not the object; if the object dies, the capture dangles. C++20's [=, this] form exists to make that explicit.

docs.title: 5. Ranges, one paragraph
docs.text:
C++20 ranges replace iterator pairs with a single object:

std::ranges::sort(v);
auto evens = v | std::views::filter([](int x) { return x % 2 == 0; });

Views are lazy and do not own data, so a view over a temporary is a dangling view — the same lifetime question as string_view. The book uses ranges in the capstone and keeps the iterator form everywhere else, because the iterator form is what every existing codebase contains.

docs.title: 6. Field note: the comparator that subtracted
docs.text:
A comparator written as:

bool cmp(int a, int b) { return a - b; }

worked for small values and produced a wrong order for large ones. a - b overflows int when the difference exceeds the range, and the sign of the overflowed result is not the sign of the true difference. qsort and std::sort both accept a comparator returning bool, so a - b converts to true whenever it is nonzero — meaning "less than" is reported for both a > b and a < b.

The repair is a < b. The general rule: a comparator returns a truth value, never a difference, and the difference form belongs to three-way comparisons where the return type is a signed integer wide enough to hold it.

docs.title: 7. Practise
docs.text: Compile code/cpp/10_algorithms/01_lambda_pipeline.cpp with -D_GLIBCXX_DEBUG, which enables the library's comparator checks, and run the deliberately broken comparator to see the diagnostic. Then read code/cpp/10_algorithms/README.md and rewrite the program into /tmp from memory: sort a struct array by two keys, remove failing records with the erase–remove idiom, and assert the surviving count and the first element — the same two properties the reference program checks.

docs.title: Capstone: Sequence Toolkit
docs.text:
The capstone is where the three tracks meet, so I state the contract before the code: a sequence type that owns its storage, a scoring function that returns a fraction, and a report that prints without allocating per line. Then I build the layers in that order, and each section ends with the check the program performs on itself. If the earlier chapters worked, this page is assembly rather than instruction; if one of them did not, the failing assertion tells you which.

The capstone assembles the C++ half of the book into one program: a FASTA reader, a composition calculator, and a report writer, with an owned buffer instead of a raw pointer, a template where the type genuinely varies, and an operator overload where the type genuinely has an invariant.

Nothing here is new. The point is that the pieces compose, and that each defect class from the previous twelve chapters has a place where it would show up if the piece were written carelessly.

docs.title: 1. The three layers
docs.text:
Sequence          owns name and residues, reads FASTA, validates the alphabet
Composition       counts residues, computes GC fraction as a Fraction
Report            formats rows, writes to stdout or a file

The layers are separated by ownership. Sequence owns its characters and never lends a pointer out. Composition borrows a const Sequence &. Report borrows a Composition and owns nothing. No layer can invalidate another layer's data, which is the structural version of the lifetime rules from chapter 3.

docs.title: 2. Layer 1: Sequence owns
docs.text:
// LAB 13-01  cpp_capstone/sequence_toolkit.cpp
class Sequence {
public:
    static std::optional<Sequence> parse(std::string_view header, std::string_view body) {
        if (header.empty() || !header.starts_with('>')) { return std::nullopt; }
        Sequence s;
        s.name_ = header.substr(1);
        s.residues_.reserve(body.size());          // known size: one allocation
        for (char c : body) {
            if (c == '\n' || c == '\r' || c == ' ') { continue; }
            if (!is_residue(c)) { return std::nullopt; }
            s.residues_.push_back(c);
        }
        return s;
    }
    std::size_t size() const { return residues_.size(); }
    char operator[](std::size_t i) const { return residues_[i]; }
    const std::string &name() const { return name_; }
private:
    static bool is_residue(char c) {
        return (c >= 'A' && c <= 'Z') || (c >= 'a' && c <= 'z') || c == '*';
    }
    std::string name_;
    std::vector<char> residues_;     // owns: no raw pointer, no manual free
};

std::optional<Sequence> rather than a partially valid object: a sequence either parsed completely or does not exist. This is chapter 11's rule applied at the boundary — invalid input produces no object rather than an object with a bad flag.

reserve before the loop is chapter 9's rule; the size is known from the body, so the one allocation is the only allocation.

docs.title: 3. Layer 2: Composition, and Fraction
docs.text:
class Fraction {
public:
    Fraction(long num, long den) : num_(num), den_(den) {
        if (den == 0) { throw std::invalid_argument("zero denominator"); }
        long g = std::gcd(num, den);
        num_ /= g; den_ /= g;
        if (den_ < 0) { num_ = -num_; den_ = -den_; }
    }
    long num() const { return num_; }
    long den() const { return den_; }
    friend Fraction operator*(const Fraction &a, const Fraction &b) {
        return Fraction(a.num_ * b.num_, a.den_ * b.den_);   // constructor reduces
    }
    friend bool operator==(const Fraction &a, const Fraction &b) {
        return a.num_ == b.num_ && a.den_ == b.den_;
    }
private:
    long num_, den_;
};

The invariant — denominator positive, fraction reduced, denominator nonzero — is established in the constructor and preserved by every operator that returns a Fraction, because every such operator goes through the constructor. This is chapter 6's argument, in the one place the capstone needs a number that is exactly representable: a GC fraction is 71/100, not 0.71, and the report prints it reduced.

class Composition {
public:
    explicit Composition(const Sequence &s) : counts_{} { for (...) ++counts_[index(c)]; }
    Fraction gc_fraction() const {
        std::size_t gc = 0, at = 0;
        for (char c : {'G', 'C', 'c', 'g'}) { gc += counts_[index(c)]; }
        for (std::size_t i = 0; i < 26; ++i) { at += counts_[i]; }
        return Fraction(long(gc), long(at));       // reduces in the constructor
    }
    std::size_t count(char c) const { return counts_[index(c)]; }
private:
    std::array<std::size_t, 26> counts_;
};

std::array with a fixed size and no allocation is chapter 7's FixedBuffer idea, and the index computation is chapter 10's masking, scaled down to a lookup.

docs.title: 4. Layer 3: Report writes, and owns nothing
docs.text:
void write_report(std::ostream &out, const std::string &name, const Composition &comp) {
    out << name << '\t' << comp.gc_fraction().num() << '/'
        << comp.gc_fraction().den() << '\n';
}

Taking std::ostream & rather than writing to std::cout is what makes the output comparable: the program assembles the report in a std::ostringstream, asserts on its prefix, and only then prints it. The same argument is why a harness could freeze this output later without touching the code.

docs.title: 5. What the program checks
docs.text:
labs/cpp/13_capstone/check.sh builds the target with the project flags and runs it; the assertions inside code/cpp/13_capstone/sequence_toolkit.cpp are what decide the result:

  1. Ubiquitin (P0CG48) parses to 76 residues and keeps its header text.
  2. The report's leading fields — name, count, reduced GC fraction — match the expected prefix, compared with rfind.
  3. Fraction reduces 6/8 to 3/4, normalises 1/-2, maps 0/5 to 0/1, and throws on a zero denominator.
  4. Three malformed records are rejected rather than sanitised: a header without >, a body with a digit, an empty record.
  5. Lowercase input is accepted and counted like uppercase.
  6. The run is clean under AddressSanitizer and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer, and the script prints any warning the build emitted.

The sanitizer is the part an output comparison cannot do: a fraction that prints correctly through a dangling reference would still match the string. That is why the harness builds with the sanitizers rather than only running the binary.

docs.title: 6. Why this capstone and not a bigger one
docs.text:
The sequence toolkit is small enough to hold in one's head and large enough to contain every chapter's failure mode: an owned buffer (chapter 8), a template (std::array, chapter 7), an operator with an invariant (chapter 6), an optional boundary (chapter 11), a move-only type (Sequence is copyable but the vector inside makes it a real candidate for moving, chapter 3), and an exception at a boundary (chapter 12).

The biology section builds on exactly this structure: the FASTA reader there is the same parse function with more validation, and the PDB parser is the same ownership discipline applied to a hierarchical format. The capstone is the bridge, which is why it is the last C++ page.

docs.text: labs/cpp/13_capstone/ holds only check.sh. Copy sequence_toolkit.cpp into /tmp, delete the bodies of Sequence::parse, Composition::gc_fraction and write_report, and rebuild them from this chapter with the signatures unchanged. Then add one test the script does not cover — a case you think of, not one given to you — and run your binary with the same sanitizer flags the project uses.

docs.title: Classes and Encapsulation
docs.text:
A class is a struct with a hidden first parameter, and I wish someone had told me that before I learned the access keywords. The page builds one type in the order the compiler sees it: the implicit this, then access control as a compile-time boundary, then the header/source split, then static members, then const member functions, and finally the rule I use to decide where an interface ends — one class, one header, one obvious responsibility.

A class is a struct with access control and member functions. The second part is the one that changes the object model: a member function is an ordinary function with an extra hidden parameter, and every use of this is a use of that parameter.

docs.title: 1. The hidden parameter
docs.text:
struct Point {
    double x, y;
    double norm() const { return std::sqrt(x * x + y * y); }
};

Point p{3, 4};
p.norm();

The compiler generates something equivalent to:

double Point_norm(const Point *this) { return std::sqrt(this->x * this->x + this->y * this->y); }
Point_norm(&p);

That rewrite explains three facts at once. Member functions do not increase the size of the object — there is one copy of the code, not one per instance. this is a pointer, so *this is the object and this->x is a member access. And a const member function is one whose hidden parameter is const Point *, which is why it cannot modify members.

Before I give the number, guess three sizes on x86-64: Point, a class holding one char and no functions, and a class holding one char and one virtual function. The answers are 16, 1 and 16, and only the first is obvious. When I first ran this, I had the third wrong: I expected 9, because a char plus a pointer is nine bytes, and forgot that the object's alignment has to match its widest member.

Point is 16 because it is two double, and the member function contributed nothing — there is one norm in the binary, not one per object. The single-char class is 1 because the standard requires every object of a class type to have a distinct address, so the compiler cannot shrink it to zero even though it holds one byte. Add a virtual function and the same class becomes 16: a pointer to the vtable is stored at offset 0, the char follows at offset 8, and the remaining seven bytes are padding inserted so the object's alignment matches the pointer's. That is the whole of the object model in three numbers: members cost their size, functions cost nothing per object, and virtual dispatch costs one pointer per object plus padding.

docs.title: 2. Access control is compile-time, not run-time
docs.text:
class Account {
public:
    explicit Account(double initial) : balance_(initial) {}
    double balance() const { return balance_; }
    void deposit(double amount);
private:
    double balance_;
};

private prevents the compiler from emitting code that touches balance_ from outside the class. It does not prevent anyone from reading the memory: reinterpret_cast and pointer arithmetic can reach it, and a debugger will show it. Encapsulation is a contract enforced by the type system, not a security mechanism.

The convention that makes it useful is the trailing underscore on members, which lets a parameter and a member share a name without shadowing confusion:

void Account::deposit(double amount) { balance_ += amount; }

explicit on the single-argument constructor is the second half of a useful class. Without it, Account a = 100.0; compiles as an implicit conversion; with it, the same line is an error and the author must write Account a(100.0);.

docs.title: 3. Declaration in the header, definition in the source
docs.text:
// account.h
class Account {
public:
    void deposit(double amount);
private:
    double balance_;
};

// account.cpp
#include "account.h"
void Account::deposit(double amount) { balance_ += amount; }

Splitting the two is what keeps compile times sane: change the body of deposit and only account.cpp recompiles; change the class layout and every file that includes the header recompiles. That is the reason headers should contain declarations and, where possible, no definitions.

Defining a member function inside the class body makes it implicitly inline, which is fine for one-line accessors and a poor choice for anything with a loop. The compiler may refuse to inline it and the definition then appears in every translation unit that includes the header.

docs.title: 4. static members have no this
docs.text:
class Counter {
public:
    static int total() { return total_; }
    static void reset() { total_ = 0; }
private:
    static int total_;
};

int Counter::total_ = 0;   // definition, exactly once, in a .cpp file

A static member function has no hidden parameter, so it cannot touch non-static members and it can be called without an object: Counter::total(). A static data member is one object shared by every instance — the file-scope variable from the C section, with a name scoped to the class.

C++17 allows the definition to be written inline in the header:

inline int Counter::total_ = 0;

which removes the "one definition in one .cpp" rule and the link error that follows from forgetting it. The book uses the C++17 form in examples and mentions the older form because it is what most existing code does.

docs.title: 5. const member functions, and the mutable exception
docs.text:
A const member function promises not to modify the object. It can be called on a const object, which is why accessors are const and mutators are not.

class Cache {
public:
    int lookup(int key) const {
        ++hits_;                 // error: modifying a member in a const function
        return value_;
    }
    mutable int hits_;           // deliberately exempt from the promise
};

mutable exists for exactly this case: a member that is logically not part of the object's observable value — a cache, a counter, a mutex — and may change inside a const function. Overusing it defeats the promise, which is the reason the keyword is rare in good code.

The const-correctness habit is worth forming early: mark every member function const unless it modifies the object, and mark every parameter const & unless it is modified or copied. Retrofitting constness onto an existing class is a day of work; writing it from the start costs nothing.

docs.title: 6. Interfaces: one class per header
docs.text:
// sequence.h
#pragma once
#include <cstddef>
#include <string>

class Sequence {
public:
    explicit Sequence(std::string bases);
    std::size_t size() const;
    double gc_content() const;
private:
    std::string bases_;
};

A header that declares one class, its member functions, and nothing else is the shape that keeps a codebase navigable. The alternatives — several unrelated classes in one header, or a header that includes five others because the class holds them by value — both increase the chance that a change ripples through the build.

Holding members by value in the header requires their complete types, which is why #include <string> appears. A pointer or reference member needs only a forward declaration, which is the one legitimate use of class Foo; at the top of a header.

docs.title: 7. Field note: the constructor that assigned instead of initialising
docs.text:
An early version of a class wrote this:

class Config {
public:
    Config(const std::string &path, int threads) {
        path_ = path;          // assignment in the body
        threads_ = threads;
    }
private:
    std::string path_;
    int threads_;
};

It compiles, works, and costs more than it should: every member is default-constructed first, then assigned. For a std::string that is an extra allocation and an extra deallocation per object. And for a member without a default constructor it does not compile at all.

The corrected form is the initialiser list, which the next chapter takes apart:

Config(const std::string &path, int threads) : path_(path), threads_(threads) {}

The lesson is not stylistic. Assignment-in-body is a different sequence of operations from initialisation, and the difference is visible in the constructor's cost and in whether some members can be initialised at all.

docs.title: 8. Practise
docs.text: Take code/cpp/02_classes/01_interface_split.cpp, which contains a working class with everything public, and split it into a header and a source file. The exercise in labs/cpp/02_classes/ is to include that header from two translation units, make every non-mutating member const, and keep the data private behind accessors — the compiler reports a missing const only when a const object calls the member, which is why the second translation unit exists.
