docs.title: STL Containers
docs.text:
A vector is three pointers, and once you accept that, every rule about invalidation becomes arithmetic. I start there, then capacity growth, then the invalidation table, then how I choose a container from the access pattern rather than from the name, then string as the character container, then map against a sorted vector with a measurement. The page is deliberately not a catalogue; four containers cover most of what I write.

The containers are the reason most people write C++. They are also the reason most people have a surprising number of copies, an invalidated iterator, and a std::map where a std::vector would have been faster. This page is about the three things that actually matter: layout, growth, and invalidation.

docs.title: 1. std::vector is three pointers
docs.text:
// LAB 09-01  cpp_containers/01_invalidation.cpp
std::vector<int> v;
std::cout << sizeof(v) << '\n';     // 24 on x86-64: begin, end, capacity end

Three pointers, no more. size() is end - begin, capacity() is cap_end - begin. The storage lives on the heap; the object itself is 24 bytes and can be moved between scopes at that cost.

push_back is amortised constant time: when capacity is exhausted the vector allocates a larger block — typically 2× with libstdc++ and 1.5× with MSVC — moves or copies the elements, and releases the old block. The growth factor matters: 2× guarantees amortised O(1) but wastes up to 50% memory; 1.5× wastes less and can reuse freed blocks better. Both are legal, which is why a program's memory profile can depend on the standard library it was built against.

The reuse argument is worth following once, because it explains why the two libraries disagree. Sizes in a 2× sequence go 1, 2, 4, 8, … and each new block is larger than the sum of every block released before it (1 + 2 + 4 = 7, and the next request is 8). No freed block, and no coalescing of freed blocks, can satisfy that request, so every growth asks the system for new memory. In a 1.5× sequence the sum of earlier blocks overtakes the next request (1 + 1.5 = 2.5 > 2.25), so an allocator that coalesces adjacent free blocks can often satisfy the growth from space it already owns. libstdc++ accepts the fragmentation for a simpler size sequence; MSVC accepts the extra arithmetic for better reuse.

v.reserve(1000);      // one allocation instead of log2(1000) reallocations

reserve is the single most effective optimisation in this chapter when the final size is known, and it is also the reason push_back in a loop with a known count is a code smell.

docs.title: 2. Invalidation, the rule that bites
3. Choosing a container
docs.text:
Container Layout Lookup Insert at end Iterator stability vector contiguous O(n) amortised O(1) invalidated by growth deque blocks of contiguous O(n) O(1) both ends stable except erased element list doubly linked O(n) O(1) anywhere stable except erased element map red-black tree O(log n) O(log n) stable unordered_map hash buckets O(1) average O(1) average invalidated by rehash

The default is vector. It wins on cache locality for almost every size that fits in memory, and the O(n) lookup is irrelevant when n is small or when the data is scanned anyway. map is for ordered iteration and stable iterators, not for "fast lookup" — a sorted vector with std::lower_bound is usually faster for read-heavy work and is what the sequence-alignment chapter uses.

unordered_map is a hash table with separate chaining in libstdc++ and a node-based design in MSVC; iteration order is unspecified and changes on rehash, so any code that depends on order is a defect. list is almost never the right answer: the pointer chasing costs more than the O(1) insert saves, and the memory overhead is two pointers per element.

docs.title: 4. std::string is a vector of characters
docs.text:
std::string has the same three-pointer layout plus a small-string optimisation in some implementations. It is contiguous, it grows the same way, and its iterators invalidate the same way. c_str() returns a pointer into the buffer that is invalidated by any operation that reallocates.

const char *p = s.c_str();
s += "more";        // may reallocate; p is now dangling

This is the most common string defect in code that mixes C and C++ APIs: the const char * is handed to a C function, the string is modified, and the pointer is used again. The fix is to keep the C call adjacent to the c_str() call, or to copy into a local std::string first.

docs.title: 5. Field note: the map that was a vector
docs.text:
The archived word-count program used std::map<std::string, int> and incremented per word:

std::map<std::string, int> counts;
while (in >> word) { ++counts[word]; }

Correct, and slow for a reason worth understanding: each operator[] walks a red-black tree of string comparisons, and each node is a separate allocation, so a 10 MB text touches thousands of cache lines in a random order. Replacing it with a vector<std::string> collected first and sorted afterwards changed the runtime by more than an order of magnitude on the test corpus, and produced the same output.

The generalisation: a hash map is faster than a tree map, a sorted vector is often faster than both, and the container should be chosen after measuring rather than by reputation.

Then attempt the exercise in labs/cpp/09_containers/, which asks for a word counter that is correct under reallocation and reports its own peak memory.

docs.title: Exceptions
docs.text:
An exception is a control transfer with a guarantee attached: during unwinding, destructors run. I start from that guarantee, then construction that throws, then noexcept as a promise about the move, then catching by reference, then the comparison with error codes that I use to decide which one a function should use. The cost section separates the zero-cost path from the table lookup, because most of the fear about exceptions is about the wrong path.

An exception is a non-local exit with a defined cleanup: the stack unwinds, every fully constructed object in the unwound frames is destroyed, and control arrives at a matching handler. That cleanup is what makes exceptions compatible with RAII and what makes them dangerous in code that has not adopted RAII.

docs.title: 1. What unwinding guarantees
docs.text:
// LAB 12-01  cpp_exceptions/01_stack_unwind.cpp
void inner() {
    Buffer b(128);            // RAII
    int *raw = new int[64];   // not RAII
    throw std::runtime_error("boom");
    // b's destructor runs during unwinding; raw leaks
}

The destructor of b runs because b is fully constructed. The raw pointer leaks because a pointer is not an owner — nothing knows to release it. This is the single argument for RAII that matters: without it, every function between the throw and the catch becomes a leak site.

The guarantee is precisely stated: objects with automatic storage duration that have completed construction are destroyed, in reverse order of construction. Objects whose construction was interrupted are not destroyed — only their already-constructed members are.

docs.title: 2. The constructor that throws
docs.text:
class Connection {
public:
    Connection(const std::string &host) : socket_(open_socket(host)), buffer_(new char[4096]) {}
    // if open_socket throws, socket_ is not constructed; nothing to destroy
    // if new throws, socket_ IS destroyed; buffer_ is not
private:
    Socket socket_;
    char *buffer_;
};

The rule is that the destructor does not run for the object whose constructor threw, but the destructors do run for its completed members. So a constructor that acquires two resources and throws after the first has already released the first correctly — as long as the first is held by an RAII member rather than a raw pointer.

This is why the labs require a constructor that throws midway: it is the case a hand-written destructor cannot handle, because the object never existed.

docs.title: 3. noexcept, and where it must be
docs.text:
class Buffer {
public:
    Buffer(Buffer &&other) noexcept;    // required for vector to move instead of copy
};

A move constructor that is not noexcept makes std::vector copy on reallocation, because a throwing move cannot be rolled back. The performance difference is measurable for large element types and invisible in the code.

vector does not test the exception specification by hand. Reallocation calls std::move_if_noexcept, a function whose return type is chosen by the traits of T: it yields an rvalue reference when the move constructor is noexcept, or when T has no copy constructor to fall back on, and a const T & otherwise. So the decision is made at compile time, per element type, and the cost of a missing noexcept is a silent switch from moving to copying for every element in every reallocation of every vector of that type. When std::string's move constructor is not marked noexcept, a std::vector<std::string> copies each element on every reallocation instead of moving it, and the cost scales with the number of reallocations and the length of each string. Nothing in the source shows it: the only difference is a missing keyword in a declaration.

A destructor is implicitly noexcept, and a destructor that throws during unwinding calls std::terminate. If a cleanup can fail, the failure belongs in an explicit close() that the caller invokes before destruction, with its error handled there.

noexcept is also an optimisation hint: a call to a noexcept function does not need the unwinding machinery around it, so the code is smaller.

docs.title: 4. Catch by reference, always
docs.text:
try { ... }
catch (const std::runtime_error &e) { std::cerr << e.what() << '\n'; }
catch (const std::exception &e) { std::cerr << "other: " << e.what() << '\n'; }

Catching by value slices the exception: a derived exception type is copied into a base object and the derived part is lost. Catching by reference preserves the dynamic type and avoids a copy. catch (...) catches everything, including non-std::exception types, and should be used only to rethrow or to log at a boundary.

Order matters: handlers are tried in order, so the most derived type must come first. A catch (const std::exception &) before a catch (const std::runtime_error &) makes the second unreachable.

The complementary failure is a handler that matches nothing. std::out_of_range derives from std::logic_error, not from std::runtime_error — the hierarchy is exception → logic_error → out_of_range — so a catch (const std::runtime_error &) written for an out-of-range index does not catch it, and the exception reaches std::terminate. The repair is to catch std::logic_error & or std::exception &. code/cpp/12_exceptions/01_stack_unwind.cpp throws an out_of_range and catches it by base class for exactly this reason.

docs.title: 5. Exceptions versus error codes
6. Performance, honestly
docs.text:
The zero-cost claim is about the non-throwing path: with table-based unwinding, entering a try block costs nothing at runtime, and the tables live in a separate section. Throwing is expensive — on the order of a microsecond for the first throw in a process, faster afterwards — which is why exceptions are for exceptional conditions and not for control flow.

A loop that throws on a missing key in a map, caught immediately, is slower than find plus a check by orders of magnitude. The rule: exceptions for "this cannot continue", return values for "this did not work, try another way".

docs.title: 7. Field note: the error code nobody checked
docs.text:
The archived mocal.c allocated an array of strings and checked every allocation:

str[i] = (char *)malloc(64);
if (str[i] == NULL) { printf("malloc failed\n"); }
// ... and then continued to use str[i] anyway

The check printed a message and fell through. A null buffer was then passed to strcpy, which is undefined behaviour and, in practice, a crash. The error was detected and not propagated: the code had the information and no way to act on it, because the function returned void.

The C++ repair is either an exception (throw std::bad_alloc{}, which is what new does) or a return type that can express failure. Both make the caller unable to ignore the failure, which is the difference between detecting an error and handling one.

docs.title: 8. Practise
docs.text: Build code/cpp/12_exceptions/01_stack_unwind.cpp and read the destructor order: the RAII member and the raw pointer are both released during unwinding, because Mixed has a destructor. Delete that destructor, rebuild, and ASan reports the block as leaked at exit — that one-line experiment is the argument for RAII. Then attempt the exercise in labs/cpp/12_exceptions/: a constructor that throws after acquiring a resource, asserting zero leaks and a correct error message.

docs.title: The Bridge from C
docs.text:
The first C++ page is not a tour of features; it is a list of what changed and what did not. I start with the reference, because 'a reference is a pointer in disguise' is the sentence that makes every later overload resolution misread. Then overload resolution, then namespaces, then the cost of iostream, then the one line I still write rarely: new. By the end you should be able to say which of your C habits survive the move and which quietly change meaning.

C++ is not C with classes added; it is a different language that happens to be source-compatible with most of C. The differences that matter first are not the famous ones — templates and virtual functions come later — but four small ones that change how you write every function: references, overloading, namespaces, and the fact that main can end without a return.

docs.title: 1. References are not pointers with nicer syntax
docs.text:
void by_pointer(int *p) { *p = 7; }
void by_reference(int &r) { r = 7; }

int x = 1;
by_pointer(&x);   // the caller writes the address
by_reference(x);  // the caller writes the object

A reference is an alias for an existing object. It has no null state, it cannot be reseated, and it cannot be used for arithmetic. Those three properties are the reason C++ functions prefer it: a const std::string & parameter means "I will not copy this and I will not modify it", and the call site cannot accidentally pass a null.

The cost is that a reference looks exactly like the object at the call site, which hides the fact that a function may modify the argument. by_reference(x) above gives no visual hint that x changes. That is a genuine readability cost, and the convention that mitigates it is const on everything that does not change — a promise visible in the signature and enforced by the compiler.

// LAB 01-01  cpp_bridge/01_ref_vs_ptr.cpp
int &pick(bool first, int &a, int &b) { return first ? a : b; }

Returning a reference is legal and is how operator[] and std::map::at work. Returning a reference to a local is the same defect as returning a pointer to a local, with the same consequence.

docs.title: 2. Overloading, and the ranking that decides
docs.text:
Two functions with the same name and different parameters are resolved by a ranking that is stricter than most readers expect:

void show(int);
void show(double);
void show(const char *);

show(42);        // exact match: int
show(3.14f);     // float -> double promotion beats float -> int conversion
show("text");    // const char[5] decays to const char *
show('a');       // char -> int promotion, so show(int)

The last line is the one to remember: 'a' is a char, char promotes to int exactly, and show(int) wins even though show(const char *) looks like the natural candidate. An overload set that makes this surprising is an overload set that should be renamed.

Ambiguity is a compile error, not a silent choice:

void f(long);
void f(unsigned long);
f(0);            // ambiguous: int converts equally to both

The fix is an explicit cast at the call site or, better, two differently named functions.

docs.title: 3. Namespaces are a naming tool, not a scope hack
docs.text:
namespace craft {
constexpr double pi = 3.14159265358979323846;
double scale(double, double);
}

A namespace prevents collisions between libraries, and it costs nothing at run time. The two habits that matter: never write using namespace std; in a header, because it imposes the entire standard library on every file that includes the header; and prefer a short namespace alias inside a .cpp file over a using directive at file scope.

using namespace in a header is the most common cause of an ambiguity that appears only when two headers are included together, which is a defect that shows up in a consumer's build and not in yours.

docs.title: 4. iostream is slower than stdio, and that is a choice
docs.text:
std::ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
std::cin.tie(nullptr);

By default std::cin and std::cout are synchronised with C's stdin and stdout, which makes every read and write go through the C library's buffer as well. The two lines above disable the synchronisation; the cost is that mixing printf and cout no longer guarantees ordering, and the gain is typically a factor of two to four on input-heavy programs.

The reason to care appears in the biology section: parsing a 30,000-atom file with cin >> unmodified is several times slower than with fscanf, and the difference is not the format but the synchronisation.

For output, '\n' rather than std::endl avoids a flush per line. std::endl flushes, which is useful for a progress indicator and ruinous for a loop.

docs.title: 5. new and delete exist, and you should rarely use them
docs.text:
int *p = new int[10];    // allocation, no initialisation
delete[] p;              // must match new[]

new throws std::bad_alloc on failure rather than returning null, which is the semantic difference from malloc. Everything else about manual new/delete is the same obligation as chapter 7 of the C section — one owner, one release — and the same defects: leaks on an early return, double delete, delete of a pointer that was not allocated by new.

The reason this book defers new to a later chapter is that the correct amount of manual new in modern C++ is close to zero. std::vector, std::string and std::unique_ptr allocate for you and release in a destructor, which is the subject of the RAII chapter. new remains in the text because it appears in every legacy codebase and because understanding it is a precondition for understanding what the containers do internally.

docs.title: 6. What carries over unchanged
docs.text: Arrays, pointers, sizeof, the object model, undefined behaviour, the stack, the heap, the preprocessor and translation units. C++ does not fix any of them. It adds tools that let you avoid them, and it adds new ways to get them wrong — which is the honest summary of the next twelve chapters.

docs.title: 7. Practise
docs.text: Copy code/cpp/01_bridge/01_ref_vs_ptr.cpp into /tmp, compile it, and change scale_ref to take a Point * instead of a Point &. Observe what happens to the call sites: how many & and * appear, whether a caller can now pass nullptr, and whether the function still compiles unchanged at the point where alias = q renames nothing. Then read code/cpp/01_bridge/README.md and run bash labs/cpp/01_bridge/check.sh: the program asserts the two properties the change breaks — a reference cannot be null, and assigning through a reference copies into the referent instead of rebinding — so the rewrite is measured against them. The rewrite is the exercise; the script only proves the baseline still holds.

  • Construction and Lifetime starts the question that dominates the section: when does an object begin and end.
  • Compiler and Flags lists the C++-specific warnings this chapter assumes.

docs.title: Inheritance
docs.text:
Every inheritance rule I know falls out of one fact: a derived object contains a complete base object at its start, followed by its own members. So I measure the base subobject first, then the constructor and destructor chain, then protected as a narrower door rather than a default, then the non-virtual destructor that leaks silently, then name hiding, then slicing, and multiple inheritance last because the diamond is the only place the layout becomes visible in a way you cannot ignore.

Inheritance is a layout decision before it is an abstraction. A derived object contains a complete base object at its start, followed by its own members, and every rule about construction, destruction, slicing and casting follows from that layout.

docs.title: 1. The base subobject
docs.text:
// LAB 04-01  cpp_inheritance/01_layout_inherit.cpp
struct Base { int a; };
struct Derived : Base { int b; };

Derived d;
std::cout << sizeof(Base) << ' ' << sizeof(Derived) << '\n';   // 4 8
std::cout << &d << ' ' << static_cast<Base *>(&d) << '\n';     // same address

Derived is 8 bytes: four for Base::a at offset 0, four for Derived::b at offset 4. The address of the derived object and the address of its base subobject are identical here, which is what makes a static_cast from Derived * to Base * free. It is not free in every case — a base with virtual functions adds a vptr, and multiple inheritance places the second base at a nonzero offset — but the single, non-virtual case is the common one.

Adding a virtual function to Base changes sizeof(Derived) to 16 on x86-64: 8 for the vptr, 4 for a, 4 for b (with padding). The vptr is the next chapter's subject; here the point is that the layout is the thing to measure, not the thing to assume.

docs.title: 2. Construction and destruction chains
docs.text:
Construction runs base first, then members, then the derived constructor body:

struct Base { Base() { std::cout << "Base\n"; } };
struct Derived : Base {
    Derived() { std::cout << "Derived\n"; }   // Base already built
};

Destruction runs the reverse: derived body, derived members, base. The asymmetry is deliberate, because a derived destructor may use members of the base that must still be alive; it is also the reason a base destructor must not assume the derived part is still intact.

The base constructor is selected in the initialiser list, and that is the only place it can be selected:

Derived(int n) : Base(n), b_(n) {}

Omitting it calls the base's default constructor, which fails if there is none.

docs.title: 3. protected is a narrow door
docs.text:
Access Same class Derived class Anyone else public yes yes yes protected yes yes no private yes no no

protected exists so a derived class can reach the base's internals without exposing them publicly. In practice it is the most fragile of the three, because it makes the base's representation part of the base's contract with every derived class, and changing it breaks code the base author cannot see.

The convention that works is private members plus protected accessor functions, which keeps the representation private while giving derived classes a stable interface. Public data members are acceptable in a struct used as a bundle and not in a class with behaviour.

docs.title: 4. Non-virtual destructors and the leak they cause
docs.text:
struct Base { ~Base() {} };                      // not virtual
struct Derived : Base { std::vector<int> v; };

Base *p = new Derived;
delete p;                                        // undefined: ~Derived never runs

delete p is a two-part operation, and both parts read the static type. First it calls the destructor that Base * selects, which is ~Base; ~Derived never runs, so the vector's destructor never runs and its buffer is never released. Second it calls operator delete, and the size handed to it is computed from sizeof(Base) unless a sized deallocation for the dynamic type is available — and with a non-virtual destructor there is no way to reach ~Derived, hence no way to learn the real size. The block was allocated as sizeof(Derived) and may be released as sizeof(Base), which is undefined behaviour before it is even a leak.

The compiler may warn (-Wdelete-non-virtual-dtor with -Wall in GCC and Clang), and the warning is one of the few that is almost always right.

The rule: a class intended to be deleted through a base pointer needs a virtual destructor. A class not intended for that does not, and adding one costs a vptr to every object.

struct Base { virtual ~Base() = default; };

docs.title: 5. Name hiding is not overriding
docs.text:
struct Base { void f(int); };
struct Derived : Base { void f(double); };   // hides Base::f(int), does not overload it

Derived d;
d.f(1);        // calls Derived::f(double); Base::f(int) is invisible

Overload resolution happens within one scope. A derived-class function with the same name as a base-class function hides every base overload, regardless of parameters. The repair is a using declaration:

struct Derived : Base {
    using Base::f;      // bring the base overloads back into this scope
    void f(double);
};

This is one of the few cases where a using declaration inside a class is necessary rather than stylistic, and it appears in real code whenever a derived class adds an overload.

docs.title: 6. Slicing, in one line
docs.text:
Derived d;
Base b = d;         // slices: only the Base part is copied

Assignment to a base object copies the base subobject and discards the rest. If Derived held a std::vector, the slice has no vector; if it held a std::string, the slice has a copy of the base's string and nothing else. No warning, no error, and the object looks valid.

Slicing is the reason polymorphic interfaces are passed by reference or pointer, never by value. The chapter on polymorphism returns to this with a virtual function, where the consequence is worse: the sliced object calls the base's implementation, so the polymorphism silently disappears.

docs.title: 7. Multiple inheritance, and the diamond
docs.text:
Two bases place the second at a nonzero offset, which is why a cast from Derived * to the second Base * adjusts the pointer. If both bases derive from a common ancestor, the object contains two copies of that ancestor unless the inheritance is virtual:

struct A { int x; };
struct B : virtual A {};
struct C : virtual A {};
struct D : B, C {};        // one shared A, reached through a pointer

Virtual inheritance solves the duplicate-ancestor problem and introduces a cost: the path from D to A is indirect, so the cast is a load rather than an addition. The book uses multiple inheritance exactly once, in the structure model, and the page states why.

docs.title: 8. Field note: the base class that was copied by value
docs.text:
A function took its parameter by value:

void report(Shape shape);        // the original signature

Shape was an abstract base with a virtual area(). Every call sliced the argument, so shape.area() always called the base's implementation — which, being pure virtual, meant the call was resolved to a stub that returned zero. The function printed zero for every shape and nobody noticed, because zero is a plausible area for an empty polygon.

The repair was one character: const Shape &. The lesson is that a polymorphic type in a by-value parameter is not a subtle bug; it is a category error, and the compiler cannot catch it because slicing a base is legal.

Then attempt the exercise in labs/cpp/04_inheritance/, which requires a base with a virtual destructor and a derived class whose members are released exactly once, verified under AddressSanitizer.

docs.title: Construction and Lifetime
docs.text:
Construction is not assignment, and the difference is invisible until a member has no default constructor. I start with the member initialisation list because that is where the difference shows up, then destructor order, then the copy constructor and the copy assignment that I got wrong in the same way twice, then the rule of three and the rule of zero. explicit is the last section because implicit conversion is the failure that happens at a call site you never wrote.

This is the chapter the rest of the C++ section rests on. An object's lifetime is a sequence with a defined order: base classes, then members in declaration order, then the constructor body; and at the end, the exact reverse. Every resource-management decision later in the book is an application of that order.

docs.title: 1. Initialisation is not assignment
docs.text:
// LAB 03-01  cpp_lifetime/01_ctor_order.cpp
#include <iostream>

struct Noisy {
    Noisy(const char *tag) { std::cout << "ctor " << tag << '\n'; }
    ~Noisy() { std::cout << "dtor " << tag_ << '\n'; }
    const char *tag_;
};

struct Host {
    Noisy a{"a"};
    Noisy b{"b"};
    Noisy c{"c"};
    Host() : c{"c"}, b{"b"}, a{"a"} { std::cout << "body\n"; }
};

The output is:

ctor a
ctor b
ctor c
body

not the order written in the initialiser list. Members are constructed in declaration order, always. The initialiser list order is ignored, and a compiler with -Wall warns (-Wreorder) when the two disagree. The warning exists because the mismatch means the author believes one thing about the object and the compiler does another.

The reason is mechanical: the object is a contiguous layout, so its members must be built from the lowest offset up. Declaration order is offset order.

docs.title: 2. Why the initialiser list matters
docs.text:
There are three cases where only the initialiser list works, and all three appear in real code:

class Buffer {
public:
    Buffer(std::size_t n)
        : data_(n),            // construct with the right size, one allocation
          size_(n),
          owner_(nullptr) {}
private:
    std::vector<int> data_;
    std::size_t size_;
    int *owner_;
};

A const member must be initialised, because it cannot be assigned afterwards. A reference member must be initialised, for the same reason. And a member without a default constructor must be initialised, because there is nothing to assign to. Assignment in the body cannot handle any of the three, and for everything else it costs an extra construct-and-destroy cycle.

docs.title: 3. Destruction runs backwards
docs.text:
Members are destroyed in reverse declaration order, after the destructor body runs. Base classes are destroyed last. The reason is the mirror of the construction order: an object may not be torn down before the things it depends on.

~Host() { std::cout << "dtor body\n"; }   // runs first
// then c, then b, then a

A destructor that throws is a defect: it may run during stack unwinding, and two exceptions in flight terminate the program. Destructors should be noexcept by default — which they are, implicitly — and anything that can fail belongs in an explicit close() called before destruction.

docs.title: 4. Copying, and the rule of three
docs.text:
The compiler generates a copy constructor, a copy assignment, a move constructor and a move assignment unless you declare them. The generated versions copy every member, which is correct exactly when every member manages itself.

class Raw {
public:
    explicit Raw(std::size_t n) : data_(new int[n]), size_(n) {}
    ~Raw() { delete[] data_; }
private:
    int *data_;
    std::size_t size_;
};

Here the generated copy constructor copies the pointer, so two objects own the same block and both destructors delete it — a double free. The rule of three says: if you need a destructor, you probably need a copy constructor and a copy assignment too, because the destructor is evidence that a member is owned rawly.

Raw(const Raw &other) : data_(new int[other.size_]), size_(other.size_) {
    std::copy(other.data_, other.data_ + size_, data_);
}
Raw &operator=(const Raw &other) {
    Raw copy(other);          // copy first: if allocation throws, *this is untouched
    std::swap(data_, copy.data_);
    std::swap(size_, copy.size_);
    return *this;             // copy's destructor releases the old block
}

Before accepting that form, write the naive one and break it three times:

Raw &operator=(const Raw &other) {
    delete[] data_;                        // 1
    data_ = new int[other.size_];          // 2
    size_ = other.size_;
    std::copy(other.data_, other.data_ + size_, data_);   // 3
}

Line 1 is the first failure: a = a deletes the block that other.data_ still points at, and line 3 then copies from freed memory. Line 2 is the second: if new throws std::bad_alloc, the object is left holding a dangling pointer, its destructor deletes it again, and one allocation is freed twice. Line 3 is the third, and it only appears once the element type is something with a throwing assignment: the object ends up with a buffer of the new size, a size field that agrees with it, and elements that were never copied.

Copy-and-swap removes all three by ordering: the new state is fully built in a temporary before anything in *this changes, so a throw at any point leaves the original intact, and self-assignment is harmless because the copy is made before the old block is released. The swap itself cannot fail, which is why it is the last step rather than the first.

That ordering is also why the assignment returns by reference: a = b = c needs the result of the inner assignment to be the object, and returning *this gives that without a copy.

docs.title: 5. Rule of zero, and why it is better
docs.text:
The modern answer is to not own anything rawly. A class whose members are std::vector, std::string and std::unique_ptr needs no destructor, no copy constructor, no assignment operator — the generated ones are correct because each member manages itself.

class Clean {
private:
    std::vector<int> data_;
    std::string name_;
};

sizeof(Clean) is the size of a vector plus the size of a string; copying it copies the buffers deeply; destruction releases them. Nothing is declared, and nothing can be forgotten. This is the target state, and the RAII chapter explains the mechanisms that make it possible.

docs.title: 6. explicit, and the conversions it prevents
docs.text:
class Threads {
public:
    explicit Threads(int n) : n_(n) {}
private:
    int n_;
};

Threads t = 4;      // error with explicit, compiles without

An implicit single-argument constructor is a conversion operator the author did not intend. It makes f(Threads) callable with an int, which is rarely wanted and occasionally catastrophic — a function taking a std::string called with a const char * is the same pattern.

docs.title: 7. Field note: the members that were assigned in the body
docs.text:
The original person.cpp in the archive constructed its object like this:

Person::person::person() {
    person::name = "";
    person::age = 0;
    person::sex = 'M';
}

Three assignments in the body, where an initialiser list belongs. Two costs follow immediately: std::string name is default-constructed and then assigned, which is an allocation followed by a deallocation for every object; and if a member were const or a reference, the code would not compile at all.

The corrected form is one line:

Person::person::person() : name_(""), age_(0), sex_('M') {}

The same file has a second defect worth recording: person.h opens with #ifndef PERSON_H and never defines the macro, so the guard does nothing and only #pragma once prevents double inclusion. A header guard without its #define is a guard that has been copied and half-edited, which is exactly the kind of defect that survives for years because every compiler in use supports #pragma once.

docs.title: 8. Practise
docs.text: Build code/cpp/03_lifetime/01_ctor_order.cpp, predict the output before running it, then move c to the front of the declaration list and predict again. The program asserts that members initialise in declaration order regardless of the initialiser list, that constructed is zero after a const-reference call, and that copies are counted rather than assumed. After that, labs/cpp/03_lifetime/ asks you to add a copy constructor and a destructor to a class that owns a new[] buffer, and to check under AddressSanitizer that no block is freed twice.

docs.title: Modern C++
docs.text:
The modern features are not a style; they are a set of defaults that remove a class of bug each. I go through the ones I actually use — auto, structured bindings, if with initialiser, string_view, optional, [[nodiscard]], constexpr — and for each I name the bug it removes. The last section lists what these features did not fix, because the point of the chapter is judgement rather than vocabulary.

This page collects the features that change how code is written rather than what it computes. Each one is here because it removes a defect class, not because it is new.

docs.title: 1. auto removes the redundant, not the type
docs.text:
// LAB 11-01  cpp_modern/01_auto_and_structured.cpp
auto n = v.size();            // std::size_t, not int
auto it = counts.find(key);   // iterator type

The reason to use auto is that the type on the left of a declaration is often a restatement of the right, and a wrong restatement is a silent conversion. int n = v.size() truncates on a 64-bit platform where size() is std::size_t; auto n = v.size() cannot.

The reason not to use it is when the type is the information — auto ratio = 1 / 2; is an int zero, and writing double ratio would have caught it. Use auto when the initialiser makes the type obvious; write the type when it does not.

auto deduces exactly as a function template would, which means it strips the reference and the top-level const unless you ask for them:

auto a = v[0];          // int: a copy
auto &b = v[0];         // int &: a reference
const auto &c = v[0];   // const int &: read-only reference
auto &&d = v[0];        // int &: forwarding reference, collapses to int&

The fourth form is the one people avoid because it looks like an rvalue reference; for a forwarding reference the && collapses to & when the initialiser is an lvalue, which is why auto && in a range-for binds both lvalues and temporaries.

There is a case where auto does not give a value at all: std::vector<bool> is a partial specialisation that stores bits, so v[0] returns a proxy object rather than a bool &. auto f = flags[0]; keeps the proxy, the proxy holds a pointer into the vector's bit storage, and it is as dangling as any iterator once the vector is gone. Writing bool f = flags[0]; forces the conversion and ends the lifetime problem — an example of the rule above, since the type here is the information.

docs.title: 2. Structured bindings
docs.text:
std::map<std::string, int> m;
for (const auto &[word, count] : m) { std::cout << word << ' ' << count << '\n'; }

auto [it, inserted] = m.try_emplace(key, 0);

The [it, inserted] form is the one that removes a real defect class: before C++17, m.insert(...) returned a pair and code often checked inserted wrongly, or ignored the returned iterator. The binding makes both parts visible and named.

Structured bindings also work on arrays and on any aggregate with public members:

struct Point { double x, y, z; };
Point p{1, 2, 3};
auto [x, y, z] = p;

docs.title: 3. if and switch with an initialiser
docs.text:
if (auto it = m.find(key); it != m.end()) { use(it->second); }

The declared name is scoped to the if, which removes the idiom of declaring an iterator before the condition and reusing it afterwards. The same form exists for switch, where it is genuinely useful for a lock or a lookup that the cases share.

docs.title: 4. string_view is a borrow, not a string
docs.text:
void report(std::string_view name);      // no copy, no allocation

string_view is a pointer and a length. It does not own the characters, it cannot grow, and it must not outlive the buffer it views.

std::string_view sv = std::string("temp");   // dangling immediately
std::string_view sv2 = s.substr(0, 10);      // s must outlive sv2

The second form is the subtle one: substr on a std::string returns a new std::string, which converts to a view whose buffer dies at the end of the expression. The two-line version is correct because the temporary lives until the next statement; the assignment to a view is a defect.

string_view parameters are the correct way to accept text without copying, and the biology section uses them for every FASTA line.

docs.title: 5. std::optional is a value that may be absent
docs.text:
std::optional<std::size_t> find_gc_start(std::string_view seq);

The return type says "there may be no answer" in the signature. The alternative — returning -1 or a sentinel — encodes the absence in a value that a caller can forget to check. optional requires a check through has_value() or the value itself, and value() throws if absent.

The cost is one byte of flag plus the size of T, and optional<T&> is not allowed — a reference has no null state to represent.

docs.title: 6. [[nodiscard]] and the attributes that matter
docs.text:
[[nodiscard]] int parse_header(std::string_view line);

The compiler warns when the return value is discarded, which catches the defect where a function returns an error code and the caller ignores it. [[nodiscard]] on a constructor-like factory is the highest-value use, because discarding its result means the work was wasted.

[[maybe_unused]] on a parameter silences the warning for a parameter kept for interface compatibility, and it documents that the silence is deliberate rather than an oversight.

docs.title: 7. constexpr moves work to compile time
docs.text:
constexpr std::size_t kMaxName = 64;
constexpr double kGasConstant = 8.314;

constexpr int popcount(std::uint32_t x) { return x == 0 ? 0 : 1 + popcount(x & (x - 1)); }

A constexpr function can be evaluated at compile time when all inputs are constant; otherwise it is an ordinary function. This is the mechanism behind std::array<int, N>, template non-type parameters, and the lookup tables in the bit-manipulation chapter.

consteval (C++20) forces compile-time evaluation; constinit forces static initialisation order. Neither is needed for this book's code, but a reader meeting them in a codebase should know they exist.

docs.title: 8. What modern C++ does not fix
docs.text: The features above reduce defect classes; they do not remove the need to understand layout. auto still copies when the initialiser is an lvalue, string_view still dangles, optional still requires the check. The features make the correct code shorter, which is the whole claim — not that the correct code is automatic.

docs.title: 9. Field note: the endl in the loop
docs.text:
A program printing one line per record used std::endl:

for (const auto &r : records) { std::cout << r.name << std::endl; }

std::endl is not a newline; it is a newline plus a stream flush. Flushing per line turns a buffered write into one system call per record, and on a ten-million-line output the difference is roughly a factor of thirty. The repair is '\n' in the loop and a single flush at the end.

The same file had using namespace std; at global scope in a header, which made every std:: name visible to every translation unit that included it and, in one case, made a local count ambiguous with std::count. The two changes — '\n' and removing the using-directive from the header — are the most common clean-ups in transitioning a course project to a codebase.

docs.title: Operator Overloading
docs.text:
An operator is a function with a strange name, and the first question is always whether it should be a member. I start with that question, then the invariant that an operator must preserve, then return types — reference for assignment, value for arithmetic — then the stream operators that must be non-members, then <=> and the rewrites it saves. The last section is the list of operators I would leave alone, with the reason for each.

An overloaded operator is a function with an unusual name. The name is chosen by the compiler from the syntax, the return type follows the usual rules, and the only genuinely new question is whether the function should be a member.

docs.title: 1. Member or non-member
2. The invariant is the whole class
docs.text:
A Fraction that does not reduce is a class that violates its own invariant, and every operator must restore it:

Fraction::Fraction(long num, long den) : num_(num), den_(den) {
    if (den_ == 0) { throw std::invalid_argument("zero denominator"); }
    normalise();
}

void Fraction::normalise() {
    if (den_ < 0) { num_ = -num_; den_ = -den_; }        // keep the sign in the numerator
    long g = std::gcd(num_, den_);
    num_ /= g;
    den_ /= g;
}

Two decisions are embedded there. The sign is normalised into the numerator so that two equal fractions have identical representations, which makes operator== a comparison of two fields. And the denominator is checked in the constructor, so no Fraction object can exist in an invalid state — the invariant is established once rather than re-checked in every operator.

std::gcd is C++17 and lives in <numeric>. Before that, a hand-written Euclid loop was the standard.

docs.title: 3. Return types carry meaning
docs.text:
Fraction operator+(const Fraction &rhs) const {          // returns a new value
    return Fraction(num_ * rhs.den_ + rhs.num_ * den_, den_ * rhs.den_);
}

Fraction &operator+=(const Fraction &rhs) {              // returns *this by reference
    *this = *this + rhs;
    return *this;
}

+ returns by value because the result is a new object; += returns by reference so that a += b += c works and so that the result can be used as an lvalue. Returning const Fraction from + was a 1990s fashion intended to prevent a + b = c; it also prevented moves and is now considered a defect.

docs.title: 4. Stream operators must be non-members
docs.text:
friend std::ostream &operator<<(std::ostream &os, const Fraction &f) {
    return os << f.num_ << '/' << f.den_;
}

The left operand is std::ostream, so a member is impossible. The function returns the stream by reference so that chaining works: os << a << b is operator<<(operator<<(os, a), b).

Making it a friend gives access to the private members without adding an accessor. The alternative — a public num() and den() — is also acceptable and is what the standard library style prefers.

docs.title: 5. Comparison, and <=>
docs.text:
friend bool operator==(const Fraction &a, const Fraction &b) {
    return a.num_ == b.num_ && a.den_ == b.den_;
}

friend auto operator<=>(const Fraction &a, const Fraction &b) {
    return a.num_ * b.den_ <=> b.num_ * a.den_;      // C++20
}

The three-way comparison returns a comparison category, and the compiler derives <, <=, >, >= from it. Because the invariant keeps denominators positive and fractions reduced, comparing cross-multiplied numerators is exact — no floating point, no tolerance question.

Exact is not the same as safe. Cross multiplication multiplies two long values, and two values near 2^31 produce a product near 2^62, which is still inside a signed 64-bit integer but only by a factor of two — one more doubling and the comparison silently wraps into a negative number, so 3/4000000000 < 2/4000000000 becomes true. The lab's five-value table never comes close to that boundary, which is exactly how such a bug survives a test suite. For a general rational type I compare through __int128 for the product, or compare by long division digit by digit and never materialise the product at all.

Pre-C++20 code writes each of the six operators by hand, which is six places to make the same mistake. The lab accepts either form and checks that all six agree on a table of values.

docs.title: 6. What not to overload
docs.text:
Three operators should be left alone in almost every codebase:

&&, || and , cannot be short-circuited or sequenced once overloaded, because the overload is an ordinary function call and both operands are evaluated. A class that overloads && has silently changed the meaning of a very common expression.

operator& on a type that also has an address is confusing, and overloading operator new/operator delete for a class changes allocation globally for that type, which is a decision for a memory chapter, not a value-type chapter.

operator T() — an implicit conversion operator — is the one to be most careful with. It allows a class to be used where a T is expected, and a bool conversion in particular makes the object usable in every condition, including the ones where the author meant to compare.

explicit operator bool() const;    // explicit: usable in if, not in int arithmetic

docs.title: 7. Field note: the division that was never reduced
docs.text:
The archived fraction.h implemented all four arithmetic operators and reduced none of them:

fraction operator*(fraction beMul) {
    fraction result(0, 1);
    result.denominator = fraction::denominator * beMul.denominator;
    result.numerator = fraction::numerator * beMul.numerator;
    return result;                       // 2/3 * 3/2 is stored as 6/6
}

2/3 * 3/2 printed as 6/6. The arithmetic was correct and the representation was not, so operator== — had one existed — would have reported 6/6 != 1/1. The class had an invariant in the author's head and nothing enforcing it in the object.

The repair is the normalise() call in the constructor, which makes the invariant structural. The lesson generalises: an invariant that is only maintained by the functions that happen to remember it is not an invariant, it is a hope.

  • STL Algorithms supplies comparators that replace operator overloads in generic code.

docs.title: Polymorphism
docs.text:
I keep the words apart: virtual dispatch is a mechanism, polymorphism is a design consequence. The page measures the vtable in a small program, then adds override and final, then derives a pure interface, then demonstrates slicing with a function that takes a base by value. The cost section is numerical rather than rhetorical: one indirection, one branch, and a devirtualisation that the optimiser will do when it can prove the dynamic type.

A virtual function is a pointer stored in the object. That single sentence explains the layout, the cost, the slicing defect, and why a virtual call cannot be inlined without devirtualisation.

mindmap
  root((Virtual call))
    Object
      vptr at offset 0
      data members after
    Vtable
      one per class
      slot for makeSound
      slot for area
    Dispatch
      load vptr from object
      index the slot
      indirect call

docs.title: 1. The layout, measured
docs.text:
// LAB 05-01  cpp_polymorphism/01_vtable_probe.cpp
struct Animal {
    virtual void speak() { std::cout << "generic\n"; }
    virtual ~Animal() = default;
    int weight;
};

sizeof(Animal) is 16 on x86-64: 8 for the vptr, 4 for weight, 4 for padding. The vptr is the first member, which is why a base subobject and the derived object share an address even when virtual functions are present.

Animal has a vtable of its own, one per class, stored once in the read-only data segment. The vptr in each object points at that table. Calling speak compiles to roughly:

Animal *a = ...;
a->vptr[0](a);      // load the pointer, index slot 0, pass this explicitly

Three operations where a non-virtual call would be one. The indirect call also defeats inlining, which is the larger cost in a tight loop.

docs.title: 2. Overriding, override, and final
docs.text:
struct Dog : Animal {
    void speak() override { std::cout << "woof\n"; }
};

override is optional and should never be omitted. It asks the compiler to verify that the function really overrides a base virtual function; without it, a signature mismatch — a missing const, a different parameter type — silently creates a new function that hides the base one. The result compiles, runs, and calls the base implementation, which is the failure mode override exists to prevent.

final on a virtual function tells the compiler no further override is possible, which enables devirtualisation in the same translation unit. final on a class does the same for all its functions.

struct Cat final : Animal { void speak() override; };

docs.title: 3. Pure virtual and abstract
docs.text:
struct Shape {
    virtual double area() const = 0;
    virtual ~Shape() = default;
};

= 0 makes the function pure: the class cannot be instantiated, and any derived class that does not define it remains abstract. The vtable slot for a pure virtual is typically a stub that calls __cxa_pure_virtual, which aborts — so a call through a partially constructed object terminates rather than returning garbage. That abort is a feature: it converts a lifetime defect into a diagnosable one.

An abstract class with a virtual destructor is the correct base for a polymorphic hierarchy. Without the virtual destructor, deleting through the base leaks the derived part, as the previous chapter showed.

docs.title: 4. Slicing removes the polymorphism, not just the data
docs.text:
struct Circle : Shape { double r; double area() const override { return 3.14 * r * r; } };

Circle c{2.0};
Shape s = c;            // sliced
s.area();               // calls Shape's slot -> the pure-virtual stub, or a wrong value

Shape s = c; reads like a conversion, and it is worth slowing down to see that it is a construction in three steps. The compiler picks Shape's copy constructor, because the declared type of s is Shape. The argument c binds to that constructor's const Shape & parameter, which exposes only the Shape subobject of Circle — for single inheritance with the base at offset 0, the address happens to equal &c. The copy constructor then copies exactly the layout it knows: the vptr and whatever else Shape declares.

The vptr is part of that layout, so the copy receives Shape's table pointer. The constructor has no way to know that the source object's dynamic type was Circle; it was generated for Shape, and it copies Shape. This is why the defect is silent: nothing illegal happened, a base object was constructed correctly from a base subobject, and the derived part — r, and the override that would have read it — was simply never brought along.

Compare Shape *p = &c;, where nothing is constructed. A pointer holds an address, converting Circle * to Shape * adjusts that address by the base offset (zero here), and the object it points at is still the original Circle with Circle's vptr. Every polymorphic call on the copy dispatches as Shape because the copy is a Shape.

The rule is short: polymorphic objects travel by reference or by pointer, never by value. A function parameter of type Shape is a defect; const Shape & is the fix.

docs.title: 5. What a virtual call costs
docs.text:
Two measurements make the cost concrete, and the lab asks for both.

A loop calling the same virtual function on the same object is devirtualised by the compiler when it can prove the dynamic type. With final on the class, GCC and Clang emit a direct call even at -O1.

A loop whose dynamic type changes per iteration cannot be devirtualised, and the cost is a load plus an indirect branch. On a modern x86-64 the difference is typically 2–4 cycles per call when the branch predictor succeeds and 15–20 when it mispredicts, which is why the order of objects in a container matters for a virtual-heavy loop.

The practical conclusion: virtual dispatch is cheap enough for anything called once per object and expensive enough to notice in a loop over a million atoms. The biology section measures exactly that case in the parallel chapter.

docs.title: 6. Field note: the derived class that forgot override
docs.text:
An early version of the animal example declared the base function as virtual void makeSound(), and the derived class as:

void MakeSound() { std::cout << "Dog Sound.\n"; }   // capital M

Different case, so no override. The derived class had two functions: the inherited makeSound and a new MakeSound that nothing called. The program printed the base's message and the author concluded that virtual dispatch was broken.

Adding override turns this into a compile error: "MakeSound marked override, but does not override". A single keyword converts a silent behavioural defect into a diagnostic, which is the best trade in the language.

docs.title: 7. Practise
docs.text: Compile code/cpp/05_polymorphism/02_slicing.cpp, which deliberately slices a Circle into a Shape by value, and read the output before and after changing the parameter to const Shape &. The exercise in labs/cpp/05_polymorphism/ is to build a two-level hierarchy, call through a base pointer, and make a pure-virtual stub abort the program if any call reaches it — the stub is the detector, since a missed override is otherwise silent.

docs.title: Continue
docs.text:
• Operator Overloading is dispatch on the static type, and the contrast is instructive.
  • Inheritance established the base subobject this chapter puts a vptr into.
  • Exceptions explains what happens when a virtual call occurs during construction.

docs.title: RAII and Smart Pointers
docs.text:
RAII is one sentence — a destructor runs when the object's lifetime ends — and everything else in this chapter follows from it. I teach it with a class of my own before any standard type, because the mechanism matters more than the header. Then unique_ptr, then shared_ptr and the control block, then move semantics, then the section that says a smart pointer is not a substitute for thinking about ownership.

RAII is the answer to chapter 7's obligation. Instead of one owner who remembers to call free, the object owns a resource and releases it in its destructor. Because destructors run when a scope exits — including during an exception — the release happens on every path, not only the paths the author remembered.

docs.title: 1. The mechanism in one class
docs.text:
// LAB 08-01  cpp_raii/01_scope_guard.cpp
class Buffer {
public:
    explicit Buffer(std::size_t n) : data_(new int[n]), size_(n) {}
    ~Buffer() { delete[] data_; }
    Buffer(const Buffer &) = delete;             // no copying: one owner
    Buffer &operator=(const Buffer &) = delete;
private:
    int *data_;
    std::size_t size_;
};

Three lines do the work: the constructor acquires, the destructor releases, and the deleted copy operations make the ownership unique. The object is now correct under every exit path, including the ones added later.

= delete is the C++11 form. Pre-C++11 code declared the copy operations private and left them undefined, which produced a link error instead of a compile error at the call site.

docs.title: 2. unique_ptr: the default
docs.text:
std::unique_ptr<Buffer> b = std::make_unique<Buffer>(128);

unique_ptr is a pointer with the destructor built in, and it is non-copyable by design. Passing it to a function that must not take ownership uses a reference:

void consume(const Buffer &b);       // borrows, does not own
void take(std::unique_ptr<Buffer> b); // takes ownership: the caller must std::move

std::move at the call site is not a cast; it is a statement that the caller is giving up the object. After the move, the source pointer is null, and using it is defined — it is a null pointer, not a dangling one.

The size cost is zero: sizeof(std::unique_ptr<T>) equals sizeof(T *) for the default deleter. The deleter is a template parameter, so a custom deleter that is empty costs nothing either.

docs.title: 3. shared_ptr: when ownership is genuinely shared
docs.text:
std::shared_ptr<Model> m = std::make_shared<Model>();
auto copy = m;      // two owners, one control block

shared_ptr keeps a reference count in a separate control block; the object is destroyed when the last owner releases. The costs are real: an atomic increment and decrement per copy, a second allocation for the control block (avoided by make_shared), and an indirection to reach the object.

shared_ptr is the right choice when two unrelated parts of a program genuinely need to keep the object alive, and the wrong choice as a default. A design in which everything is a shared_ptr hides the ownership graph rather than expressing it, and cycles in the graph leak because the counts never reach zero.

struct Node {
    std::shared_ptr<Node> next;
    std::weak_ptr<Node> prev;      // weak breaks the cycle
};

weak_ptr observes without owning: it does not change the count, and lock() returns a shared_ptr or null if the object is gone.

docs.title: 4. Move semantics, at the level RAII needs
docs.text:
A class that owns a resource can often be moved instead of copied, which turns a deep copy into a pointer transfer:

class Buffer {
public:
    Buffer(Buffer &&other) noexcept : data_(other.data_), size_(other.size_) {
        other.data_ = nullptr;      // the moved-from object must still be destructible
        other.size_ = 0;
    }
    Buffer &operator=(Buffer &&other) noexcept { ... }
};

The noexcept is load-bearing: a std::vector reallocating its storage will move elements only if the move constructor is noexcept; otherwise it copies, because a throwing move during reallocation cannot be undone.

The moved-from object must be left in a valid state — destructible, assignable, and with no ownership of the transferred resource. Setting the pointer to null accomplishes exactly that, since delete[] nullptr is defined.

docs.title: 5. Smart pointers are not a substitute for a destructor
docs.text:
A class holding a FILE * still needs a destructor, because unique_ptr's default deleter calls delete, not fclose:

struct FileCloser { void operator()(std::FILE *fp) const { if (fp) std::fclose(fp); } };
std::unique_ptr<std::FILE, FileCloser> fp(std::fopen(path, "rb"), FileCloser{});

The custom deleter is a function object, empty in this case, so the unique_ptr remains pointer-sized. This is the pattern for every C resource: sockets, handles, HDF5 identifiers, MPI communicators.

docs.title: 6. Field note: the three defects in one stack class
docs.text:
The archived Stack.cpp contained three independent errors in about thirty lines:

this.data = new T[n];        // 1. missing ->, so this.data is a syntax error
delete this.data;            // 2. should be delete[], and it deletes a member of *this
if (!isFull) { ... }         // 3. calls the function pointer's truth value, always true

The first is a compile error and therefore harmless. The second is undefined behaviour: delete on an array allocated with new[] fails to run the destructors of the elements and may corrupt the allocator. The third is worse, because it compiles: isFull without parentheses converts the member function to a pointer, which is never null, so !isFull is always false and the guard never runs — the stack silently overruns its capacity.

The repair for all three is a single change of representation: use std::vector<T> as the member, and the allocation, the deallocation, the capacity check and the copy semantics all become correct at once.

template <typename T>
class Stack {
public:
    explicit Stack(std::size_t cap) : data_(cap) {}
    void push(const T &v) { data_.push_back(v); }   // vector grows; no fixed capacity
private:
    std::vector<T> data_;
};

The lesson is the chapter's thesis: the best fix for a resource defect is to stop holding the resource manually.

docs.title: 7. Practise
docs.text: Run code/cpp/08_raii/01_scope_guard.cpp, then delete the explicit destructor and see what LeakSanitizer reports. Then attempt the exercise in labs/cpp/08_raii/, which requires a unique_ptr-owning class that survives a throw in the middle of its constructor — the case a destructor alone cannot handle, because the object was never fully built.

docs.text:
