  • Exceptions explains why the constructor that throws is the hardest RAII case.
  • Error Handling is the C-side contract this chapter replaces.

docs.title: Templates
docs.text:
A template is not a type; it is a recipe the compiler follows once it knows the argument types, and until then the body is barely checked. That is why the errors arrive late and why this chapter spends its space on diagnosis. I begin with deduction, then a class template with a non-type parameter, then lazy instantiation and the errors it hides, then two-phase lookup, then concepts as the constraint that turns a page of errors into a sentence. The Field Note is a template that compiled and returned a reference to a temporary.

A template is a recipe the compiler follows when it has the argument types. Until then the body is not checked for much of anything, which is why template errors arrive late, arrive with long messages, and are the reason this chapter spends most of its space on diagnosis rather than syntax.

docs.title: 1. Function templates and deduction
docs.text:
// LAB 07-01  cpp_templates/01_template_diag.cpp
template <typename T>
T larger(T a, T b) { return a > b ? a : b; }

larger(3, 4);          // T = int
larger(3.0, 4.0);      // T = double
larger(3, 4.0);        // error: conflicting deduction, T cannot be both

Deduction works on the declared parameter types, not on the argument values. Passing an int and a double for two T parameters asks the compiler to deduce T twice with different answers, which is an error rather than a conversion. The fixes are a cast at the call site or two template parameters with a std::common_type_t.

Explicit arguments bypass deduction:

larger<double>(3, 4.0);   // T = double, the int converts

docs.title: 2. Class templates and non-type parameters
docs.text:
template <typename T, std::size_t N>
class FixedBuffer {
public:
    explicit FixedBuffer(const T (&src)[N]) { std::copy(src, src + N, data_); }
    std::size_t size() const { return N; }
private:
    T data_[N];
};

N is a non-type parameter: it must be a compile-time constant, and it becomes part of the class's identity. FixedBuffer<int, 4> and FixedBuffer<int, 8> are unrelated types with unrelated layouts. This is the mechanism behind std::array, and it is why std::array<int, 4> has no dynamic allocation and no runtime size field.

docs.title: 3. Instantiation is lazy, and that is the source of the late error
docs.text:
A class template's member functions are instantiated only when used. A function that is never called is never compiled, so a defect inside it is invisible until someone calls it — and the error then points at the call site rather than at the defect.

template <typename T>
T minimum(T *arr, std::size_t n) {
    T min = arr[0];
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
        if (arr[0] < min) { min = arr[0]; }   // never true: compares arr[0] with itself
    }
    return min;
}

This function compiles for every T that supports <, returns arr[0] for every input, and produces no warning. The body looks plausible, the loop variable i is unused in the condition, and the flaw is a leftover from a version that compared arr[i].

The reason it survived is exactly the laziness: nothing in the template's declaration suggests a problem, and the call site gets a correct-looking value, so no error is ever raised. A test with a three-element array where the minimum is not first would have caught it immediately.

docs.title: 4. Two-phase lookup
docs.text:
Names inside a template are looked up in two phases, and the split explains a class of errors:

  1. At definition: names that do not depend on a template parameter must be visible, along with everything from the enclosing namespaces.
  2. At instantiation: names that depend on a template parameter are resolved, including argument-dependent lookup (ADL).
template <typename T>
void scale(T &v, double f) { v.scale(f); }   // v.scale resolved at instantiation

A dependent call is resolved at instantiation, which is why a free function found only by ADL works and a function declared after the template definition may not. The practical rule: declare everything the template needs before the template, or move the definition into the same header as the declaration.

The single most common symptom is "the compiler says my function does not exist, but it clearly does". The declaration order is usually the answer.

docs.title: 5. Constraints, and what concepts replace
docs.text:
Before C++20, constraining a template meant static_assert inside the body or SFINAE in the signature. Both produce errors that are hard to read:

template <typename T>
T sum(const std::vector<T> &v) {
    static_assert(std::is_arithmetic_v<T>, "sum requires an arithmetic type");
    ...
}

C++20 concepts move the constraint into the signature and improve the diagnostic:

template <std::arithmetic T>
T sum(const std::vector<T> &v);

The book uses concepts in the capstone and mentions the older forms because existing code is full of them. The diagnostic quality difference is large enough to be worth the standard bump.

docs.title: 6. Field note: the sort that sorted backwards
docs.text:
The archived funTemplate.h contained a class template whose sort() member compared and swapped like this:

if (a[i] < a[j]) {
    T temp = a[i];
    a[i] = a[j];
    a[j] = temp;
}

With i < j and the condition a[i] < a[j], the larger element moves to the earlier position, so the result is descending order. The function is named sort, so a caller expecting ascending order gets an array that is sorted and wrong.

There was no test, because a template has no obvious place for one, and the only caller was a commented-out main. Two lessons: name a function for what it guarantees, and give a template at least one instantiation that runs in the test suite — otherwise it is code that has never been compiled.

The same file's Stack template had the sibling defect: an array allocated with new[] and released with delete rather than delete[], which is undefined behaviour and reported by ASan as an allocation/deallocation mismatch.

docs.title: 7. Practise
docs.text: Build code/cpp/07_templates/01_template_diag.cpp, which contains the sort defect above, and make its assertions pass: ascending order for int, double and std::string, a minimum of 1 from a five-element array, w descending as 5 … 1, and larger<double>(3, 4.5) resolving to 4.5 only when the argument is explicit.

docs.title: Continue
docs.text:
• RAII and Smart Pointers is what a template like FixedBuffer needs instead of a raw array member.
  • STL Containers are templates instantiated far more often than you might expect.
  • Construction and Lifetime explains why FixedBuffer's copy constructor is implicit and correct.

docs.title: CMake and Build Systems
docs.text:
I build the build system before the labs, because a lab you cannot rebuild in ten seconds is a lab you will not repeat. The page reads the top-level file line by line, then registers one lab, then runs it, and only then compares Linux, Visual Studio 2022 and conda — three routes, one CMake logic underneath. The field note is a header I compiled twice and lost an afternoon to.

The repository builds with CMake because the same three-line command must work on Linux, in WSL2, under MSVC, and inside a conda environment. This page explains what this repository's CMakeLists.txt actually does, in the order a reader will meet it.

docs.title: 1. The shape of the tree
docs.text:
code/
├── CMakeLists.txt          # the only entry point
├── c/CMakeLists.txt        # per-language registration
├── cpp/CMakeLists.txt
├── bio/CMakeLists.txt
├── include/                # shared headers: craft_assert.h, craft_bench.h, craft_io.h
└── c/07_heap/01_growth_trace.c

cmake is run against code/, never against code/c/. A single entry point means one build directory and one set of options, which is what makes the labs reproducible.

docs.title: 2. The top-level file, line by line
docs.text:
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.20)
project(craft LANGUAGES C CXX)

The version floor is 3.20 because target_link_libraries with an interface target and generator expressions needs it, and because 3.20 is what Ubuntu 22.04 ships. Declaring both languages up front means the C and C++ standards are set once.

set(CMAKE_C_STANDARD 17)
set(CMAKE_C_STANDARD_REQUIRED ON)
set(CMAKE_C_EXTENSIONS OFF)
set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 20)
set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD_REQUIRED ON)
set(CMAKE_CXX_EXTENSIONS OFF)

EXTENSIONS OFF means -std=c17 rather than -std=gnu17. This matters more than it looks: gnu17 accepts several GNU extensions that MSVC does not, so a lab that compiles under gnu17 may fail on Route B. Turning extensions off keeps the code portable by construction.

add_library(craft_common INTERFACE)
target_include_directories(craft_common INTERFACE ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/include)
target_link_libraries(craft_common INTERFACE m)

craft_common is an interface library: it has no source files, it only carries usage requirements. Every lab links it, so every lab gets the shared headers without repeating the include path. The difference between INTERFACE and PUBLIC is that INTERFACE requirements apply only to consumers, never to the library itself — correct here because there is no library.

function(craft_lab target source)
    add_executable(${target} ${source})
    target_link_libraries(${target} PRIVATE craft_common)
    target_compile_options(${target} PRIVATE
        -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Wconversion -Wshadow)
    if(CMAKE_C_COMPILER_ID STREQUAL "GNU" OR CMAKE_C_COMPILER_ID MATCHES "Clang")
        target_compile_options(${target} PRIVATE -fsanitize=address,undefined -fno-omit-frame-pointer)
        target_link_options(${target} PRIVATE -fsanitize=address,undefined)
    endif()
    add_test(NAME ${target} COMMAND ${target})
endfunction()

One function, called once per lab. add_test in the same function is what makes ctest a complete test suite without a second declaration. The sanitizer flags are added only for GCC and Clang: MSVC has /fsanitize=address but does not support the combination with UBSan in the same way, and Route B's chapter notes say so.

-Wconversion is in the list because the C chapters are about type width, and it is the flag that reports a narrowing conversion at the point of the conversion rather than as a wrong result later. It is also the noisiest flag in the list, which is why chapter 2's examples are written to satisfy it deliberately.

docs.title: 3. Registering a lab
docs.text:
craft_lab(01_sizeof_table c/01_objects_in_memory/01_sizeof_table.c)

The target name is the lab's identity in ctest, in the file tree, and in the book's LAB numbering. Keeping the three identical means the error message from ctest names a file the reader can open.

The reason for one line per lab rather than file(GLOB_RECURSE ...):

  • A glob is evaluated at configure time, so a new file requires re-running CMake and produces a build that silently omits it. Explicit registration fails loudly.
  • A glob cannot express per-file options, and the sanitizer exception for MSVC is per-target.
  • git log on CMakeLists.txt becomes a list of what was added, which is the closest thing to a changelog the code has.

docs.title: 4. Building and testing
docs.text:
cmake -S code -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug
cmake --build build -j
ctest --test-dir build --output-on-failure

-S/-B is the modern form and does not depend on the working directory. --output-on-failure is not optional: without it, ctest prints a pass/fail summary and hides the assertion message, which is the only useful part.

The tools/Makefile wraps the three commands:

make configure
make build
make test

It exists for readers who prefer make, and it calls cmake rather than replacing it. There is exactly one build description, and it is the CMakeLists.txt.

docs.title: 5. Route differences
docs.text:
Linux GCC/Clang MSVC (Route B) conda (Route C) Configure cmake -S code -B build cmake -S code -B build -G "Visual Studio 17 2022" cmake -S code -B build -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=$CC Build cmake --build build -j cmake --build build --config Debug same as Linux Test ctest --test-dir build ctest --test-dir build -C Debug same as Linux Sanitizers automatic automatic per-target check automatic

The --config argument appears because a multi-config generator puts the binaries in build/Debug/ rather than build/. A reader who forgets it gets "test executable not found", which is a path problem rather than a code problem.

docs.title: 6. Field note: the header that was compiled twice
docs.text:
The archived C++ project listed both person.cpp and main.cpp, and the latter included person.h — correctly, a declaration. The build worked. Later a person.cpp was added to the list a second time through a wildcard, and the link failed with multiple definition of Person::Person().

The cause was not the duplicate: it was that the course project's person.h contained the constructor body.

#ifndef PERSON_H
#define PERSON_H
class Person {
public:
    Person(std::string n) : name(n) {}    // defined in a header
};
#endif

The include guard makes the definition appear once per translation unit, which is exactly once too many when two units include it. The guard solves multiple inclusion, not multiple definition — those are different problems, and the guard's name makes the difference easy to forget.

The repair is the rule the book follows everywhere: a header declares, a .c or .cpp defines. inline is the exception for functions that must live in a header, and it is the reason craft_io.h's functions are static inline.

docs.title: Continue
docs.text:
• Compilation Pipeline is what the commands ultimately run.
  • Testing and Sanitizers explains what ctest executes.
  • Translation Units is the rule the include guard does not solve.

docs.title: Compilation Pipeline
docs.text:
Four stages sound abstract until one of them explains an error you have already seen. I take preprocessing first because it is pure text, then the translation unit, then sections in the object file, then linking as symbol resolution and relocation. Static against dynamic, then optimisation, then a 24 KB binary for a four-line program — by the end each stage has a size you can point at.

One gcc main.c hides four programs and seven file extensions. This page opens them, because every warning and every link error in this book comes from one of those stages, and knowing which stage produced it is most of the diagnosis.

docs.title: 1. The four stages
docs.text:
main.c ──► [cpp] ──► main.i ──► [cc1] ──► main.s ──► [as] ──► main.o ──► [ld] ──► a.out
           preprocess          compile            assemble          link
Stage Program Input Output What it does Preprocess cpp .c .h .i includes, macros, #if, comments stripped Compile cc1 / cc1plus .i .s parse, type-check, optimise, emit assembly Assemble as .s .o assembly to machine code and a symbol table Link ld .o .a .so executable resolve symbols, relocate, lay out segments

The driver runs all four and deletes the intermediates. Each stage can be stopped and inspected:

gcc -E main.c -o main.i        # preprocess only
gcc -S main.c -o main.s        # stop before assembling
gcc -c main.c -o main.o        # stop before linking

docs.title: 2. Preprocessing is textual, and that is the whole problem
docs.text:
#include is a file insertion, not an import. #define is a token replacement, not a constant. The consequences are visible in the first chapter's examples: a macro without parentheses around its parameters expands wrongly, and an include that is missing a header produces a "unknown type" error in the file that included it, with no mention of the real culprit.

gcc -E -P main.c | head -40      # -P drops line markers

Reading the preprocessed output is the fastest way to answer "why does the compiler think this macro is that?" — the expansion is right there, one line, already wrong.

The other use is size: a translation unit that includes <stdio.h>, <stdlib.h> and <string.h> is several thousand lines after preprocessing, which is why compile times are dominated by headers rather than by the source file. This is the reason for the forward-declaration habit in chapter 13: an include that could have been a declaration costs every includer the parse time.

docs.title: 3. The compiler sees one translation unit at a time
docs.text:
cc1 never sees other.c. It type-checks the .i file in isolation, and any name it cannot resolve becomes an external symbol to be resolved later. That is why:

  • A function called without a prototype is assumed to take int (C89) or rejected (C23), and never checked against the definition in another file.
  • A static function with no caller produces a "defined but not used" warning — the compiler knows it is invisible outside this unit.
  • A missing #include produces an error in this unit even though the definition exists elsewhere.
gcc -c main.c -o main.o
nm main.o

nm lists the symbol table: T for a defined text symbol, U for undefined, t for a local one. A U main in your .o and a T main nowhere is the classic "undefined reference to main" in reverse; a U craft_read_file with no T anywhere is the classic missing object file.

docs.title: 4. Assembling produces sections, not just code
docs.text:
gcc -c main.c -o main.o
size main.o
readelf -S main.o

The object file has .text (code), .data (initialised globals), .bss (zero-initialised globals), .rodata (constants and string literals), and .comment. Two consequences worth knowing:

  • A global initialised to zero costs nothing on disk (.bss is not stored), which is why static int table[1024]; is free and static int table[1024] = {1}; is 4 KB of .data.
  • A string literal lives in .rodata, so writing to it is a segfault. This is the mechanism behind the char *s = "abc"; s[0] = 'x'; crash in the strings chapter.

docs.title: 5. Linking resolves and relocates
docs.text:
gcc main.o util.o -o app

ld reads the symbol table of every input, matches each U against a T, and rewrites the addresses in the code. Three errors come from here and nowhere else:

Message Meaning undefined reference to 'foo' a U with no matching T in any input multiple definition of 'foo' a T in two objects — usually a function defined in a header relocation truncated to fit a code model problem, rare and always about a huge binary

The second one is the reason headers declare and .c files define. Chapter 13 covers the translation-unit rules that produce it.

docs.title: 6. Static and dynamic linking
docs.text:
gcc main.c -o app              # dynamic: libc resolved at run time
gcc main.c -static -o app      # static: libc copied into the binary
ldd app                        # list dynamic dependencies

A dynamic executable is small and shares libc with the system; a static one is portable and independent, at the cost of size and of never receiving libc security updates. ldd on a binary you did not build is a security question, not a size question.

The book builds dynamically, because the sanitizers require it and because a 40 KB binary is easier to read with nm.

docs.title: 7. Optimisation changes what you can debug
docs.text:
gcc -O0 -g main.c -o app        # debug build: every variable has an address
gcc -O2 main.c -o app           # release build: variables are registers or gone

At -O2 the compiler may reorder statements, delete variables, and inline functions, so a debugger shows values that no longer exist and a breakpoint lands on a line that is not the one you expected. The book builds every lab at -O0 -g and measures timing at -O2, and the two are separate builds for exactly this reason.

The first symptom a reader meets is <optimized out>. It is not a debugger failure: the variable was placed in a register, that register was reused by later code, and the DWARF location description has no answer for the current instruction pointer. info locals lists the variables that still have a location; the ones missing are gone, not hidden. -Og is the middle setting — it keeps the variables and line table a debugger needs while still doing inlining and a little scheduling — which is why I use -O0 -g for the labs and -Og -g when a defect only appears with optimisation enabled.

docs.title: 8. Field note: the binary that was 24 KB for a four-line program
docs.text:
The first chapter's warn.c prints a diagnostic and exits. Built with gcc warn.c, the binary is about 24 KB — and the source is four lines. Almost all of it is the startup code, the dynamic loader stubs, and the section alignment that the linker inserts by default.

Knowing this matters for two reasons. It stops the intuition that "small program means small binary" from becoming a diagnostic rule that misleads; and it explains why size reports a .text far larger than the code you wrote. gcc -Os -s warn.c gets the file under 16 KB, mostly by dropping symbols.

The lesson: the ratio between source and binary is not a measure of anything, and a binary's size is a property of the link, not of the code.

docs.title: Debugging
docs.text:
A crash is not a mystery; it is a state you have not read yet. I begin with the backtrace because it costs one command and answers most questions, then frames and prints, then breakpoints with conditions, then printf done properly, then bisection for wrong results, then sanitizers beside the debugger. The order is the order I actually follow at two in the morning.

The debugger is slower than printf and faster than guessing. This page covers the four operations that solve almost every crash in this book, and the two habits that decide whether a debugging session ends in ten minutes or in an hour.

docs.title: 1. The first crash: get a backtrace before anything else
docs.text:
gdb ./app
(gdb) run
Program received signal SIGSEGV, Segmentation fault.
0x0000555555555163 in read_records (path=0x0) at records.c:41
41          std::fread(buf, 1, size, fp);

The three lines that matter are SIGSEGV, the function and line, and the arguments. path=0x0 is the answer in this case: the caller passed a null path, and fopen(NULL, ...) returned null, and fread on a null FILE * crashed.

gdb -batch -ex run -ex bt ./app       # same, without an interactive session

The batch form is what goes into a script: it runs, and on a signal prints the backtrace and exits. A harness that runs binaries unattended wants this form, so that a crash produces a report rather than a timeout.

The transcripts on this page use a two-function toy — load.c calling records.c — rather than a file from code/. The argument does not depend on which program crashed, and a toy keeps the frames short enough to read; the two files under code/c/16_error_handling/ are the repository's own examples of the same pattern.

docs.title: 2. bt is the map, frame and print are the inspection
docs.text:
(gdb) bt
#0  read_records (path=0x0) at records.c:41
#1  load (cfg=0x7fffffffd9d0) at main.c:63
#2  main () at main.c:12

(gdb) frame 1
(gdb) info locals
(gdb) print cfg->path

bt numbered from the innermost frame. frame N moves the inspection context to that frame, and info locals and print then show that frame's values. The most common mistake is inspecting frame 0 when the bad value was computed in frame 1 — the crash site is rarely the defect site.

up and down move by one frame; info args shows the parameters; x/8gx addr dumps memory as eight 8-byte hexadecimal words, which is what reads a struct or a buffer correctly.

docs.title: 3. Breakpoints, and the conditional form
docs.text:
(gdb) break records.c:41
(gdb) break read_records if size > 1000     # conditional
(gdb) info breakpoints
(gdb) delete 2

A conditional breakpoint is the tool that makes a loop debuggable: set it on the iteration where the invariant fails, not on the first iteration. ignore N 1000 skips the first thousand hits, which is the same idea without a predicate.

watch -l buf[0] stops when the memory changes, which is how a buffer overrun is caught at the write rather than at the read that follows. rwatch and awatch are the read and read/write variants.

docs.title: 4. Printing is legitimate, and there is a right way
docs.text:
printf debugging gets a bad reputation from being used badly. Done well it is the fastest tool:

fprintf(stderr, "%s:%d path=%p size=%zu\n", __FILE__, __LINE__, (void *)path, size);

Three rules: write to stderr so the output is not mixed with the program's real output; include the file and line so a later copy of the message is unambiguous; print in one statement so the line is atomic with respect to other output. A loop that prints ten thousand lines is a loop that needed a conditional print, not a smaller buffer.

The advantage over a breakpoint is that a printed log survives the run and can be diffed. The disadvantage is that it changes the timing and the code. When both are needed, assert-style checks plus a log are usually enough, and the debugger is for the case where the value is unknown in advance.

docs.title: 5. Bisecting a wrong result
docs.text:
A crash has a site; a wrong answer has a range. The technique is to narrow the range by halving:

  1. Print the input and the output at the function boundary. If the input is already wrong, the defect is upstream.
  2. If the boundary is clean, print at the midpoint of the function's body.
  3. Repeat, halving each time. A function of 100 lines is located in 7 prints.

This is faster than stepping through the function, because each print eliminates half the remaining lines rather than one line.

docs.title: 6. Sanitizers and the debugger, together
docs.text:
The labs build with ASan and -g, so a report includes line numbers:

./app
==12345==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow
    #0 0x... in fill at buffer.c:18

ASan aborts at the first bad access, so gdb --args ./app followed by run lands in the debugger with the full stack at the moment of the illegal access — the best of both tools. ASAN_OPTIONS=abort_on_error=1 makes that reliable.

LeakSanitizer reports at exit and does not abort, so a leak is diagnosed after the program has finished. To stop at the first leak, ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_leaks=1:abort_on_error=1 with a breakpoint on __lsan_do_leak_check.

docs.title: 7. Field note: the crash that was three lines upstream
docs.text:
The archived mocal.c crashed inside strcpy, and the backtrace pointed at strcpy in libc with no useful frame.

char *str[10];
for (int i = 0; i < 10; ++i) { str[i] = (char *)malloc(64); }
strcpy(str[0], "hello");

The crash was reported inside strcpy, but the defect was one line up: if (str[i] == NULL) printed a message and continued, so a null destination reached strcpy. The library function cannot know the pointer is null until it writes to address 0, and the report names the library rather than the caller.

The habit that finds this in one step: when the backtrace's innermost frame is inside libc, the defect is in the frame above it, and that frame's arguments are the ones to inspect. frame 1 plus print str[0] would have shown (char *) 0x0 immediately.

docs.title: 8. Practise
docs.text: Take a lab that passes, introduce one defect of your own (a null dereference, an off-by-one write, or a leaked allocation), and diagnose it three ways: with ASan alone, with gdb on the sanitizer abort, and with a print bisection. Record which one found the line first.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
I refuse to start with a profiler, because most slow programs are slow for three reasons a timer can show you for free. I take the clock first and its resolution limits, then layout at small n, then the constant factor, then allocation, and only then the tool. Amdahl's law is one paragraph because it is one fraction. The field note is a benchmark that timed the optimiser away.

A performance claim without a measurement is a guess, and most of the guesses in this book turned out wrong when measured. This page is the measurement, kept deliberately small: one timer, one counter, and the three effects that account for almost every surprise in the labs.

docs.title: 1. The timer, and what it can and cannot see
docs.text:
// code/include/craft_bench.h
static inline double craft_cpu_seconds(void) {
    return (double)clock() / (double)CLOCKS_PER_SEC;
}

clock() measures CPU time consumed by the process, not wall time. That is the right choice for a single-threaded lab: it excludes time the process spent descheduled, so a noisy machine does not change the number. It is the wrong choice for the parallel labs, where the whole point is to compare wall time across threads — those use clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC, ...) and say so.

The resolution is typically 1 ms on Linux, which means a function that takes 10 µs cannot be timed by one call. The pattern is to time N repetitions and divide:

double t0 = craft_cpu_seconds();
for (int i = 0; i < 1000; ++i) { work(); }
double t1 = craft_cpu_seconds();
printf("%.3f us/call\n", (t1 - t0) * 1e6 / 1000);

Three rules for a number worth quoting: the loop body must not be optimisable away (accumulate into a global and print it), the run must be long enough to exceed the resolution by two orders of magnitude, and the build must be -O2 — a -O0 measurement is a measurement of the debug build.

docs.title: 2. Effect one: layout beats algorithm at small n
docs.text:
The row-major walk lab compares two traversals of the same matrix:

for (i) for (j) sum += a[i][j];      // row-major: sequential
for (j) for (i) sum += a[i][j];      // column-major: stride 400 bytes

Both are O(n²) and both perform the same number of additions. On a 2000×2000 int matrix the second is typically several times slower — the exact factor depends on the machine and the cache size, the direction does not — entirely because each access misses the cache line that the next access in the loop needed. If you want a number rather than a direction, this is the one lab in the book worth running on your own hardware. The mechanism:

  • A cache line is 64 bytes = 16 ints.
  • Row-major: 16 consecutive sums use one line, then one miss.
  • Column-major: every sum uses a different line, so every sum misses.

At small n the matrix fits in L2 and the two loops are identical. The effect appears at a threshold, not gradually, which is why a benchmark at n = 100 proves nothing and a benchmark at n = 4000 proves everything.

docs.title: 3. Effect two: the constant factor is the code
docs.text:
The same algorithm written two ways can differ by 10× with no change in complexity. Three concrete cases from the book:

Code Operation Why it differs s += strlen(s) in a loop O(n²) hidden strlen rescans the prefix each time std::endl per line one write per line flush is a syscall printf("%d\n") vs fputs format parse per call printf walks the format string

The third one is the one people under-estimate: printf is roughly 10× slower than fputs for a fixed string, because it parses the format every call. In a loop that prints a million lines, the difference is a second.

docs.title: 4. Effect three: allocation is the hidden cost
docs.text:
malloc and free are cheap individually and expensive in aggregate. A program that allocates one small block per record pays for the bookkeeping, the fragmentation, and the cache misses that come from touching a new block each time.

The fix is structural rather than a faster allocator: allocate once, reuse. This is what std::vector's capacity does, what the ring buffer lab does, and what the sequence reader does with reserve.

// one allocation for N records, instead of N allocations
Record *records = malloc(N * sizeof *records);

The measurement that makes this believable: run the lab with N allocations and with one, and compare. On a typical machine the ratio is 3–10× for N = 10^6, and the larger the record, the worse the per-allocation version gets.

docs.title: 5. The tool, when the three effects are not enough
docs.text:
perf stat ./app                    # cycles, instructions, cache misses, branch misses
perf record -g ./app && perf report
valgrind --tool=callgrind ./app     # instruction counts per function, cross-platform

perf stat answers "is it cache, branch, or instruction count" in one line, and the cache-miss count is the fastest way to confirm effect one. callgrind is slower but deterministic and works without kernel permissions, which makes it the tool for a shared machine or a container.

Both are Linux tools. Route B and Route C readers get the same information from Visual Studio's profiler or from valgrind, and the chapter notes say so.

docs.title: 6. Amdahl's law, in one paragraph
docs.text:
If a fraction p of the work can be parallelised across N processors, the speedup is at most

\[ S(N) = \frac{1}{(1-p) + p/N} \]

With p = 0.9 and N = 8, the ceiling is about 4.7×, not 8×. With p = 0.5, it is 1.6×. This is the reason the parallel-scoring chapter measures the serial fraction before adding threads: a program with a 50% serial part cannot be saved by more cores, and the measurement is what tells you which part to attack.

docs.title: 7. Field note: the benchmark that measured nothing
docs.text:
A lab measured the cost of a function like this:

clock_t t0 = clock();
compute(data);
clock_t t1 = clock();
printf("took %ld ticks\n", (long)(t1 - t0));

The output was took 0 ticks for every input. Two causes: clock()'s resolution is 1 ms and compute took microseconds; and at -O2 with the result unused, the compiler was entitled to delete the call entirely.

The repair is both, not one: repeat enough times to exceed the resolution and consume the result so it cannot be removed. A benchmark that prints zero is not a fast function — it is a measurement that failed, and the number is not evidence of anything.

docs.title: 8. Practise
docs.text: Run code/c/14_sorting/01_sort_bench.c at -O0 and at -O2 and explain the difference in the two lines it prints. Then attempt the exercise in labs/c/04_arrays_layout/: the row-major walk at n = 4000 must be measurably faster than the column-major one, and a measurement inside the timer's noise must be rejected rather than reported.

docs.title: Testing and Sanitizers
docs.text:
An assertion is a statement about one state; a test is a statement about a contract, and conflating them is why people say they test and still ship bugs. I start from that distinction, then ctest registration, then AddressSanitizer as the default build rather than an occasional flag, then Valgrind for the cases ASan cannot reach, then golden files with their escaping problem. The field note is a file that compiled and did nothing.

The repository has no test framework. It has assertions, ctest, and three sanitizers, which together cover the defect classes this book is about. This page is the manual for that combination.

docs.title: 1. Assertions are not tests, and the difference matters
docs.text:
// code/include/craft_assert.h
#define CRAFT_ASSERT(cond) do {                                          \
    if (!(cond)) {                                                       \
        fprintf(stderr, "%s:%d: assertion failed: %s\n",                 \
                __FILE__, __LINE__, #cond);                              \
        abort();                                                         \
    }                                                                    \
} while (0)

CRAFT_ASSERT checks an invariant and stops the process with the file, line and expression. It is a debugging tool: it answers "did this hold", not "did the program do the right thing".

The distinction from a test is what happens on failure. An assertion that fires stops the run, so the first failure hides every subsequent one. A test suite reports each case and continues, so one run tells you how many things broke. For a lab with three checks, an assertion is enough; for the capstone with six, a suite is worth the extra file.

assert from <assert.h> is the standard version, and it has one trap: NDEBUG removes it entirely, so a release build silently drops every check. That is why craft_assert.h does not depend on NDEBUG — a check that disappears in the build you ship is worse than no check.

docs.title: 2. ctest runs what CMake registered
docs.text:
ctest --test-dir build --output-on-failure

Every craft_lab() call adds one test named after the target. A lab with no assertions still runs, and the test passes if the process exits zero — which is why a lab that is supposed to fail a check must be written to exit non-zero, not to print an error and continue.

docs.title: 3. AddressSanitizer is the default build
docs.text:
gcc -fsanitize=address,undefined -g main.c -o app

ASan wraps every allocation with red zones and checks every access against them. The report names the access type (heap-buffer-overflow, heap-use-after-free, stack-buffer-overflow), the address, the allocation site, and the free site. That is four facts in one report, which is why the labs build with it by default rather than adding it when something crashes.

Three reports worth recognising:

heap-buffer-overflow on address ... READ of size 4
  #0 main in main.c:12      ← where the bad read happened
  ...
  0x... is located 0 bytes after 40-byte region   ← how far past the end
  allocated by thread T0 here:                    ← where the block came from

stack-use-after-return is the one ASan catches by default only with -fsanitize-address-use-after-scope, and it is the report for the function that returns a pointer to a local:

int *bad(void) { int local = 42; return &local; }   // report on use, sometimes much later

UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer catches the things ASan cannot: signed overflow, shift by an out-of-range amount, misaligned access, null dereference. It does not wrap memory, so its reports are one line and its false-negative rate is higher.

LeakSanitizer runs at exit on Linux and reports every block still reachable — with a caveat: "still reachable" from a global is not the same as "definitely lost". The report distinguishes them, and only definitely lost is a defect.

docs.title: 4. Valgrind covers the case ASan cannot see
docs.text:
Valgrind does not instrument at compile time; it runs the binary on a synthetic CPU. That makes it slower (20–50×) and able to see things ASan cannot: uninitialised reads (Conditional jump or move depends on uninitialised value), and use of memory that ASan's red zones do not cover because the access is inside a valid block.

valgrind --leak-check=full --track-origins=yes ./app

--track-origins=yes is the flag that makes the uninitialised-value report useful: without it, the report says a branch depends on an uninitialised value; with it, the report says which allocation it came from.

The rule of thumb: ASan for a fast loop while developing, Valgrind once on a suspect, because Valgrind's uninitialised-value detection has no ASan equivalent.

docs.title: 5. Golden files for output
docs.text:
./app > out.txt
diff out.txt /tmp/baseline.txt        # the file you saved after reading the output once

diff on exact output is the cheapest possible regression test. Two conditions make it work: the program must write to stdout or a file the script controls, and the output must not contain timings, addresses, or floating-point values formatted differently on different platforms.

The second condition is the reason the capstone prints a Fraction rather than a double: 71/100 is byte-identical everywhere, while 0.71 may print as 0.710000 or 0.71 depending on the default precision. The capstone's own check.sh stops at exit status, and the program checks its report with rfind on the tab-separated prefix rather than by diffing a whole file — the header field is the part a reader is expected to edit, so a byte-for-byte comparison in the harness would fail on a legitimate change. The golden-file pattern above is what to use when the output is meant to be frozen.

For floating point that must be compared numerically, the rule is a relative tolerance:

static int close_enough(double a, double b, double rel) {
    double d = a > b ? a - b : b - a;
    double m = (a > b ? a : b);
    return d <= rel * (m > 1.0 ? m : 1.0);
}

The m > 1.0 guard is what makes the tolerance work near zero, where a relative comparison would demand impossible precision.

docs.title: 6. Field note: the file that compiled and did nothing
docs.text:
The archived C++ project contained src/tesxt.cpp — a typo in the name, and zero bytes of content. It appeared in the source list and compiled without complaint, because an empty translation unit is a legal translation unit.

The cost was invisible: a class declared in tesxt.cpp's header, defined nowhere, produced an "undefined reference" at link time in a completely different file, and the search started from the link error rather than from the empty file.

Two habits prevent this. Compile with -Wall -Wextra, which does not warn about an empty file but does warn about the unused declarations; and let the build fail on emptiness — -Werror=empty-body covers the function-level case, and a wc -c check in a wrapper script covers the file-level one.

docs.title: 7. Practise
docs.text: Build one of the C labs deliberately broken — introduce a one-past-the-end write — and read the ASan report until you can name the function, the line, the block size, and the distance past the end without looking anything up. Then attempt the exercise in labs/bio/04_alignment/: the full-table and two-row scores must agree exactly, and the self-alignment score for an eight-residue sequence must come out at 8 — the two assertions the reference program makes, which is why the run is also built under both sanitizers.

docs.title: C Reference
docs.text:
This page is the one I open while writing, not while reading, so it is organised by the mistakes rather than by the standard. Widths, then the precedence rows people actually get wrong, then conversions, then the headers this book uses, then qualifiers, then the short list of undefined behaviour, then one page of rules I apply without thinking.

A lookup table, not a tutorial. Every row here has a chapter that explains it, and the chapter is what to read when the row does not settle the question.

docs.title: 1. Types and widths
docs.text:
Type x86-64 Linux Windows MSVC Minimum guaranteed char 1 1 1 short 2 2 2 int 4 4 2 long 8 4 4 long long 8 8 8 float 4 4 4 double 8 8 8 long double 16 (80-bit used) 8 8 pointer 8 8 ≥ 2

The long row is the one that breaks code: on Linux it is 64-bit, on Windows it is 32-bit, and a file format or a network protocol that assumes either will fail on the other. Use int64_t when the width matters.

#include <stdint.h>
int8_t  int16_t  int32_t  int64_t      /* exact width, present or absent */
int_fast32_t  int_least16_t            /* at least this wide, fastest / smallest */
size_t  ptrdiff_t                      /* unsigned length, signed difference */

size_t is the unsigned type of sizeof and of array indices; ptrdiff_t is the signed type of pointer difference. Mixing them in a comparison produces -Wsign-compare, which is the warning that exists because the mixed comparison is usually a defect.

docs.title: 2. Operator precedence, the rows people get wrong
docs.text:
Precedence Operators Associativity 1 () [] . -> left 2 ! ~ ++ -- + - (unary) * & sizeof (cast) right 3 * / % left 4 + - left 5 << >> left 6 < <= > >= left 7 == != left 8 & left 9 ^ left 10 \| left 11 && left 12 \|\| left 13 ?: right 14 = += -= … right 15 , left

The three traps: & binds tighter than == (x & 1 == 0 is x & (1 == 0), always zero), << binds tighter than + (1 << 2 + 1 is 1 << 3), and * in a declaration binds to the name (int *a, b declares one pointer).

docs.title: 3. Conversion rules
docs.text:
• Integer promotion: char and short promote to int in arithmetic.
  • Usual arithmetic conversions: int + unsigned int → unsigned int, which is the defect where -1 > 0u is true.
  • Integer to floating: exact up to 2²⁴ for float and 2⁵³ for double.
  • Floating to integer: truncation toward zero, undefined if out of range.

-Wconversion reports every one of these that narrows. The book's labs are built with it.

docs.title: 4. Standard headers actually used
docs.text:
Header Used for Chapter stdio.h printf, fopen, fread, getline (POSIX) files and streams stdlib.h malloc, free, qsort, strtol, exit heap, sorting string.h strlen, memcpy, strncpy, strcmp strings stdint.h fixed-width integers bit operations stddef.h size_t, ptrdiff_t, offsetof structs limits.h INT_MAX, CHAR_BIT overflow errno.h errno, strerror error handling assert.h assert (compiled out under NDEBUG) testing time.h clock, clock_gettime performance math.h sqrt, atan2, fabs, isfinite geometry

getline is POSIX, not ISO C: it needs _POSIX_C_SOURCE on strict builds and is absent on MSVC. The portability note is in the FASTA chapter.

docs.title: 5. Qualifiers
docs.text: Qualifier Meaning Trap const not modified through this name does not make the object immutable volatile may change outside the program's control not a thread primitive static (file scope) internal linkage not "persistent" static (block scope) static storage duration initialised once, not per call restrict no aliasing through this pointer violating it is UB register obsolete ignored

docs.title: 6. Undefined behaviour, the short list
docs.text: Signed overflow, shift by ≥ width or negative, null or misaligned pointer access, out-of-bounds array access, free of a non-heap pointer or double free, reading an uninitialised object, modifying a string literal, memcpy with overlapping regions. Each has a row in Undefined Behaviour with the detector that catches it.

docs.title: 7. The one-page rule set
docs.text:
1. Every allocation has exactly one owner and one free.
  2. Every array index is checked by the function that computes it.
  3. Every function returning a pointer documents how long the pointer is valid.
  4. Every sizeof is applied to the object, not the type: malloc(n * sizeof *p.
  5. Every integer that can be large is size_t or int64_t, not int.
  6. Every comparison between signed and unsigned is cast explicitly.

These are the six rules behind every Field Note in the C chapters, written as rules rather than as stories.

docs.title: Compiler Flags
docs.text:
Flags are grouped by what they change, not by compiler. Warnings and the standard first, then sanitizers, then linking, then the flags that change behaviour rather than diagnostics, then conda, because the third route has its own flag names and its own traps.

Three compilers, one table. The GCC column is the reference; MSVC is what Route B uses, and the differences are the reason a lab can build on Linux and fail on Windows.

docs.title: 1. Warning and standard flags
docs.text:
Purpose GCC / Clang MSVC C standard -std=c17 /std:c17 C++ standard -std=c++20 /std:c++20 Warning level -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic /W4 Warnings are errors -Werror /WX Narrowing conversions -Wconversion part of /W4, no separate flag Shadowing -Wshadow /W4 (partial) Non-virtual dtor -Wnon-virtual-dtor /W4 (partial) Old-style cast -Wold-style-cast — Debug info -g /Zi Optimisation -O0 -O2 -Os /Od /O2 /O1 Standard conformance (default) /permissive- Source charset -finput-charset=UTF-8 /utf-8 Exceptions (default) /EHsc Preprocessor only -E /E Assembly output -S /FA Object only -c /c

/permissive- is not optional on MSVC: without it the compiler accepts constructs that are not standard C++, and a lab that builds only on Route B can hide a non-portable construct. /utf-8 matters when the source contains non-ASCII characters, which the biology comments do.

The mismatch worth knowing: -Wconversion has no MSVC equivalent, so a narrowing conversion that GCC reports as a warning is /W4's C4244 — reported on a different line, with a different name, and sometimes not at all for template instantiations. A reader on Route B who sees no warning where the book says there is one should assume the warning exists and check with -Wconversion on Route A before concluding the code is clean.

docs.title: 2. Sanitizers
docs.text:
Detector GCC / Clang MSVC AddressSanitizer -fsanitize=address /fsanitize=address UndefinedBehaviour -fsanitize=undefined — (no equivalent) LeakSanitizer included in ASan on Linux /fsanitize=address includes it on recent versions ThreadSanitizer -fsanitize=thread — Stack protector -fstack-protector-strong /GS (default) Frame pointer -fno-omit-frame-pointer /Oy-

UBSan has no MSVC equivalent, which is a real gap: the signed-overflow and shift checks in the C chapters are only available on Routes A and C. Route B readers get ASan's memory checks and the compiler's own /W4 diagnostics, and the chapter notes say so explicitly rather than pretending the coverage is equal.

Combining ASan and UBSan is supported on GCC and Clang:

gcc -fsanitize=address,undefined -fno-omit-frame-pointer -g main.c -o app

The -fno-omit-frame-pointer is what makes the stack traces usable; without it, the report's frames are sometimes missing.

docs.title: 3. Linking
docs.text:
Purpose GCC / Clang MSVC Link a library -lfoo foo.lib on the command line Library search path -Lpath /LIBPATH:path Static -static or libfoo.a /MT (static CRT) OpenMP -fopenmp /openmp Math library -lm (last) (linked by default) pthread -pthread (built in)

-lm must come after the object files that use it; the linker resolves left to right and a library before its user is ignored. This is the single most common link-order error.

docs.title: 4. The flags that change behaviour, not just diagnostics
docs.text:
Flag Effect Why it matters -O2 aggressive optimisation deletes unused computations; a benchmark at -O0 is not a benchmark -fno-strict-aliasing relaxes aliasing rules some legacy code needs it; the book's code does not -ffast-math relaxes IEEE semantics changes results; never in the labs -fwrapv signed overflow wraps turns UB into defined behaviour; hides defects -DNDEBUG removes assert a check that disappears in release -fsigned-char / -funsigned-char plain char signedness a file format that relies on it is not portable

-ffast-math and -fwrapv are the two that most often turn a failing lab into a passing one, and both do it by removing the check rather than the defect. The labs do not use either.

docs.title: 5. Route C: conda
docs.text:
conda install -c conda-forge gxx_linux-64 cmake make
export CC=$(which x86_64-conda-linux-gnu-gcc)
export CXX=$(which x86_64-conda-linux-gnu-g++)

The compiler binary is prefixed, so the plain gcc on PATH may be the system one. Setting CC and CXX explicitly is what makes CMake use the conda toolchain; without it, CMake finds the system compiler and the sanitizer runtimes from the two toolchains conflict at link time.

The conda packages are gxx_linux-64 on Linux and vs2019_win-64 on Windows, and the compiler is generally one major version behind the system one. The C++20 requirement means checking $CXX --version before starting, not after a failed build.

docs.title: C++ Reference
docs.text:
Six tables, each answering a question that comes up in review. Special member functions and when the compiler writes them, value categories in one table, overload resolution order, the containers and algorithms worth memorising, the C++20 flags, and the three rules that prevent most of the defects I have seen.

The C++ counterpart, organised by what a reader looks up rather than by what a chapter teaches.

docs.title: 1. The special member functions
2. Value categories, in one table
docs.text:
Category Example Binds to lvalue named object, *p, a[i] T & xvalue std::move(x), T{} member access T && prvalue 42, f() returning by value T &&, materialises to T — const lvalue const T & only

std::move is an unconditional cast to T &&; it does not move anything by itself. std::forward<T> preserves the value category and is what a forwarding constructor needs.

docs.title: 3. Overload resolution order
docs.text:
1. Exact match.
  2. Promotion (char → int).
  3. Standard conversion (int → double).
  4. User-defined conversion (one, at most).
  5. Ellipsis.

Two candidates reached at the same step make the call ambiguous. The book's rule: a function taking double and one taking int64_t makes every int call ambiguous, which is why overloads should differ in arity or in a way the caller can see.

docs.title: 4. Standard library, the containers and the algorithms
docs.text: Need Use Note dynamic array std::vector<T> default choice fixed size array std::array<T, N> no allocation text std::string owns text parameter std::string_view borrows, must not outlive key-value, ordered std::map O(log n), stable iterators key-value, unordered std::unordered_map O(1) average, order unspecified maybe a value std::optional<T> explicit absence exclusive owner std::unique_ptr<T> zero overhead shared owner std::shared_ptr<T> atomic count, cycles leak observer std::weak_ptr<T> lock() to use Need Algorithm sort std::sort, std::stable_sort select k-th std::nth_element find std::find, std::find_if transform std::transform remove std::remove_if + erase accumulate std::accumulate (numeric) min / max std::min_element, std::max_element binary search std::lower_bound, std::upper_bound

docs.title: 5. Compiler flags for C++20
docs.text:
Flag Effect -std=c++20 the standard (MSVC: /std:c++20) -Wall -Wextra the useful warnings -Wconversion narrowing conversions -Wshadow a local shadows an outer name -Wnon-virtual-dtor a polymorphic class with a non-virtual dtor -Wold-style-cast C-style casts in C++ -Werror warnings become errors (the chapter rule is zero warnings) -g debug info for the sanitizer reports -fsanitize=address,undefined ASan + UBSan -D_GLIBCXX_DEBUG libstdc++ container checks -D_GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS cheaper subset of the above

-Wnon-virtual-dtor is the flag that catches deleting a derived object through a base pointer without a virtual destructor — the defect that compiles, runs, and leaks.

docs.title: 6. The three rules that prevent most C++ defects
docs.text:
1. Own with RAII. A raw new, malloc, fopen, or socket() in a constructor-less context is a leak waiting for the second exit path.
  2. Pass by reference for input, by value only for cheap copies. A const T & parameter costs nothing and accepts everything; a T parameter copies.
  3. noexcept on move operations. Without it, containers copy instead of move, and the performance claim of move semantics does not hold.

docs.title: Error Cookbook
docs.text:
Errors are indexed by the moment they appear, because that is how you meet them. Compile time in C, link time in C, compile time in C++, link time in C++, sanitizer reports at runtime, then wrong answers, which are the only ones with no message at all. Each entry is a real message with the cause underneath it.

Message first, cause second, chapter third. Every entry is a message this book's code has actually produced.

docs.title: 1. C: compile time
docs.text: Message Cause Read warning: implicit declaration of function 'foo' missing #include, or the function is declared later translation units error: 'foo' undeclared missing declaration, or a typo in the name translation units warning: incompatible implicit declaration of built-in missing header for a standard function — the compiler guessed the signature strings error: expected ';' before ... the error is usually one line earlier — warning: unused variable 'x' a leftover; -Werror turns it into a stop first program warning: conversion to 'unsigned int' from 'int' may change the sign -Wconversion; a size_t compared with an int types warning: comparison of integer expressions of different signedness same as above at a comparison undefined behaviour warning: format '%d' expects 'int' but argument is 'size_t' wrong format specifier; %zu for size_t files and streams warning: control reaches end of non-void function a missing return; the behaviour is undefined error handling error: array size missing in 'a' int a[] with no initialiser arrays and layout error: invalid use of incomplete type a pointer to a struct whose definition is not visible translation units

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
Definitions only, grouped by the section that uses them first: memory, C and C++, build, numbers, biology. I keep them short, because a glossary that argues is a chapter in disguise.

Terms as this book uses them, which is not always how the standard defines them. Where the two differ, the book's usage is what the chapters rely on.

docs.title: 1. Memory
docs.text:
Object — a region of storage with a type. A variable is a named object; an expression's result is usually an unnamed one.

Storage duration — how long the storage exists: automatic (a scope), static (the program), dynamic (until freed), thread (the thread).

Alignment — the requirement that an object's address be a multiple of its alignof. A misaligned access is undefined behaviour and, on x86, a performance penalty.

Padding — bytes inserted between members to satisfy alignment. Never readable through a member, always present in sizeof.

Undefined behaviour (UB) — the standard imposes no requirement on the result. Not "a random value": the compiler may assume it never happens and delete the branch that checks for it.

Unspecified behaviour — a set of allowed results; the implementation picks one and does not have to document which.

Implementation-defined — a documented choice, such as the width of int.

Strict aliasing — the rule that two pointers of incompatible types do not point at the same object. Violating it is UB, and -fno-strict-aliasing relaxes it.

Effective type — the type of the last store to an allocated object; the aliasing rule is stated in terms of it.

Arena / region — a block of memory from which many small objects are carved, with one free for the whole block. The alternative to one malloc per object.

docs.title: 2. C and C++
docs.text:
Translation unit (TU) — one source file after preprocessing, including every header it pulled in. The compiler sees only TUs.

ODR — the one-definition rule: a function or object with external linkage is defined once across all TUs. Class definitions may repeat, but must be token-identical.

Internal linkage — a name visible only within its TU: static at file scope, or an anonymous namespace in C++.

Lvalue / rvalue — a value with an identity (address) versus a value without one. C++'s value categories refine this into lvalue, xvalue and prvalue.

RAII — resource acquisition is initialisation: an object acquires a resource in its constructor and releases it in its destructor, so every exit path releases it.

Special member functions — default constructor, copy, move, destructor. Declaring one suppresses others; this is the rule of five.

Rule of zero — the recommendation that a class declare none of the five, because its members are RAII types that already do it correctly.

Slicing — copying a derived object into a base object, losing the derived part. Happens when a polymorphic object is passed by value.

Virtual dispatch — the call through a vtable that reaches the most-derived override. Two indirections: object to vtable pointer, vtable to function pointer.

Template instantiation — generating a concrete function or class from a template and its arguments. Lazy: a member function is instantiated only when used.

Two-phase lookup — names in a template are resolved at definition (non-dependent) and at instantiation (dependent), which is why a declaration order can break a template.

Concept (C++20) — a named set of constraints on template parameters, checked at the call site with a readable diagnostic.

docs.title: 3. Build
docs.text:
Object file — the output of assembling one TU: code, data, and a symbol table. Not yet linked.

Symbol — a name in an object file, marked defined (T) or undefined (U).

Linkage — how a symbol is resolved across TUs: external, internal, or none.

Static library — an archive of object files, copied into the executable at link time. .a on Linux, .lib on Windows.

Shared library — loaded at run time, shared between processes. .so on Linux, .dll on Windows.

Sanitizer — a compiler instrumented runtime check. ASan wraps memory, UBSan checks operations, LSan scans at exit, TSan checks data races.

Golden file — expected output stored in the repository and compared byte-for-byte. The cheapest regression test and the reason output formatting must be platform-independent.

docs.title: 4. Numbers
docs.text:
ULP — unit in the last place: the gap between a floating-point value and the next representable one. Error bounds are stated in ULPs.

Kahan summation — compensated summation that carries the rounding error in a second variable, reducing the error from \(O(n\epsilon)\) to \(O(\epsilon)\).

Log-sum-exp — the numerically stable form of \(\log \sum e^{x_i}\), factoring out the maximum to avoid overflow and underflow.

Amortised cost — the average over a sequence of operations, used for push_back where a single call may be O(n) but the average is O(1).

NaN — a floating-point value that is not a number, produced by 0/0, acos of an out-of-range argument, or an invalid operation. It propagates through arithmetic and compares false with everything, including itself.

Strict weak ordering — the requirement on a comparator: irreflexive, transitive, and with transitive incomparability. <= is not one, which is why a comparator must use <.

docs.title: 5. Biology
docs.text:
Residue — one amino acid in a chain, identified by chain, sequence number and insertion code.

Altloc — alternate location indicator: a structure may have two conformations of the same atom, labelled A, B in column 17.

Backbone — the N, CA, C, O atoms of a residue, which define the chain's path.

Dihedral — the angle between two planes defined by four consecutive atoms, measured about the middle bond. A peptide's \(\phi\) and \(\psi\) are dihedrals.

RMSD — root mean square deviation, the square root of the mean squared distance between corresponding atoms. Meaningful only after optimal superposition.

Kabsch algorithm — the SVD-based computation of the optimal rotation between two point sets. What makes an RMSD a structural comparison.

Radius of gyration — the root mean square distance of atoms from the centroid, a measure of compactness.

Contact map — an n×n matrix marking residue pairs within a cutoff distance. The simplest tertiary-structure descriptor.

k-mer — a substring of length k, used for composition and feature encoding.

PDB format — the Protein Data Bank's fixed-column text format. Every field is defined by columns, not by delimiters.

FASTA format — a header line starting with > followed by residues. The format specifies no line length, case, or uniqueness.

docs.title: References
docs.text: This is a course, not a paper, so the list is short and deliberately narrow: only the work whose results the chapters actually use. The derivations, the code and the chapter numbering are this project's own; where a number in the text came from a run, the lab that produced it is named in the text.

docs.title: 1. Sequence algorithms
docs.text:
• Needleman, S. B. & Wunsch, C. D. (1970). A general method applicable to the search for similarities in the amino acid sequence of two proteins. Journal of Molecular Biology 48(3), 443–453. — the recurrence and the traceback in the alignment chapter.
  • Hirschberg, D. S. (1975). A linear space algorithm for computing maximal common subsequences. Communications of the ACM 18(6), 341–343. — the O(min(n, m)) traceback that the alignment chapter leaves as an exercise.
  • Henikoff, S. & Henikoff, J. G. (1992). Amino acid substitution matrices from protein blocks. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 89(22), 10915–10919. — BLOSUM62 and the half-bit log-odds scale used for scoring.

docs.title: 2. Numerical methods
docs.text:
• Kahan, W. (1965). Further remarks on reducing truncation errors. Communications of the ACM 8(1), 40. — compensated summation in the numerics chapter.
  • Goldberg, D. (1991). What every computer scientist should know about floating-point arithmetic. ACM Computing Surveys 23(1), 5–48. — background for the floating-point behaviour the C chapters treat as undefined or unspecified.

docs.title: 3. Bit-level programming
docs.text: • Kernighan, B. W. & Ritchie, D. M. (1988). The C Programming Language, 2nd edition. Prentice Hall. — the v &= v - 1 loop, still the standard name for "clear the lowest set bit".

docs.title: 4. Parallelism and memory
docs.text:
• Amdahl, G. M. (1967). Validity of the single processor approach to achieving large scale computing capabilities. AFIPS Conference Proceedings 30, 483–485. — the bound behind every "how much faster can this get" argument in the performance chapter.
  • Drepper, U. (2007). What Every Programmer Should Know About Memory. Red Hat. — cache lines, prefetchers and the reason a stride costs what it costs.

docs.title: 5. Standards
docs.text:
• ISO/IEC 9899:2018 — C17. The final committee draft is free: N2176. Clause numbers in this book follow it.
  • ISO/IEC 14882:2020 — C++20. The working draft is free: N4861.

docs.title: 6. File formats
docs.text:
• wwPDB. Protein Data Bank Contents Guide: Atomic Coordinate Entry Format Description, version 3.30. — the fixed columns and the record types parsed in the PDB chapter.
  • wwPDB. PDBx/mmCIF dictionary. — the hierarchy of data blocks, categories and loops behind the structure model.

docs.title: 7. Deliberately not cited
docs.text:
Two things a reader may expect are absent on purpose.

  • BLAST and other aligners. The book does not run an aligner; the algorithm is what chapter 04 teaches, and running someone else's binary is a shell exercise rather than a computing one. The original paper is not cited because no result in the book depends on it.
  • C and C++ textbooks. Nothing in the text is taken from one, and a reading list of them would suggest otherwise. If you want one, the standard drafts above are the primary source and are more accurate than any summary of them.

If a citation here is wrong, or a chapter uses a result that is missing from this list, that is a defect worth reporting and will be fixed in the next version.

docs.title: Repository Layout
docs.text:
The tree is a contract, and this page states the four rules that make it one: numbered stage directories, a lab number in every source file's header, one check.sh per stage that builds one target, and a four-line README. Then the order for registering a new lab, then what I deliberately left out and why.

Where everything lives, and the four naming rules that keep the book, the code and the tests pointing at each other.

docs.title: 1. The tree
docs.text:
CorCraft/
├── mkdocs.yml                  site configuration (theme section untouched)
├── docs/
│   ├── start-here/             preface, author, toolchain, first program, how to use
│   ├── c/                      16 chapters, memory-first
│   ├── cpp/                    13 chapters, one Practise section each
│   ├── engineering/            5 chapters on build, test, measure, debug
│   ├── bio/                    10 chapters, sequence to structure
│   ├── reference/              6 lookups
│   ├── about/                  roadmap, projects, AI workflow
│   ├── material/overrides/     home.html and theme overrides
│   ├── assets/                 images, favicon
│   └── includes/mkdocs.md      snippets appended by the snippet extension
├── code/
│   ├── CMakeLists.txt          the single build entry point
│   ├── include/                craft_assert.h, craft_bench.h, craft_io.h
│   ├── c/01_objects_in_memory/ … 16_/error_handling/
│   ├── cpp/01_bridge/ … 13_capstone/
│   └── bio/01_fasta/ … 09_parallel/
├── labs/
│   ├── c/  cpp/  bio/          one check.sh per lab, one directory per stage
├── data/                       README with fetch commands; coordinates not committed
├── kb/                         local knowledge base notes (see kb/README.md)
└── tools/
    ├── Makefile                configure / build / test / sanitize / labs / clean
    └── run_labs.sh             runs every labs/*/*/check.sh

docs.title: 2. Rule 1: a stage directory is numbered and named
docs.text:
code/c/07_heap/               documents a topic
code/bio/05_pdb_parse/        documents a topic

The number matches the chapter order and appears in the chapter's path. A stage added between two existing ones gets a decimal (07a_), not a renumbering — renumbering breaks every LAB identifier in the prose and in the tests.

docs.title: 3. Rule 2: a source file carries its lab number
docs.text:
code/c/07_heap/01_growth_trace.c      LAB 07-01
code/cpp/05_polymorphism/02_slicing.cpp   LAB 05-02

The two-level number in the file name is stage-file. LAB 07-02 in the prose refers to exactly one file, and the file's header comment repeats it:

/* LAB 07-02  heap/02_double_free.c
 * Drills: the second free, and why setting the pointer to NULL is the guard.
 * Build:  cmake --build build --target c_07_double
 */

Three labelled lines, always in that order, because the reader who lands in a file mid-chapter needs the link back to the prose and the reader in the prose needs the one command that produces the binary. A stage that needs a sentence of context puts it after a blank line, as 02_double_free.c does for its --unsafe mode.

docs.title: 4. Rule 3: the acceptance script is named check.sh and builds one target
docs.text:
labs/cpp/13_capstone/
└── check.sh        configures `code/`, builds that target, runs it, exits 0

The directory holds one file on purpose. The exercise is in code/<track>/<stage>/README.md and in the chapter's Lab section; a starter.c beside a working solution.c teaches reading, not writing, and two copies of the same program drift apart. check.sh is the regression harness: it proves the reference implementation still produces the stated result under the flags the chapter quotes, so that when a reader's own attempt fails, the toolchain is already ruled out.

No lab depends on a downloaded file. Every program in code/bio/ carries its coordinates or sequences as a literal, so check.sh never skips and never reports a missing data/ file as a lab failure. The reader's later prototypes — the ones that do read a PDB file — are the place where data/README.md matters.

docs.title: 5. Rule 4: one README per stage, four lines
docs.text:
# 07_heap

Drills: realloc growth, double free, leak hunt.
Chapter: docs/c/heap.md
Labs: `01_growth_trace.c`, `02_double_free.c`, `03_leak_hunt.c`

The README is the index for a directory a reader may land in without the prose. The Labs: line lists the files that are actually in the directory, not the ones intended for it — a README that advertises a file the repository does not contain is the cheapest possible broken link.

docs.title: 6. Registering a new lab, in order
docs.text:
1. Write the source in the stage directory with its sequence number.
  2. Add one line to the stage's CMakeLists.txt: craft_lab(c_07_growth 07_heap/01_growth_trace.c).
  3. Write the chapter paragraph that references LAB 07-02 and the file path.
  4. Add the check.sh under labs/<track>/<stage>/, naming the same target.
  5. Add the chapter to mkdocs.yml's nav.
  6. Run make test and tools/run_labs.sh.

Steps 2 and 3 were the ones skipped in the first draft of this repository, and the result was prose that referenced files which did not exist. The order above exists because the reference is a link and a link must resolve.

docs.title: 7. What is deliberately absent
docs.text:
• No vendored structure files. data/README.md explains why and gives the fetch commands.
  • No pre-built documentation site in the repository. The site is generated from docs/; committing site/ would double every edit.
  • No theme fork. docs/material/overrides holds home.html and a few partials; the Material theme itself is a dependency, not a copy.
  • No license file yet. The repository has not declared one, and the pages do not claim one. Adding it is a decision for the owner, not a default.

docs.text:

docs.title: About the Author
docs.text: I keep this page short, because a biography is not an argument. What matters for the book is narrower: which problems I have actually had to solve, because those decide which chapters exist and which Field Notes are mine.

docs.title: 1. What I actually build
docs.text:
I am an undergraduate at Henan University of Technology, majoring in Biological Engineering with a minor in Computer Science, and I work where the two meet: genome and transcriptome analysis, differential expression, molecular dynamics, and the structure work that is cheap to state and expensive to compute. My GROMACS pipelines cover four system types — protein–ligand, protein–protein, protein-only, protein–metal — from topology and equilibration through production, and a post-processing toolkit turns trajectories into RMSD, RMSF, Rg, DCCM, MM-PBSA and secondary-structure plots without manual steps. A trajectory that has not been reduced to a number is not evidence.

Enzyme engineering is where that lands: an automated workflow runs sequence retrieval, alignment, conservation analysis, pocket detection and mutation screening in one pass, calling FoldX, DynaMut2 and CataPro and returning a ΔΔG heat map, with site-saturation scans for activity as the same loop and a different scoring function. Two Python packages came out of it and are not published — a high-throughput docking wrapper (pocket, AutoDock Vina, PLIP) and a peptide generator. Protein Phaser, a C++ library that reads PDB and mmCIF into a chain/residue/atom hierarchy, became the input layer for a feature engine computing pocket centres, residue depth, SASA and per-residue flexibility, and FlexTrimmer is trained on those features; BioCUDA is its GPU counterpart, and I have written enough CUDA to know which parts belong on the device. None of it has produced a marketed compound, and this book does not pretend otherwise.

docs.title: 2. Why I wrote this book
docs.text:
Every one of those projects eventually ran into the same class of problem: a structure parsed correctly but with the wrong padding, a buffer that grew one element too late, an object destroyed while a pointer to it was still alive. The fixes were small. Finding them was not.

What I wanted, and could not find, was a text that put the object model first and the syntax second, and then carried the same model into the domain where it pays off — a PDB file, a distance matrix, a contact map. So the C half of this book is about bytes and lifetimes rather than about statements, and the C++ half assumes that model rather than restarting from "what is a class". The biology section is the test: if the earlier chapters worked, a protein structure is a layout problem and a scoring loop is a numeric one.

The Field Notes are mine. Each one is a defect I actually shipped, with the compiler message or the sanitiser report that finally explained it. I kept them because a defect that looked plausible is more instructive than a defect that looked obviously wrong, and because the alternative — a book of correct examples — would have taught you less about your own code.
