docs.title: First Program
docs.text:
The first program has two defects on purpose, because I want the reader to meet the compiler as a critic rather than as a gate. I compile it, ask for warnings, fix the program instead of the output, turn warnings into errors, look at what was produced, then ask the runtime as well. The rule at the end is the one I still follow: the warning is the bug, arriving early.

This page builds one small program four times, with increasingly strict compiler settings, and reads what comes back. The goal is not to print a greeting; it is to establish that the compiler is the first reviewer of every line you write, and that its complaints are evidence rather than noise.

docs.title: 1. A program with two defects
docs.text:
Create warn.c — the repository ships this exact file as code/warn.c, and the line numbers below refer to it:

#include <stdio.h>

int main(void) {
    int unused_flag = 1;
    unsigned int total = 0;
    int delta = -5;

    total = delta;
    printf("total = %u\n", total);
    return 0;
}

Compile it the way most tutorials do, with no warning flags at all:

gcc warn.c -o warn
./warn

It prints total = 4294967291 and exits 0. Nothing failed. The program is nevertheless wrong in two places, and the compiler knew about both.

docs.title: 2. Ask for warnings
docs.text:
gcc -Wall -Wextra -Wconversion warn.c -o warn

Two messages appear, in this order:

warn.c:4:9: warning: unused variable 'unused_flag' [-Wunused-variable]
    4 |     int unused_flag = 1;
      |         ^~~~~~~~~~~
warn.c:8:11: warning: conversion to 'unsigned int' from 'int' may change the sign of the result [-Wsign-conversion]
    8 |     total = delta;
      |           ^~~~~

Read them as three separate pieces of information each: the location, the rule that fired, and the flag that controls it. The flag name is the important part, because it tells you what category of mistake you made and how to ask for the same check elsewhere.

-Wunused-variable is bookkeeping. A variable that is written and never read is either a leftover or a symptom that a computation was forgotten. In a 2,000-line file this warning is usually a real bug.

-Wsign-conversion is a semantic error wearing a warning's clothes. delta holds -5; assigning it to an unsigned int does not store -5, it stores the value that results from converting a negative signed integer to an unsigned type, which the standard defines as adding 2³². The printed 4294967291 is not a curiosity: it is the number that will be used in every subsequent arithmetic operation, including the bounds check that was supposed to reject it.

docs.title: 3. Fix the program, not the output
docs.text:
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void) {
    unsigned int total = 0;
    int delta = -5;

    if (delta < 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "delta must be non-negative, got %d\n", delta);
        return 1;
    }

    total = (unsigned int)delta;
    printf("total = %u\n", total);
    return 0;
}

Two changes, and only one of them is about types. The conversion is now explicit, because the cast is a place where the author asserts that the range has already been checked. And the range is checked, on the line above, so the assertion is true. A cast without a preceding check is the same defect with the evidence removed.

Rebuild with the same flags. There is no output, which is the only acceptable result:

gcc -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Wconversion warn.c -o warn
echo $?

docs.title: 4. Turn warnings into errors
docs.text:
Warnings are easy to ignore when there are forty of them and the program still runs. The habit worth forming is to make ignoring impossible during development:

gcc -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Wconversion -Werror warn.c -o warn

Now any warning aborts the build. Every lab in code/ is compiled with that same warning set, and labs/<track>/<stage>/check.sh prints any warning it sees rather than aborting — the zero-warning rule is enforced by review, and the script keeps the evidence in front of the reader.

-Werror is a development setting, not a release setting. Third-party headers occasionally emit warnings you cannot fix without patching them; the usual compromise is to keep -Werror for your own translation units and to isolate the third-party include behind -isystem, which suppresses warnings from headers found there.

docs.title: 5. Look at what was produced
docs.text:
The compiler emitted an executable, not a script. Two commands make that visible:

file warn
nm warn | grep -E ' main| printf'

file reports an ELF 64-bit executable, dynamically linked. nm lists the symbol table: main is defined in this object (T), while printf is undefined (U) and will be resolved at load time by the dynamic linker. That U is the reason a C program needs the C library at runtime and a statically linked one does not.

This distinction becomes the subject of Compile Pipeline. For now it is enough to know that "compiled successfully" means four separate stages agreed, and the executable is the artefact of the last one.

docs.title: 6. Ask the runtime as well
docs.text:
The compiler checks what it can see. AddressSanitizer and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer check what happens while the program runs. Add this line before the printf, deliberately out of bounds:

int probe[4] = {1, 2, 3, 4};
probe[4] = 99;

Compile and run:

gcc -fsanitize=address,undefined -g warn.c -o warn_san
./warn_san
echo $?

The program now stops with a report naming stack-buffer-overflow, the address, and the line. Without the sanitizer, the same write usually succeeds silently, corrupting whatever the compiler happened to place after probe; the defect then surfaces somewhere unrelated, often in a different function.

docs.title: 7. The rule this page establishes
docs.text:
Every example in this book is compiled with -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic, run under a sanitizer where memory is involved, and judged by exit status as well as output. If a program prints the right number but triggers a warning or a sanitizer report, it has not passed. That standard applies to the reader's own code from this page onward, which is why the lab check scripts enforce it automatically.

Two things to carry forward: a warning names the rule that fired, and the rule is usually a category of bug rather than a single line; and an explicit cast is a claim, so it must be preceded by the check that makes the claim true.

docs.title: How to Use This Book
docs.text:
This page is the map, and I keep it concrete: what lives where, how the numbering works, two ways to run an example, the lab protocol, how to use a model without outsourcing the thinking, three routes through the book, and what done means. If you are unsure whether to read or to type, the answer is here.

Three things determine whether this book works for you: how the examples are numbered, how the exercises are graded, and what you do when you are stuck. Each is mechanical, and each is worth ten minutes before you write any code.

docs.title: 1. What lives where
docs.text:
The repository has five directories, and each has exactly one job.

Path Holds You touch it when docs/ This book Reading code/ Every example, grouped by chapter number Following a page, or copying a snippet to modify labs/ One check.sh per chapter, recording that the lab still runs on your machine Practising data/ Download instructions for public structures and sequences Starting the biology section kb/ A local knowledge base, with notes you write yourself When a question keeps recurring

Nothing in docs/ is generated from code/ or the reverse. The page and the source are written together and reviewed against each other, which is why a page never claims behaviour that the source does not exhibit.

docs.title: 2. The numbering
docs.text:
Every example carries a label of the form LAB 07-02, meaning chapter 7, example 2. The chapter number is also the numeric prefix of the stage directory, so the label resolves to a path without a lookup table:

LAB 07-01  →  code/c/07_heap/01_growth_trace.c
             docs/c/heap.md  (chapter 7)

The same numbering is used in labs/: labs/c/07_heap/ belongs to the same chapter. A page, a source file and an exercise that share a number are guaranteed to be about the same subject.

Each source file begins with a header comment that answers three questions before the reader compiles anything:

/* LAB 07-01  heap/01_growth_trace.c
 * Drills: realloc growth, the address that changes, and the capacity policy.
 * Build:  cmake --build build --target c_07_growth
 *
 * The trace is the point: the addresses are the evidence that realloc moves
 * the block, which is why every pointer into the old block becomes invalid.
 */

LAB is the label the prose uses and the path from the repository root. Drills is what the program is evidence for, not what it contains. Build is the exact one-line command that produces the binary; the CMake target name is the one labs/ uses too. Anything after the blank line is the sentence the chapter would otherwise have to repeat. When a page and a header disagree, the header is authoritative: it was compiled.

docs.title: 3. Two ways to run an example
docs.text:
Build everything at once through CMake, from the repository root:

cmake -S code -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=RelWithDebInfo
cmake --build build -j"$(nproc)"
ctest --test-dir build --output-on-failure

ctest runs each example as a test, so a chapter is "done" when the suite is green. This is also the fastest way to check that your toolchain matches the one the book assumes.

Build a single file when you are studying one page and do not want to wait for the whole tree:

cd code/c/07_heap
gcc -std=c17 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -I../../include \
    01_growth_trace.c -o /tmp/growth
/tmp/growth

Compile to /tmp rather than into the source directory. Binaries in the source tree end up in git status, and a stale binary is a reliable way to spend an evening debugging code you already fixed.

docs.title: 4. The lab protocol
docs.text:
Each lab directory holds one file, check.sh, and the task itself lives in code/<track>/<stage>/README.md plus the Lab section of the chapter. There is no starter file by design: the point of the exercise is to write the program, not to fill three blanks in someone else's. The protocol is deliberately rigid, because the value of an exercise is in the prediction, not the answer:

  1. Read the chapter's Lab section and the stage README.md, and write down, on paper, what you expect the program to print.
  2. Write the program into /tmp/lab from memory, with the chapter closed. Do not read code/ yet.
  3. Compile it with the flags from the chapter and run it. Compare the output with your note, not with the book.
  4. Only when it differs, open the chapter section, then code/. A difference you predicted is a gap in your model; one you did not predict is a gap in your reading.
  5. Run bash check.sh in the lab directory to confirm the reference implementation still produces the expected result on your machine — a toolchain regression, not your answer, is what it rules out.
  6. Change one thing, rerun. Two changes at once makes the next failure uninterpretable.

Run every lab at once from the repository root:

bash tools/run_labs.sh

The script prints one line per lab and exits non-zero if any failed. A build that emits a warning prints the warning text and continues, so the zero-warning rule stays visible without turning a known diagnostic into a false failure.

docs.title: 5. Using a model without outsourcing the thinking
docs.text:
This book contains prompts at the points where readers most often get stuck, marked Prompt the model. They are meant to be used after you have formed your own guess, not before. Three rules make that work:

Read the diagnostic first, then ask. A compiler message contains the file, the line, the rule name, and often a note explaining the fix. Handing the message to a model without reading it transfers the work you were supposed to do. Read it, form a hypothesis, then ask whether the hypothesis is right.

Demand evidence, not confidence. A useful answer cites a standard clause, a compiler version, or a program that can be compiled and run. An answer that says "in most implementations" without naming one is a guess wearing a lab coat. Ask for the code, then compile it.

Treat the answer as a hypothesis. The compiler and the sanitizer are the arbiters, not the model. When the two disagree, the compiler is right, and the disagreement itself is worth understanding — it usually means the model learned a rule from a different standard version or a different compiler.

The full method, including how to build the local knowledge base that grounds these questions, is in How I Use AI to Build a Project.

docs.title: 6. Three routes through the book
docs.text:
Not every reader needs all sixty pages in order. Three routes cover the common cases.

Route For Path Time Inspection Readers who already write C and want the object model Preface → Objects in Memory → Stack Frames → Pointers → Structs and Padding → Undefined Behavior → RAII → PDB Parsing 2–3 weeks part-time Complete Readers learning both languages properly Everything, in navigation order, with every lab attempted One semester Domain-first Biologists who need working code, not a curriculum Preface → First Program → Strings → Files → Bit-Level Programming → the whole Computational Biology section, consulting the C chapters on demand 4–6 weeks

The domain-first route works because the biology section assumes only the C chapters it links back to. Each page in it names its prerequisites at the top and repeats the two or three facts it borrows, so a reader arriving from a different direction does not have to reconstruct the whole earlier section.

docs.title: 7. What "done" means
docs.text: A chapter is finished when three things hold: the example builds with no warnings, its Expect line matches what you observed, and you can explain the Probe result without rereading the page. If the third condition fails, the chapter is not finished even though the code runs; that is the difference between having executed a program and having learned from it.

docs.title: Linux Toolchain
docs.text:
Three routes, one compiler underneath, and I say so before the instructions: Linux or WSL2 is what this book uses, Visual Studio 2022 is a first-class alternative on Windows, and conda-forge gives you GCC or Clang without touching the system. I give commands for all three, then one verification program that has to pass on any of them.

Three routes lead to a usable C and C++ compiler, and all three run every example in this book. The difference is what the book's commands assume: this text is written against Linux, because a compiler that reports identical warnings on every machine is what makes the examples reproducible, and because the clusters that run the biology code are Linux machines.

That is a choice of reference implementation, not a claim about the only correct environment. Visual Studio 2022 on Windows is a complete, first-class toolchain, and a conda-forge environment gives you a compiler that travels with your analysis code. Sections 3 and 4 describe both, including the few places where a chapter needs a note.

docs.title: 1. Three routes at a glance
docs.text:
Route Best for Compiler What changes in the book A. Linux or WSL2 The reference route; all fifty-eight chapters GCC 11+ or Clang 14+ Nothing B. Visual Studio 2022 Windows-native work, MSVC debugger, C++20 MSVC 19.3x Compiler flags differ; perf and a few POSIX calls are replaced by chapter notes C. conda-forge Readers already living in conda; reproducible scientific environments GCC or Clang from conda Toolchain paths are long; set CC/CXX explicitly

Whichever route you take, the language standards are fixed: C17 and C++20. A compiler that cannot accept -std=c17 and -std=c++20 will fail on the first C++ chapter, and it is worth checking that before reading further.

docs.title: 2. Route A — Linux or WSL2
docs.text:
Any of the following is sufficient:

Environment Notes Ubuntu 22.04 or 24.04 LTS The reference platform; every command in this book was written against it Debian 12 Same packages, same paths WSL2 with Ubuntu 22.04 Identical inside the distribution; keep project files on the Linux filesystem A container based on ubuntu:22.04 Fine for the build chapters, awkward for the debugger chapters

Two version floors matter. CMake must be at least 3.20, because the top-level CMakeLists.txt declares cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.20). GCC must be at least 11 for the C++20 chapters; GCC 9 covers everything in the C sections. Ubuntu 20.04 ships CMake 3.16 and is therefore below the floor — install a newer copy from Kitware's repository rather than fighting the system package.

Install in one command:

sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y build-essential clang gdb cmake valgrind git curl

build-essential pulls in gcc, g++, make and the C library headers. clang is installed alongside GCC, not instead of it: the two compilers disagree on some diagnostics, and reading both opinions on the same file is one of the fastest ways to learn what a warning means. valgrind covers the one chapter where AddressSanitizer cannot see the problem.

On WSL2, install the distribution first, then run the same commands inside it:

wsl --install -d Ubuntu-22.04

Keep the repository inside the Linux home directory — /home/<user>/craft — and not under /mnt/c/.... Cross-filesystem access through the WSL mount is an order of magnitude slower, which makes the performance chapter meaningless and the build chapters tedious.

docs.title: 3. Route B — Visual Studio 2022
docs.text:
Visual Studio 2022 with the Desktop development with C++ workload provides the MSVC compiler, a debugger, CMake integration and AddressSanitizer. Nothing in the book's object model depends on GCC, so the C and C++ chapters work unchanged once the flags are translated.

Install the workload through the Visual Studio Installer: open Modify, tick Desktop development with C++, and confirm that MSVC v143, Windows SDK and C++ CMake tools are selected. About 3 GB.

Build from the Developer Command Prompt for VS 2022, not from an ordinary terminal; the prompt sets PATH, INCLUDE and LIB:

cl /std:c17 /W4 /WX /Zi hello.c
cl /std:c++20 /W4 /WX /EHsc /Zi hello.cpp

The mapping from the book's flags is direct but not identical:

Book MSVC Note -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic /W4 MSVC's /W4 is roughly -Wall -Wextra; there is no pedantic tier -Werror /WX Any warning becomes an error -g /Zi Debug information, used by the VS debugger -fsanitize=address /fsanitize=address Supported since VS 2019 16.9; needs the ASan runtime DLL on PATH -std=c17 /std:c17 Supported since VS 2019 16.7 -std=c++20 /std:c++20 Supported since VS 2019 16.11 -O2 /O2 Same intent, different inlining thresholds

The CMake project builds with the Visual Studio generator:

cmake -S code -B build -G "Visual Studio 17 2022" -A x64
cmake --build build --config RelWithDebInfo
ctest --test-dir build -C RelWithDebInfo --output-on-failure

Three chapters need a substitution note, and each carries one on the page itself: engineering/performance.md uses perf stat, which has no MSVC equivalent (use the VS profiler or Measure-Command); bio/parallel-scoring.md uses OpenMP, which MSVC supports through /openmp with a different runtime; and c/files-and-streams.md uses fopen only, so it is unaffected, but the errno values differ in wording.

Two things to expect. First, MSVC's diagnostics are worded differently from GCC's, so the verbatim warning text quoted in the field notes will not match your screen; the flag or the rule name is what to compare, not the sentence. Second, MSVC does not implement every C99 variable-length array case and rejects some forms GCC accepts; where a lab relies on one, the page says so.

docs.title: 4. Route C — conda-forge
docs.text:
A conda environment is a reasonable choice when the compiler has to travel with an analysis stack: the same environment then holds the compiler, CMake, a Python interpreter and the scientific packages, and it can be reproduced from a file.

conda create -n craft -c conda-forge cmake make gdb
conda activate craft

The compiler packages are platform-specific, and the names change across platforms, so confirm rather than guess:

conda search -c conda-forge 'gcc*'

On Linux the packages are gcc_linux-64 and gxx_linux-64 (or the newer gcc/gxx metapackages); on macOS they are clang_osx-64 and clangxx_osx-64; on Windows the practical option is m2w64-toolchain, a MinGW-w64 port. Install the pair that matches your platform:

conda install -c conda-forge gcc_linux-64 gxx_linux-64      # Linux
conda install -c conda-forge m2w64-toolchain                # Windows

Conda compilers are installed with a target triplet in the filename, so the generic gcc command may not exist. List what actually landed and point CMake at it:

ls "$CONDA_PREFIX/bin" | grep -E 'gcc|g\+\+'
export CC="$CONDA_PREFIX/bin/x86_64-conda-linux-gnu-gcc"
export CXX="$CONDA_PREFIX/bin/x86_64-conda-linux-gnu-g++"

The exact triplet varies by platform; the two lines above are for linux-64. On macOS the prefix is x86_64-apple-darwin or arm64-apple-darwin, and on Windows the binaries are named x86_64-w64-mingw32-gcc. Setting CC and CXX before invoking CMake is what makes cmake -S code -B build use the conda compiler rather than the system one:

CC="$CC" CXX="$CXX" cmake -S code -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=RelWithDebInfo

Two caveats. Sanitizers are not shipped with every conda GCC build; check with gcc -fsanitize=address -x c - -o /tmp/probe <<< 'int main(void){return 0;}' before relying on them. And gdb from conda sometimes cannot read debug info produced by a different compiler build; if that happens, use the system gdb.

docs.title: 5. Verify whichever route you chose
docs.text:
The checks are the same idea everywhere: prove that C17 and C++20 are accepted, and prove that the memory checker works.

On Linux, WSL and conda:

gcc --version | head -n1
clang --version | head -n1        # optional
cmake --version | head -n1

printf 'int main(void){return 0;}\n' > /tmp/probe.c
gcc -std=c17 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic /tmp/probe.c -o /tmp/probe && /tmp/probe
g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -x c++ /tmp/probe.c -o /tmp/probe && /tmp/probe
gcc -fsanitize=address,undefined -g /tmp/probe.c -o /tmp/probe_san && /tmp/probe_san
echo $?

On Windows with MSVC:

cl /std:c17 /W4 /WX /Zi probe.c
cl /std:c++20 /W4 /WX /EHsc /Zi probe.cpp
cl /std:c17 /fsanitize=address /Zi probe.c

Expected results: no diagnostics, exit status 0 everywhere, and an ASan run that terminates normally. A loader error mentioning libasan on Linux means the sanitizer runtime package is missing (libasan5, or libasan8 on newer releases); on Windows it means the ASan runtime DLL is not on PATH.

The version floors, once more, as a table to check against:

Tool Floor Reason GCC 11 C++20 chapters Clang 14 Comparable C++20 support MSVC 19.3x (VS 2022) /std:c++20 and ASan CMake 3.20 CMakeLists.txt floor GDB 9 Pretty-printing and -O1 debugging

docs.title: 6. Workspace layout
docs.text:
All three routes use the same directory shape: the repository, the build tree beside it, and the downloaded data.

mkdir -p ~/craft && cd ~/craft
git clone https://github.com/GuiHui-huimy/CorCraft.git
cd CorCraft
cmake -S code -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=RelWithDebInfo
cmake --build build -j"$(nproc)"

The build tree lives outside the source tree so that git status stays clean and a broken build can be deleted with a single rm -rf build. Nothing in the repository writes into the source tree; the labs write their binaries into build/ or /tmp.

The layout is described in Repository Layout. For now two paths matter: code/ holds the sources and the CMake project, and labs/ holds the exercises.

docs.title: 7. When the install goes wrong
docs.text:
apt cannot find clang. The package index is stale, or the sources list points at a release that does not carry it. Run sudo apt update; if that fails, compare /etc/apt/sources.list with lsb_release -cs.

CMake reports a version below 3.20. Either install a newer release from Kitware, or keep an isolated copy: python3 -m pip install --user cmake. The second route is the one to prefer on a shared machine.

GCC accepts -std=c17 but rejects -std=c++20. GCC 9 and 10 accept the flag and implement only part of the standard. Install g++-11 and select it with CXX=g++-11.

AddressSanitizer reports a shadow-memory conflict. Some sandboxed containers reserve the address space ASan needs. Run the same binary outside the sandbox, or use Valgrind for that chapter; the diagnostic content is equivalent, only slower.

MSVC cannot find cl. An ordinary terminal has no INCLUDE or LIB paths. Open the Developer Command Prompt, or run vcvars64.bat first.

Conda's gcc is not found after activation. The binary carries a triplet prefix. List $CONDA_PREFIX/bin and set CC and CXX as in section 4.

docs.title: Continue
docs.text: With a compiler verified, the next step is to compile something and read what it says: First Program. If you would rather see how the exercises are structured before starting, read How to Use This Book. The per-flag comparison table lives in Compiler and Flags.

docs.title: Preface
docs.text:
The preface is where I say what this book is not: not a reference, not a tour of every feature, not a promise that C++ is C with classes. I state the one skill the book aims at, how the four parts are organised, how each chapter is written, what the code is and is not, and where to start depending on what you already know.

The first C program I wrote that mattered was a PDB parser. It read a file, filled a struct, and crashed on the third chain. I had been taught that a struct is a group of related variables, which is true the way that a house is a group of bricks: accurate, and useless when the roof leaks. What I needed to know was where the padding went, why sizeof disagreed with the sum of the fields, and why the pointer I had stored in the struct was still valid in one function and garbage in the next.

That gap between the definition and the layout is what this book is about. Not C as a list of syntax rules, and not C++ as a list of features, but the object model underneath both: how a value occupies bytes, how long it lives, who is allowed to name it, and what happens when the answer changes.

docs.title: 1. Why this book exists
docs.text:
Most introductory material teaches C by describing what a statement does. This book teaches C by describing what a statement builds. A declaration does not merely introduce a name; it reserves a region of memory with a width, an alignment, and a lifetime. A pointer is not merely an arrow; it is an integer that has been granted permission to be dereferenced, and that permission expires with the object it points at. A virtual function is not merely a keyword; it inserts a pointer at the front of every object of that class, and every polymorphic call is an indirect jump through that pointer.

Once the layout is visible, the rules stop being arbitrary. const is not a style preference: it is a promise about which bytes may be written. restrict is not a hint: it is a promise that no other pointer aliases the same region, which is why the optimiser is allowed to reorder reads. Undefined behaviour is not a punishment: it is the set of cases where the standard declines to describe what the bytes mean, and the compiler is therefore free to assume they mean nothing at all.

docs.title: 2. What the reader will be able to do
docs.text:
By the end, a reader should be able to take a program they did not write, and answer four questions without running it: how much memory does it touch, how long does each object live, which pointer owns each allocation, and which line will fail first under a sanitizer. Those four questions cover most of what separates a program that compiles from a program that works.

The last section of the book applies all four to protein structures: parsing a PDB file by column position, computing bond angles and dihedrals from coordinates, building a contact map with a grid instead of a double loop, and scoring a library of conformations across threads. The biology is not decoration. It is the reason the earlier chapters insist on layout: a structure with 30,000 atoms is where a wrong sizeof becomes a five-minute parse and a wrong ownership rule becomes a leak per chain.

docs.title: 4. How each chapter is written
docs.text:
Chapters do not share a template. The memory chapters run as one continuous argument: a single picture of an object grows across nine chapters, from a lone int to a stack frame to an array to a struct with padding to a heap block with an owner. Reading them out of order breaks the picture, which is why they are numbered.

The craft chapters change register. Each one starts from a failure — a sort that loses a comparison, a file that reads one line short, a translation unit that links but calls the wrong function — and works forward to the tool or the rule that prevents it. They read like laboratory notes because they were written from laboratory notes.

The C++ chapters are organised around a single question repeated with increasing difficulty: when does this object begin, and when does it end. The build chapters are organised around commands and their artefacts, because that is what a build system is. The biology chapters are organised around data flow: file in, structure out, number out, error estimate.

What the chapters do share is a floor: every page carries code that compiles, every claim carries evidence in the form of a sizeof value, a compiler message, a timing, or an assertion, and every page ends with links into specific subsections rather than a generic "next chapter".

docs.title: 5. A note on the code in this book
docs.text:
The examples are not a curated set of correct programs. Several of them are wrong on purpose, and they are wrong in the way the original versions were wrong: a function whose name promises the absolute value and whose body returns the absolute value of something else; a loop condition with == where != was meant; a two-level allocation where only the outer block is freed; a stack whose capacity check compares against the wrong bound.

Each of these appears in the chapter that would have caught it, labelled as a field note, with the original snippet, the compiler's or the debugger's actual response, and the smallest correction. A reader who only ever sees correct code learns to recognise correctness by shape. A reader who has debugged these learns to recognise it by behaviour.

docs.text:

docs.title: 8. Where to start
docs.text: If the toolchain is already installed, go to First Program and build something. If it is not, Linux Toolchain takes about twenty minutes. If you want to know how the exercises are meant to be used before writing any code, read How to Use This Book first; it is the shortest of the three.
